D5.p: A person is put under a magic spell (enchanted), which may change their form or affect their mind or character without necessarily changing their appearance.

D5.1.p: An enchanted person is unable to move.

D5.1.1.p: A stepson is cursed to stay stuck in a grave mound until a pretty girl offers to take his place.

D5.2.p: An enchanted person lies on a bier (a funeral couch or stretcher).

D6.p: A castle or building is enchanted by magic.

D7.p: A magic valley or place that has been enchanted, so that whoever enters it is changed or put under a spell.

D10.p: A person is magically changed into a person of the opposite sex.

D10.1.p: An ogre has the special power to swap sex with a human being.

D10.2.p: A person changes sex after crossing a body of water.

D11.p: A woman is magically transformed into a man.

D11.1.p: An ogress is transformed into a man.

D11.2.p: A woman turns herself into a bird and lends her female organ to a boy. He fails to give it back, so when she returns to human form she becomes a man.

D12.p: A man is magically transformed into a woman.

D12.1.p: A god is transformed into a giantess.

D20.p: A person is magically transformed into someone of a different social class or rank.

D22.p: A common man is magically transformed into a person of high rank.

D22.1.p: A common man is magically transformed into a grand officer.

D22.2.p: A man of low caste takes on a prince's appearance and magically changes the prince into his own appearance.

D23.p: A person is magically transformed into a craftsman or skilled worker.

D23.1.p: A person is magically transformed into a boatman.

D24.p: A person is magically transformed into a humble or low-status person.

D24.1.p: A king is magically transformed into a menial servant.

D24.2.p: A king and queen are magically transformed into a peasant and his wife.

D24.3.p: A person is magically transformed into a swineherd, one who tends pigs.

D25.p: A person who is an ordinary layman is magically changed into a professional, such as a doctor or a religious official.

D25.1.p: A person is magically changed into a doctor.

D25.2.p: A person is magically changed into a cleric or monk.

D27.p: A person is magically changed into a leper.

D28.p: A person is magically changed into a giant.

D29.p: A miscellaneous magical change of a person into someone of a different social class or rank.

D29.1.p: A person is magically changed into a churl, a lowborn peasant of the common class.

D29.2.p: A person is magically changed into a juggler, an entertainer who performs tricks.

D30.p: A person is magically changed into someone of a different race.

D31.r: (Cf. D57)—Chauvin II 183 No. 23; *Fb “jomfru”, “hvid” I 700b, “sort” III 467b, “pige” II 816b.—Spanish Boggs FFC XC 57 No. 425; Jewish: *Neuman.

D40.1.p: A person magically takes on the appearance of the owner of a shield he is carrying.

D40.2.p: A person magically takes on the appearance of another woman.

D40.2.1.p: A woman magically takes on the appearance of a man's mistress so she can get close enough to kill him.

D41.p: A humble man magically takes on the appearance of someone of high rank.

D41.1.p: A man magically takes on the likeness of a ruler, using the last of three wishes granted to him.

D42.2.p: A spirit takes on the shape of a man.

D43.p: A mortal is magically changed into the likeness of a god.

D43.1.p: A creature, such as an animal, is magically changed so that it takes on the form of a god.

D43.1.1.p: A dog is magically changed into a god.

D44.r: Africa (Upoto): Einstein 142, (Buin) Wheeler 51. See also D47.
D44.p: A living human takes on the appearance of a spirit or supernatural being.

D44.1.p: A human is magically changed into an angel.

D45.p: Two persons magically swap their outward forms or shapes with one another.

D45.2.p: Two gods magically swap forms with one another.

D45.3.p: Two friends magically swap forms with one another.

D45.4.p: A girl magically exchanges her form with a sorceress so she can visit her brother and become pregnant by him.

D47.r: Irish myth: Cross (D94, D95); Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D47.p: A person is magically changed to look like a monster.

D47.1.p: A mortal temporarily takes on the shape of a demon.

D47.2.p: Ordinary men are magically changed into ogres.

D47.3.p: A princess is magically changed into an ogress.

D49.p: Miscellaneous magical transformations in which a person takes on the likeness of another person.

D49.1.p: A dwarf magically takes on human form.

D49.2.p: A spirit can take on any form it chooses.

D50.r: Irish: Plummer clxxxiv (changes in form, complexion, height, and age).
D50.p: A person is magically changed in his own body or appearance, rather than being given another person's form.

D52.1.p: A man is magically changed so that he becomes hideous to look at.

D52.2.p: A man who is ugly is magically changed into a handsome man.

D53.p: A person's health or physical condition is magically changed.

D53.1.r: Icelandic: Sturlaugs saga 642; Africa (Boloki): Weeks Congo 200ff.
D53.1.p: A person is magically transformed into a sick or ailing man.

D55.2.2.p: A devil or troll magically makes himself small.

D55.2.3.p: A giant magically changes from his huge size to normal human size.

D55.2.4.p: Ten serving-women are magically carried in a bottle, since they can change their size at will.

D56.1.p: A person is magically transformed into an older person.

D57.4.p: A person is magically transformed into a black man.

D57.5.p: A person is magically changed so that his color becomes rusty brown.

D93.p: A young prince is magically changed into an old man.

D97.p: A man is magically changed into a witch.

D454.15.p: A magic transformation in which a statue turns into drinking vessels or cups.

D454.16.p: A magic transformation in which instruments of torture turn into lotus flowers.

D457.p: A magic transformation in which a part of a person or animal, such as blood, hair or meat, becomes some other object. This heading covers the more specific motifs listed under it.

D457.1.p: A magic transformation in which a person's or animal's blood turns into some other object. The specific object is given in the subentries.

D457.1.1.p: Blood turns into rubies as it drops to the ground.

D457.1.2.p: A bird is caught and ordered to make milk; it bleeds, and its blood turns into milk.

D457.1.3.p: Drops of blood turn into flowers.

D457.2.p: A magic transformation in which milk turns into blood.

D457.3.r: *BP I 276 n. 2, II 535; Sébillot Incidents s.v. “tête”.
D457.3.p: A magic transformation in which a calf's head turns into a death's head, that is, a skull.

D457.4.p: A magic transformation in which a person's or animal's hair turns into some other object. The specific object is given in the subentries.

D457.5.p: A magic transformation in which meat turns into some other object. The specific object is given in the subentries.

D457.5.1.p: Meat that has been stolen turns into roses.

D457.5.2.p: Meat received from spirits turns into banana leaves.

D457.6.p: Magic transformation in which a person's scurf (dry skin flakes) turns into a palm tree.

D457.7.p: Magic transformation in which a feather turns into a tree.

D457.8.r: Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges; Norse: Herrmann Saxo II 596.
D457.8.p: Magic transformation in which a tooth turns into the head of an ax.

D457.9.r: Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 131 No. 89.
D457.9.p: Magic transformation in which a finger turns into the handle of an ax.

D457.9.1.p: Magic transformation in which a cut-off hand turns into a plant.

D457.10.p: Magic transformation in which a moustache turns into grass.

D457.11.p: Magic transformation in which an eye turns into some other object.

D457.11.1.p: Magic transformation in which a bull's eye turns into hornets.

D457.11.2.p: Magic transformation in which eyeballs turn into torches.

D457.12.p: Magic transformation in which a bone turns into some other object.

D457.12.1.p: Magic transformation in which bone dust turns into a blazing fire.

D457.12.2.p: Magic transformation in which a bone turns into a skeleton.

D457.13.p: Magic transformation in which animal dung turns into some other object.

D457.14.p: Magic transformation in which a tongue turns into some other object.

D457.14.1.p: Magic transformation in which an ogress's tongue turns into a surfboard.

D457.14.2.p: Magic transformation in which a tongue turns into a flame.

D457.15.p: Magic transformation in which an animal's heart turns into some other object.

D457.15.1.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 138.
D457.15.1.p: Magic transformation in which a fox's heart turns into a rattle.

D457.16.p: Magic transformation in which a saint's relics turn into some other object.

D457.16.1.p: A saint's relics take on the form of a Buddha image.

D457.17.p: Magical transformation in which parts of a person or animal, such as flesh, turn into some other object.

D457.17.1.p: A magical transformation in which flesh turns into fire.

D457.18.p: Magical transformation in which a person's or animal's tears turn into some other object.

D457.18.1.p: A magical transformation in which tears turn into a fountain.

D457.18.2.p: A magical transformation in which tears turn into a river.

D457.19.p: A magical transformation in which the tips of an animal's ears turn into pelts or furs.

D469.p: A general category of magical transformations in which one miscellaneous object turns into other objects.

D469.1.p: A magical transformation in which an egg turns into mist.

D469.1.1.p: A magical transformation in which an egg turns into a house.

D469.2.p: A magical transformation in which smoke turns into a bridge.

D469.3.p: A magical transformation in which a chain of arrows turns into a bridge.

D469.4.p: A magical transformation in which sea-scum turns into ice.

D469.5.p: A magical transformation in which a furnace of fire turns into a garden.

D470.p: A general category of magical transformations in which the material of an object is changed into a different material.

D471.p: A magical transformation in which an object turns into stone.

D471.1.r: As punishment. (Cf. D441.1, D444.2, D444.4, D476.)—Type 368*; *BP III 168, 462; Fb “sten” III 553b, 554a; Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 1599; Icelandic: *Boberg.
D471.1.p: A magical transformation in which bread turns into stone.

D471.2.r: N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 212 No. 41, 398 No. 70, 409 No. 73.
D471.2.p: A magical transformation in which a house turns into stone.

D471.2.1.r: N. A. Indian (Shasta): Farrand-Frachtenberg JAFL XXVIII 216 No. 6.
D471.2.1.p: A magical transformation in which the door of a house turns into stone.

D471.3.p: A magical transformation in which a ship turns into stone.

D471.4.p: A magical transformation in which cheese turns into stone.

D471.4.1.p: Milk is magically changed into stone, a specific case of an object turning to stone in a tale of enchantment.

D471.5.p: Salt is magically changed into stone.

D471.6.p: A tree is magically changed into stone.

D471.7.p: Poison is magically changed into stone.

D471.8.p: Animals are magically changed into stones.

D471.8.1.p: Chickens that were stolen turn into stones while they are being cooked.

D471.9.p: A candle is magically changed into stone.

D471.10.p: Water is magically changed into rocks.

D472.p: An object is magically changed into muck, filth, or mud.

D472.1.r: As punishment. Fb “mog” II 603; India: Thompson-Balys.
D472.1.p: Food is magically changed into muck or filth.

D473.p: An object is magically changed into wood.

D473.1.p: A sword is magically changed into wood.

D474.p: An object is magically changed so that it becomes bloody.

D474.1.p: A key is magically changed so that it becomes bloody.

D474.2.r: Loomis White Magic 78; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 358.
D474.2.p: Water is magically changed into blood.

D474.3.p: A cake is magically changed so that it becomes bloody.

D474.4.p: An egg is magically changed into blood.

D474.5.p: Butter, made from milk, is magically changed into blood.

D474.6.p: Tears are magically changed into blood.

D474.7.p: Spittle, or saliva, is magically changed into blood.

D474.8.p: Fruit juice magically turns into blood.

D474.9.p: The eyes of a stone lion magically become bloody.

D475.p: An object magically changes into treasure, or treasure changes back into an ordinary object.

D475.1.r: Encyc. Religion and Ethics s.v. “Alchemy”; *Loomis White Magic 79, 81.—Irish: Cross, Plummer xliv, clxxxv; German: Hartland Science 49; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 383.
D475.1.p: Various objects magically turn into gold.

D475.1.1.p: Burning coals magically turn into gold.

D475.1.2.p: Wood shavings magically turn into gold.

D475.1.3.p: Dead leaves magically turn into gold.

D475.1.3.1.p: Banyan leaves magically turn into gold.

D475.1.7.p: A brick or tile magically turns into gold.

D475.1.8.p: Earth or soil magically turns into gold.

D475.1.11.p: A paste smeared on a princess's body magically turns to gold.

D475.1.12.p: Putrescence (rotting matter) magically turns into gold.

D475.1.13.p: Mucus magically turns into gold as a reward for piety.

D475.1.14.p: Magic transforms a bottle into gold. An ordinary bottle is turned into solid gold by supernatural power.

D475.1.15.p: Magic turns a palace into gold. A palace is changed into solid gold by supernatural power.

D475.1.16.p: Magic turns food into gold. Something to eat is changed into gold by supernatural power.

D475.1.17.p: Magic turns an axe into gold. An axe becomes golden by supernatural power.

D475.1.18.p: Magic turns flowers into gold and silver. Flowers are changed into precious metal by supernatural power.

D475.1.19.p: The leaves on which a meal is served turn into gold plates. Leaves used as dishes are changed into gold by magic.

D475.1.20.p: Magic turns straw into gold. Straw is changed into gold by supernatural power.

D475.1.21.p: Magic turns fingernails into gold. A person's fingernail clippings or nails are changed into gold by supernatural power.

D475.2.p: An object is transformed into money, or money is transformed into an object. Magic changes things into coins or changes coins into something else.

D475.2.1.p: Magic turns stones into gold coins. Ordinary stones become gold money by supernatural power.

D475.2.2.r: Africa (Kpelle): Westermann Zs. f. afrikan., ozean., u. ostasiat. Spr. VI 161 No. 29a.
D475.2.2.p: Magic turns water into money. Water is changed into coins by supernatural power.

D475.2.3.p: Magic turns money into ashes or leaves. Coins are changed into ash or leaves by supernatural power.

D475.2.4.p: Magic turns money into pewter. Coins are changed into cheap pewter metal by supernatural power.

D475.3.p: Various objects are transformed into silver by magic. Things are changed into silver by supernatural power.

D475.3.1.p: Magic turns earth or soil into silver. Dirt is changed into silver by supernatural power.

D475.3.2.p: Magic changes tin into silver. Tin is turned into silver by supernatural power.

D475.3.3.p: Magic turns a stone into silver. An ordinary stone becomes silver by supernatural power.

D475.3.4.p: Magic turns the iron in an axe into silver. The iron blade of an axe is changed into silver by supernatural power.

D475.3.5.p: A silver dish turns into wood. Magic changes a silver dish into a wooden one.

D475.4.p: An object is transformed into jewels, or jewels are transformed into an object. Magic changes things into gems or gems into something else.

D475.4.1.p: Stones are magically changed into jewels.

D475.4.2.p: Lice are magically changed into gems.

D475.4.3.p: Dishes are magically changed into jewels.

D475.4.4.p: Peas are magically changed into pearls.

D475.4.5.r: German: Grimm No. 179; Greek: Grote 134; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.

D475.4.6.p: Fingernail clippings are magically changed into jewels.

D475.4.7.p: Hairs are magically changed into jewels.

D475.4.8.p: Water dripping off a person's body is magically changed into agates.

D475.4.9.p: Oil is magically changed into jewels.

D475.5.p: A cup made of marble is magically changed into one made of crystal.

D476.p: Food is magically transformed, usually from something that is not food into something edible.

D476.1.p: A substance that cannot be eaten is magically changed into food.

D476.1.1.p: Bread is magically made out of mud.

D476.1.2.p: A loaf of bread is magically made from a tree leaf.

D476.1.3.p: Wood is magically changed into grain.

D476.1.4.p: Lard is magically made from tree bark.

D476.1.5.p: Butter is magically made from nettles.

D476.1.6.p: Pancakes are magically made out of snow.

D476.1.7.p: A rock is magically changed into milk.

D476.1.8.p: A stream is magically changed into an egg.

D476.1.9.r: N. A. Indian (Menomini): Skinner and Satterlee PaAM XIII 270, (Crow): Lowie PaAM XXV 23ff., (Southern Ute): Lowie JAFL XXXVII 11 No. 5.
D476.1.9.p: Magic transforms ice into grease, turning a cold, inedible substance into a usable food fat.

D476.1.10.p: Magic turns powdered bone into cheese, changing an inedible substance into food.

D476.1.11.p: Magic turns sand into rice, so something worthless becomes edible grain.

D476.2.p: Magic changes a food that can be eaten into something that cannot be eaten.

D476.2.1.p: Magic turns food into dust, so it crumbles and can no longer be eaten.

D476.2.2.p: Cooked meat is magically turned back into raw meat.

D476.2.3.p: Milk is magically changed into some other substance that is not drinkable milk.

D476.2.3.1.p: Milk is magically changed into blood.

D476.2.3.2.p: Milk is magically changed into lye, a caustic alkaline liquid.

D476.2.4.p: Magic turns sugar into ashes, so a sweet food becomes worthless residue.

D476.3.p: Meat is magically transformed in some way; the headline gives no further detail.

D476.3.1.p: Meat magically takes on the flavor of whatever delicacy one wishes for.

D476.3.2.p: Bacon is magically changed into iron.

D476.3.2.1.p: Bacon is magically changed into various other kinds of food.

D476.3.3.p: Horse meat is magically changed into mutton.

D476.3.4.p: On a feast day, meat is miraculously turned into fish, and fish into meat.

D477.p: Magic transforms an object into wine, or wine into an object.

D477.0.1.p: Wine is miraculously changed into some other object.

D477.0.1.1.p: Wine is magically changed into blood.

D477.0.1.2.p: A wine is magically changed into some other object or substance, here honey.

D477.1.r: Fb “vand” III 1000a.; St. John 2:9; Grimm Deutsche Mythologie I 486; Hartland Science 69; Farnell Cults of the Greek States V 156; Wuttke Volksaberglaube (Berlin 1900) 66ff.; *Toldo VI 310ff.; *Saintyves Essais 206ff.; Günter 246 s.v. “Wein”; *Loomis White Magic 78; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
D477.1.p: Water is magically changed into wine.

D477.1.1.p: The Devil takes a man who waits at midnight on Old Christmas Eve for water to turn into wine.

D477.1.2.p: A woman goes to a well at midnight on Old Christmas Eve, when the water turns to wine, and loses an eye.

D477.2.p: Salt water (brine) is magically changed into wine.

D477.3.p: Beer is magically changed into wine.

D478.p: Water is magically changed into some other substance, or some other substance is changed into water.

D478.1.p: Water is magically changed into milk.

D478.2.p: Water is magically changed into ale.

D478.3.p: Water is magically changed into fire.

D478.4.p: Water is magically changed into a marvelous drink.

D478.5.p: Water is magically changed into honey.

D478.6.p: Water is magically changed into mead, a honey-based alcoholic drink.

D478.7.p: Water is magically changed into oil.

D478.8.p: Water is magically changed into balsam, a fragrant healing ointment or resin.

D478.9.p: A magician turns the water of a river into copper.

D478.10.p: Salty water is magically turned into fresh, drinkable liquid.

D478.11.p: Water is magically changed into butter and cream.

D478.12.p: Water is magically changed into rocks or stone.

D478.13.p: Water is magically changed into brimstone (sulfur), or the reverse.

D478.14.p: Boiling pitch is magically turned back into cold water.

D479.p: Various ordinary objects are magically changed from one material into another.

D479.1.p: A bog or swamp is magically transformed into a meadow full of flowers, through a saint's power.

D479.2.p: Iron tools are magically turned into earth or soil.

D479.3.p: A magic charm makes a root taste bitter.

D479.4.p: A goose's egg is magically changed into a hen's egg.

D479.5.p: A basket of miscellaneous things is magically changed into iron.

D479.6.p: Wax is magically turned into earth.

D479.7.p: Bad smells are magically turned into sweet fragrances, or sweet smells into bad ones.

D479.8.p: A humble hut is magically transformed into a golden palace.

D480.p: The size of an object is magically changed, making it larger or smaller.

D480.0.1.p: A saint miraculously stretches or shortens things when they are needed.

D482.p: Objects are magically stretched to become longer or taller.

D482.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Batak: Warneck Religion der Batak 50; Melanesian: Codrington 165.—N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 332 n. 199; S. A. Indian (Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 35; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 188, 306.
D482.1.p: A tree magically stretches and shoots upward.

D482.2.p: A lily plant grows miraculously quickly, stretching tall.

D482.3.p: A lance or spear is magically stretched to a greater length.

D482.4.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “precipice”.—Hawaii: Dixon 90; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 76.
D482.4.p: A cliff magically rises up into the air, stretching upward.

D482.5.p: A sepulchre, or tomb, magically becomes longer.

D482.5.1.p: A grave is magically made five times as long as any person's foot-length.

D482.5.2.p: A sepulchre's gate is magically enlarged, usually so that something or someone can pass through it.

D483.p: A sea comes into being from the spittle of a giant.

D483.1.r: S. A. Indian (Apapocuvú-Guaraní): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 138.
D483.1.p: A river magically swells until it becomes a sea.

D485.p: A person stretches their fingers magically so that they form a ladder.

D486.p: A person magically becomes larger in size.

D486.1.p: A demon magically becomes larger in size.

D487.p: An animal magically becomes larger in size.

D487.1.p: A snake magically grows to a length of 300 leagues.

D487.2.p: A monkey magically grows to a height of 100,000 feet.

D487.3.p: An ox-demon magically grows to a length of 10,000 feet.

D489.p: Miscellaneous objects are magically made larger.

D489.2.p: A magic amulet enlarges until it becomes a cloak.

D490.p: Miscellaneous magical transformations of objects not covered by more specific headings.

D491.r: N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 336 n. 210a.
D491.p: Objects that can be magically shrunk or compressed to a small size and later restored.

D491.1.p: Magic animals that can be shrunk or compressed to a small size.

D491.1.1.p: A whole herd of cattle is magically put into a small cup.

D491.1.2.p: A magic mule can fold itself up like a sheet of paper.

D491.1.3.p: A magic dog shrinks to a smaller size.

D491.2.p: Magic objects that can be shrunk down to a much smaller size, often to be carried around easily.

D491.2.1.p: A magic box that can be made smaller by magic, so that it can be carried or hidden easily.

D491.2.1.1.r: East Africa: Frobenius Atlantis IV 134ff. No. 13.
D491.2.1.1.p: A magic box that can be made small and holds many people and objects inside it.

D491.2.2.p: A table that can be magically compressed into a smaller size.

D491.3.p: A saint magically keeps a large amount of water confined within a small ditch.

D491.4.p: A piece of ice or a snowflake is made small by magic.

D491.5.p: A castle is magically made smaller in size.

D491.6.p: Twelve stones join together magically and become a single stone.

D491.7.p: A large ship is magically made into a small boat.

D492.p: The color of some object is magically changed.

D492.1.p: A rooster's comb magically turns white.

D492.3.p: A person's hair suddenly changes color.

D493.p: A spirit takes the form of an animal.

D494.p: A person is magically transformed into a monster.

D500.p: General heading for the ways or means by which transformation (magical change of shape or form) is brought about.

D502.p: A person who has the power to change shape cannot do so while other people are watching.

D510.r: Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 468; Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 154.
D510.p: A person is transformed into another form because they broke a taboo, a forbidden act or rule.

D511.p: A person is transformed because someone breaks a taboo against speaking or using a certain name.

D511.1.p: A man calls his wife "my swallow", a forbidden name, and as a result she turns into a swallow bird.

D512.p: A person is transformed into something else by showing astonishment or amazement at a marvel. The wonder itself triggers the change.

D512.1.p: A smith draws water in an eggshell, and a person who expresses astonishment at this feat is transformed.

D513.p: A person is transformed by breaking a prohibition against looking at something forbidden.

D513.1.p: A man watches snakes mating, and as a result he is changed into a woman.

D515.p: A person is transformed into something else for picking flowers in an enchanted garden.

D516.r: Greek: Roscher s.v. “Itys”; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian (Thompson): Alexander N. Am. 137.
D516.p: A person is transformed into something else because of overwhelming grief.

D517.p: A person is transformed into something else as punishment for disobeying a command.

D518.r: Eskimo (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 176, (Greenland): Rink 413, Rasmussen III 81, (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 638.
D518.p: A woman is transformed as punishment for feeding or nursing an animal.

D520.p: A person or thing is transformed by means of a spoken word, wish, song, curse, or similar utterance.

D521.r: Type 451; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 398 No. 70, 409 No. 73, (Shasta): Farrand-Frachtenberg JAFL XXVIII 216 No. 6; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 172.
D521.p: A person is transformed simply because someone wishes it to happen.

D521.1.p: A parent carelessly wishes a change on a child, and the child is transformed as a result.

D522.r: (Cf. D1273.)—Irish myth: Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys, Penzer I 136, II 20, VI 8, 59.—Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/203); Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 271 No. 84.
D522.p: A person is transformed by saying a magic word or charm.

D523.p: A person is transformed by means of a song.

D523.1.p: A person is transformed by playing a musical instrument.

D523.1.1.p: A person is transformed by playing a flute.

D525.r: Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer VI 16, VIII 140ff.; Icelandic: *Boberg.
D525.p: A person is transformed by a curse pronounced against them or by someone's curse.

D525.1.p: A mother in despair curses herself and her children, and they are turned into trees.

D526.p: Whoever or whatever is first greeted is transformed, so the greeting itself causes the change.

D527.p: A person is transformed by being scolded.

D529.p: Miscellaneous transformations caused by the power of the spoken word that do not fit the more specific categories above.

D529.1.p: A person is turned to stone at the moment a woman's voice is heard.

D530.p: A person is transformed into another being by putting on a skin, clothing, or similar covering.

D531.r: Fb “and”; Icel.: Völsunga saga ch. 8; Irish myth: *Cross; English: Child II 494, III 518, IV 495a, V495 s.v. “seals”; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 313 n. 132; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 364, II 13, III 75, 143, 262, Rink 146, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 181, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 617, (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 468, (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 95; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 271 No. 84; North Carolina Negro: Parsons JAFL XXX 187; Surinam: Alexander Lat. Am. 274.—See also all references under D361.1. (Swan Maiden).
D531.p: A person becomes an animal by putting on the animal's skin, feathers, or similar covering, taking on that animal's form.

D532.r: Types 552A, 553; *BP III 434; Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XXII 13.
D532.p: A person is transformed by putting on a claw, feather, or other part of a helpful animal.

D533.p: A person is transformed into a fish when caught in a fish-trap.

D535.r: *Fb “hest” I 598b, “grime” I 484, “bidsel” IV 37b; Köhler-Bolte I 220, 586.—Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 130 No. 71; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 45 No. 71; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3656; India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer VI 56 n. 2, *59.
D535.p: A person is transformed into a horse (or donkey or similar animal) by having a bridle or halter put on.

D535.1.p: A person is transformed into a horse by having horseshoes fitted to them.

D536.p: A person is transformed when chains are removed from their neck.

D536.1.r: (Cf. D161.)—**O. Rank Die Lohengrinsage (1911) 65f.; *Wehrhan 50; *Wesselski Märchen 255 No. 64; *Chauvin VIII 206 No. 248; *G. Huet Romania XXXIV (1905) 206ff.; H. A. Todd MLN VI 2.—Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 263; English Romance: Wells 97 (Chevalere Assigne).
D536.1.p: People are turned into swans when chains are taken off their necks.

D537.r: Icelandic: Arnason (Powell and Magnusson tr.) II 246, Boberg.—N. A. Indian (Micmac): Rand Nos. 5, 16, 17. (Caughnawaga): Harrington JAFL XIX 127f., cf. (Yana): Curtin Creation Myths of Primitive America (Boston 1898) 312ff.—Cf. Fb. “klæder” II 200a.
D537.p: A person is transformed by changing their clothes.

D537.1.p: A person is transformed by putting on a hood.

D537.2.p: A person is transformed by putting on a cloak.

D537.2.1.p: A man grows to giant size when he puts on a giantess's cloak.

D537.3.p: A person is transformed by putting on a moustache.

D537.4.p: A person is transformed by putting on a wig.

D550.r: *MacCulloch Childhood 158.—Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 313 n. 132a.
D550.p: A person is transformed by eating or drinking something.

D551.p: A person is transformed by eating something.

D551.1.p: A person is transformed by eating a fruit.

D551.1.1.r: *Fb “æble” III 1136a; Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Apfel” n. 11.—Icelandic: Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “pomme”; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 62 No. 449. Cf. Type 566.
D551.1.1.p: A person is transformed by eating an apple.

D551.1.2.p: A person is transformed by eating an apricot.

D551.1.3.p: A person is changed into another form by eating a pear.

D551.2.p: A person is changed into another form by eating a vegetable.

D551.2.1.p: A person is changed into another form by eating cabbage.

D551.2.2.p: A person is changed into another form by eating cicuta, a poisonous plant (water hemlock).

D551.2.3.p: A person is changed into another form by eating magic seeds.

D551.2.4.p: A person is changed into another form by eating a flower.

D551.2.5.p: A person is changed into another form by eating onions.

D655.p: A character deliberately changes shape in order to get food.

D655.1.p: A character turns into a buffalo so that it can graze on grass.

D655.2.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 166, 484 nn. 21, 22; England, Ireland, U.S.: *Baughman.
D655.2.p: A witch changes into an animal, such as a hare or a pig, in order to suck milk from cows.

D657.r: (Cf. K300.)—Icelandic MacCulloch Eddic 54; Chinese: Werner 360f.; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 306 n. 109x, (Calif.): Gayton and Newman 63; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 220 No. 32.
D657.p: A character changes shape in order to steal something.

D657.1.p: A character changes into a small form so that it can be carried off hidden in a food bag.

D657.2.p: A character changes into a flying horse in order to carry off a king.

D657.3.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 7, (Choco): ibid. 112.
D657.3.p: A character changes shape in order to steal fire.

D658.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 319 n. 2. 395; India: Thompson-Balys.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 305 n. 109v.
D658.p: A character changes shape in order to seduce someone.

D658.1.p: A character turns into an animal in order to seduce a woman.

D658.2.r: *Penzer III 126f.; *Toldo Zs. f. Vksk. XV 367; *Frazer Apollodorus I 174 n. 1; *Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Betrüger überführt”; Roscher Lexikon s.v. “Alkmene”; Euphorion I 589f.; Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XVI 138ff.; Wells 30 (Geoffrey of Monmouth), 32 (Layamon’s Brut), 43 (Arthour and Merlin), 103 (Alliterative Alexander, Fragment A).—Irish myth: *Cross, MacCulloch Celtic 52, 56, 63, 75; Welsh: ibid. 185; German: Boberg; Indonesian: DeVries’s list No. 150.
D658.2.p: A character takes on the appearance of a woman's husband or lover in order to seduce her.

D658.3.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Danish: Boberg; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 49.
D658.3.p: A character changes sex in order to seduce someone.

D658.3.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Hindu: Keith 151.
D658.3.1.p: A character changes into a man in order to seduce a man.

D658.3.2.p: An animal changes into a woman in order to seduce a man.

D658.3.2.1.r: Icelandic: De la Saussaye 261 (Loki); India: Thompson-Balys.
D658.3.2.1.p: A goddess takes the form of a mare in order to seduce a stallion.

D658.3.3.p: Seven girls take the form of seven parrots to approach a boy who has rejected them.

D659.p: A character changes shape voluntarily for some other reason not covered by the more specific headings.

D659.1.r: (Cf. D621.1.1.) Done by otherworld people.—New Britain: Dixon 117.
D659.1.p: A character turns into snakes at night so that it can sleep.

D659.2.r: (Cf. D615)—Icelandic: Boberg; Irish myth: *Cross; Persian: Carnoy 269; Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 38.
D659.2.p: A character changes into animals in order to fight.

D659.3.p: A character changes shape to show displeasure or anger.

D659.4.p: A character voluntarily changes into an animal in order to help someone, for example by guarding or assisting them.

D659.4.1.r: (Cf. D112.1, D621.1.)—Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 62 No. 451.
D659.4.1.p: A character changes into a lion so as to stand guard over a palace.

D659.4.2.p: A sea dragon takes the form of a serpent in order to travel alongside and accompany the hero.

D659.4.3.p: A character changes into an eagle to carry the hero to safety.

D659.4.4.p: A character changes into an eagle in order to guard a princess.

D659.5.p: A character changes shape in order to obtain a blessing.

D659.6.p: A character transforms into a friar in order to teach people.

D659.7.p: A wife transforms herself into the likeness of her husband's mistress, so that she takes the mistress's place with him.

D659.8.p: A character changes shape in order to test whether another person is faithful.

D659.9.p: A character changes into another form in order to persuade a man to go to battle.

D659.10.p: A character changes shape in order to lure hunters to a certain place.

D659.11.p: A character changes shape in order to recover stolen goods.

D659.12.r: French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule. (Cf. D23.1.)
D659.12.p: A character changes into a tramp or beggar so as not to be recognized.

D659.13.p: A character transforms in order to drive buffaloes to be milked.

D659.14.p: A woman transforms so that she can fly, helping the hero pick out the right weapons from among many.

D660.p: The reasons why one character transforms another into a different form.

Bolte) No. 413.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Finnish: Kalevala rune 33; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 97 No. 836A*; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “amoureux”; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 313 No. 82; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 343 (Niobe), Fox 29 (Io); Jewish: Neuman; Tahiti: Dixon 65; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 89 No. 22, 105 No. 29.
D661.p: A person is transformed into another form as a punishment.

D661.1.p: A person is transformed as revenge for rejecting amorous advances.

D661.2.r: Der Heiligen Leben und Leiden 100ff. (Santa Barbara).
D661.2.p: A person is transformed as punishment for denouncing a saint.

D661.3.p: A person is transformed as punishment for breaking a vow.

D662.r: He falls in love with another woman: his wife changes him to negro. He then falls in love with negress: wife changes him to ass. He then falls in love with she-ass. Finally restored to his original form.—*Chauvin II 183 No. 23.
D662.p: A husband who has been unfaithful is changed into another form by magic, usually so that his wife can cure him of his wandering ways.

D663.p: Someone is magically transformed as a reward for a good deed or service.

D664.p: A goddess magically changes a woman's appearance or form to protect her chastity from an attacker or suitor.

D665.p: Someone magically transforms an enemy into another form to get rid of him.

D665.1.p: A person magically transforms a rival for another's love or marriage so as to remove him from the competition.

D665.2.p: A person magically transforms a stepchild into another form to get rid of the child.

D665.3.p: A jealous co-wife magically transforms the other wife, usually into an animal or object.

D666.r: Icelandic: Hjálmtèrs saga ok Ölvers 472, Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
D666.p: Someone is magically transformed in order to save that person from danger.

D666.1.p: A king of birds turns his quails into sticks and pebbles so that the king, his hunters and hawks cannot catch or kill them.

D670.r: Irish myth: Cross; *Krappe The Legend of Walther and Hildegund (Journal of English and Germanic Philology XXII [1923] 75—88).
D670.p: A flight from pursuers accomplished by magic, in which the fugitives use supernatural means to get away.

D671.r: *Types 313, 325, 327; **Aarne Die magische Flucht (FFC XCII); *Fb “and” IV 12b, “rose” III 80a.—Irish myth: *Cross; English: Child V 499 s.v. “transformations”; Greek: Grote I 182; Jewish: Neuman; Arabian: Burton Nights V 353; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 75, 17 n. 1; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 327, 367, III 124, Rink 195, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 182; N. Indian (Sharanti, Comacan, Mashacalí): Horton BBAE CXLIII 3 294, (Mundurucu): Horton ibid. 3 281; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 274 No. 86.—Africa (Kaffir): Theal 98, (Zulu): Callaway 21, (Basuto): Jacottet 206 No. 30, Casalis Les Bassoutos (Paris 1859) 349.
D671.p: Fugitives escape pursuit by changing their own shape so the pursuer does not recognize them.

D671.0.1.r: Africa (Zulu): Held 144ff., (Bechuana): Brown, J. T. Among the Bantu Nomads (London, 1926) 181ff., (Northern Rhodesia): Worthington The Little Wise One (London, 1930) 135ff. No. 19, (Gan): Westermann Die Sprache der Guang (Berlin, 1922) 86f.
D671.0.1.p: A fugitive escapes by turning himself into stone, and the pursuer throws him to safety.

D671.0.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Grote I 238.
D671.0.2.p: A helper transforms the fugitive so the pursuer cannot detect him.

D671.1.r: Transformed pursuer. Koryak: Jochelson JE VI 363.
D671.1.p: The fugitives are transformed to escape, but the pursuer reverses the transformation in order to find them.

D672.p: Fugitives throw objects behind them that magically become obstacles blocking the pursuer.

D672.1.r: S. A. Indian (Ceiuci): Alexander Lat. Am. 304.
D672.1.p: Magic objects are dropped to distract the pursuer, who stops to pick up what has been transformed into animals.

D673.r: Type 450; BP III 205.—Arabic: A. Jahn Die Mehri-Sprache in Südarabien (Wien, 1902) 124 No. 28, D. H. Müller Mehri und Hadrami-Texte (Wien, 1909) 99 No. 39, ibid. Mehri und Soquotri Sprache (Wien, 1905) II 99 No. 20.
D673.p: Magic obstacles are raised in front of a fugitive to block his escape, the reverse of the usual obstacle flight.

D674.p: A speaking he-goat helps a girl escape a bargain with the devil, in which she was promised to him.

D675.r: Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 328, 367, III 124, 260, Rink 195, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 182.
D675.p: The sea freezes over so that fugitives can cross it and escape.

D680.p: Miscellaneous details about how a transformation happens, not covered by more specific categories.

Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 170 No. 32, (White Mountain Apache): Goddard PaAM XXIV 128, (Joshua): Farrand-Frachtenberg JAFL XXVIII 241 No. 20;—Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 85.
D681.p: A transformation that happens slowly, step by step, rather than all at once.

D682.p: A transformation in which only part of a person or animal changes, while the rest stays the same.

D682.1.r: Hartland Science 198; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 150, (Central Eskimo): Boas BAM XV 182, 253, (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 49.
D682.1.p: A person who has the head of an animal while the rest of the body stays human.

D682.2.p: A person who has animal hair growing on the body while otherwise remaining human.

D682.3.p: An animal that has been changed so it keeps a human mind or understanding.

D682.3.1.r: Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 456, Rasmussen III 73, (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 173, (Central Eskimo): Boas BAM XV 217.
D682.3.1.p: Animals in human form keep their animal diet and habits, even though they look human.

D682.3.2.p: An animal that still has human eyes, showing it is secretly a person.

D682.4.p: A partial transformation in which only the color of something or someone changes.

D682.4.1.p: A magic mantle whose color changes every hour.

D682.4.2.p: A spirit of poetry that appears as a hideous young man and then becomes beautiful.

D683.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 184 n. 97; Irish myth: *Cross; See also all notes to D615.1.
D683.p: A transformation carried out by a magician.

D683.1.r: See all references for motifs A900—A999 for work of transformers. (Cf. D272.)—Marshall Islands: Davenport JAFL LXVI 222.
D683.1.p: Demigods who change things at will so that they take on their present form.

D683.2.r: *Types 403, 405, 410, 450, 451; *Kittredge Witchcraft 183f. nn. 91—96; *Fb “grime” I 484.—Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Fox 137 (Circe); Spanish: *Boggs FFC XC No. 449; India: Thompson-Balys.
D683.2.p: A transformation carried out by a witch or sorceress.

D683.3.p: A troll changes a person's shape by magic.

D683.4.r: *Toldo Studien zur vgl. Littgsch. V 343; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
D683.4.p: A transformation carried out by a saint.

D683.5.p: A transformation carried out by a god or goddess.

D683.6.p: A transformation carried out by evil spirits.

D683.7.p: A transformation carried out by a fairy.

D683.7.1.p: A transformation carried out by the child of a fairy and a mortal.

D683.8.p: A transformation carried out by an angel, acting for God.

D683.9.p: A transformation carried out by a druid.

D684.p: Someone is changed into an animal or other form by animals that help them. The helpful animals are the means of the transformation.

D684.0.1.p: A person is changed into another form by a magic animal, which performs the transformation.

D686.p: A person who has been turned into an animal will not touch the flesh of that same kind of animal, because it would be like eating their own kind.

D686.1.p: A person turned into an animal refuses ordinary human food and eats only what suits the enchanted animal form.

D688.r: *Types 403, 450; BP I 79ff., 99ff.—India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman; Japanese: Ikeda.—Africa (Bushman): Bleek and Lloyd 87, (Kaffir): Theal 61.
D688.p: A mother who has been transformed into an animal still nurses her child.

D688.1.p: A mother transformed into a cow gives advice to her daughter.

D691.p: Men who have been turned into dogs are beaten every day. The beating is required to keep the spell in force, unless the hero himself is to be transformed.

D692.p: The inhabitants of a city are turned into fish. Different social classes become fish of different colors.

D693.p: A man who has been turned into a donkey plays the lyre.

D694.p: Food is left out for a person who has been transformed, so they can eat while in their changed form.

D695.p: A man who has been transformed into a woman has children.

D696.p: A person is transformed while asleep, or the change happens during sleep.

D697.p: A magic object has the power to change its own form without anyone's help.

D697.1.p: A magic loincloth can change itself into any form.

D698.r: Greek myth: passim; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 2, and chapt. 1 passim.
D698.p: Gods have the power to change their own shape.

D699.p: A grouping of miscellaneous transformation motifs that do not fit elsewhere in the index.

D699.1.p: The eyes of a hero's buffalo friend turn into two strong dogs, which then protect his wife.

D700.r: Types 314, 402, 434*, 442, 502; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 925 s.v. “Erlösung”.—Irish myth: Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “métamorphose”; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 285, 356, 364.
D700.p: A person is freed from an enchantment or magic spell that had changed them.

D701.r: (Cf. D617.)—*Type 307; Wimberly 381; Moe Samlede Skrifter I 52; German: Grimm Nos. 108, 121, 137; India: Thompson-Balys.
D701.p: A person is freed from enchantment little by little, not all at once.

D702.p: A person is only partly freed from enchantment, so some of the transformation remains.

D702.1.r: Many of the references to E33 may refer to this motif.
D702.1.p: A person who was turned into an animal or other form loses a body part during the transformation and, once restored to human shape, still lacks that part.

D702.1.1.r: (Cf. D142, D621.1.1.)—*Taylor MPh XVII 59 n. 8; Tobler 43; Eng., Ire., U.S.: *Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
D702.1.1.p: A man spends a night in a haunted mill and cuts off a cat's paw; in the morning the miller's wife is found missing a hand, because she was the cat.

D702.1.2.p: A hog's forefoot is cut off, and the woman who was the hog is then found missing a hand.

D702.2.p: A person changed back into human form still keeps some animal features, such as a tail, ears, or fur.

D705.p: A whole place, such as a building or district, is freed from an enchantment that had been laid on it.

D705.1.p: A castle that had been under an enchantment is freed from it, so that it returns to normal.

D710.r: Types 507A, 507C; India: Thompson-Balys; Irish myth: Cross.
D710.p: An enchantment is broken by treating the enchanted person or object roughly, rather than by gentle or magical means.

D711.r: *Types 314, 402, 425, 440, 441, 471, 506, 507, 531, 545A, 545B, 550, 708; *Fb “hoved” I 655a, “løse” II 517a; **Kittredge JAFL XVIII 1; BP I 9, III 60; Hartland Science 241.—Irish myth: *Cross; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 17; French: Sébillot France III 52, 140; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 39 No. 5.
D711.p: An enchantment is broken by cutting off the enchanted being's head.

D711.1.p: An enchantment is broken by cutting off the head, and then a head is put back on the body, sometimes a different one.

D711.1.1.p: The head of one man is transferred to another man's body, so that the second man's head ends up in the first man's hand.

D711.2.p: An enchanted person is broken free of the spell by being cut in two.

D711.3.p: A bird is freed from enchantment by having its bill cut off.

D711.4.r: Type 407.—Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. *368, 407; India: Thompson-Balys.
D711.4.p: A flower is disenchanted by having its stalk broken.

D711.4.1.p: A flower is disenchanted by being plucked from its plant.

D711.5.p: A leaf is disenchanted by being broken off the tree it grows on.

D711.6.p: A fruit is disenchanted by being picked from the tree.

D712.p: An enchantment is broken by violence, meaning rough or harmful physical treatment of the enchanted being.

D712.1.r: (Cf. D711.1.)—Kittredge JAFL XVIII 13; Fb “flå”; Irish myth: Cross.
D712.1.p: An enchantment is broken by cutting off bodily parts of the enchanted being and reversing them, such as putting them back on the wrong way.

D712.1.1.p: An enchanted animal is freed by having one of its limbs cut off.

D712.1.2.p: An enchanted being is freed by being cut in two.

D712.2.r: Type 440; Hartland Science 242.—Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 510; Chile: Pino Saavedra 402.
D712.2.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being hurled or slung against something, which breaks the enchantment.

D712.2.1.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being thrown into a fire.

D712.3.r: Wimberly 343.—Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 57 No. 412; Missouri-French: Carrière; Chinese: Werner 309; India: Thompson-Balys.
D712.3.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being struck or hit.

D712.3.1.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being struck with a missile, such as a thrown object.

D712.3.2.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being hit with a thrown stone.

D712.3.3.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being struck with a thrown flower.

D712.4.r: *Fb “blod” IV 48a; Child I 178, 337 n.; Wimberly 342; *Jijena Sanchez 19f., 36.
D712.4.p: A transformed person is disenchanted when blood is drawn from them.

D712.4.1.p: A transformed person is disenchanted when someone drinks their blood.

D712.5.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 348 n. 249a; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 187, (Ungava): Turner RBAE XI 265, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 630, (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 158, (Greenland): Rink 93, Rasmussen II 38, III 104.
D712.5.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being beaten.

D712.6.r: Kittredge JAFL XVIII 11; *Jijena Sanchez 35, 49; Chinese: Graham.
D712.6.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being wounded.

D712.7.r: Kittredge JAFL XVIII 11; Fb “and” IV 12b.—Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 76 No. 15.
D712.7.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being shot.

D712.8.p: A transformed person is disenchanted when their armor is ripped open.

D712.9.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being killed.

D712.9.1.p: A person transformed into a lizard is killed, and the body that remains is a lizard rather than a human.

D712.10.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by having a stake driven through their body.

D712.11.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by having objects thrown at them.

D714.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being rubbed.

D716.p: A person under an enchantment is freed by defeating them in a physical fight or contest.

D717.p: A transformed person is disenchanted when bones are gathered and put back together.

D717.1.p: The collected bones are laid in a seven-fold cloth with another spread above them, and this disenchants the person.

D718.p: A transformed person is disenchanted by being shaved.

D719.p: A general heading for miscellaneous ways of breaking a magic spell by treating the enchanted person roughly. No single specific method is named here.

D719.1.p: The spell is broken when the enchanted victim is buried and grain is sown over the grave.

D719.1.1.p: The enchanted person is buried, then dug up again and brought back to life, which ends the enchantment.

D719.2.p: A wife destroys the crab form her husband has been turned into, and he is permanently freed from the enchantment.

D720.p: A general heading for breaking a spell by removing or destroying the covering, such as a skin or outer form, that the enchanted person is wearing.

D721.r: See all references to D361.1, Swan Maiden.—Irish myth: *Cross: India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XX 299, (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 51; Koryak: Jochelson JE VI 131, 156, 335; Africa (Pangwe): Tessman 368f.
D721.p: A spell is broken by removing or stripping away the covering, such as a skin, that hides or encloses the enchanted person.

D721.1.p: The enchanted person is freed when their animal skin is stripped off, as if flayed.

D721.2.r: *Type 400; *Fb “sælhund”.—Scandinavian: Krappe Scandinavian Studies XVIII (1944) 156—162; Slavic: Máchal 258; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Surinam: Alexander Lat. Am. 274; Indonesian: DeVries’s list No. 151; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 146 No. 30, (Kaffir): Theal 38.
D721.2.p: The enchanted person briefly takes off their skin covering, and it is stolen, so they stay in the enchanted form until it is found.

D721.3.r: *Type 425, 430, 440, 441; Köhler-Bolte I *319, 511; *Chauvin VII 37 No. 212B.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Turkish: Giese Türkische Märchen (Jena 1925) 120; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Korean: Zong in-Sob 177.—Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 89, (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 55, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 224; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 347 n. 249; S. A. Indian: Jijena Sanchez 23; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis IV 69, 287.
D721.3.p: The enchanted person's skin or covering is destroyed, which frees them from the spell.

D721.4.p: The enchanted person is freed by someone holding them while they are temporarily in the disenchanted state.

D721.5.p: The enchantment is broken when a fruit or flower containing the enchanted person is opened.

D722.r: See references in D535.—*Type 325; *BP II 67; Chauvin V 150 No. 73.—French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 17; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.
D722.p: A man transformed into a horse or donkey is freed when his bridle is taken off.

D723.p: A general heading for breaking a spell by putting on or taking off a chain worn around the neck.

D723.1.p: The enchantment is broken when a chain is put around the enchanted person's neck.

D723.2.r: French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 17; India: *Thompson-Balys.
D723.2.p: The enchantment is broken when a chain is taken off the enchanted person's neck.

D723.2.1.p: The enchantment is broken when a string is removed from the enchanted person's neck.

D730.r: Icelandic: Hjálmthèrs saga ok Ölvis 510, 515; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 17.
D730.p: A general heading for breaking a spell by submitting to the will of the enchanted person, who must be obeyed.

D731.p: The enchantment is broken through the helper's obedience and kindness toward the enchanted person.

D732.r: Maynadier The Wife of Bath’s Tale; Taylor Washington Univ. Studies IV (2) (1917) 177 n. 9; Vogt MLN XXXVII 339; Coomaraswamy On the Loathly Bride (Speculum 1945, 391ff.); Krappe Philological Quarterly XXVI 352ff.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.—Ila (Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 404 No. 1; India: Thompson-Balys.
D732.p: A loathsome, ugly woman under a spell is freed when a man embraces her despite her ugliness.

D732.1.p: A girl under a spell is freed when someone carries her on their back.

D733.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 16; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 329 n. 188; S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 44, 87.
D733.p: A loathsome, ugly man under a spell is freed when a woman embraces him despite his ugliness.

D733.1.r: *C. A. Williams Oriental Affinities of the Legend of the Hairy Anchorite (U. of Illinois, 1925) 15; Gaster Oldest Stories 43.
D733.1.p: A hairy, beast-like man becomes a handsome human when a beautiful woman seduces him.

D733.2.p: A bridegroom who has been turned into a pig is restored to his original human form by his bride's love.

D733.3.p: The ugly, loathsome husband turns out to be a god who has taken a repulsive disguise.

D734.r: *BP I 9; Type 440; Fb “løse” II 517a.—English: Child I 298, II 502b, IV 454a, V 213a, 215b; Indonesian: Dixon 210; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 63, 321, 327.
D734.p: An animal is freed from its enchantment when it is allowed into a woman's bed.

D735.r: *Type 410; BP I 9, II 236 n., 271, 561; Wimberly 335ff.; Hartland Science 238 f., 241; Taylor Washington Univ. Studies IV (2) (1917) 177 n. 9; Klapper 112.—Irish myth: *Cross; English: Child I 306ff., Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII xxxv, *Boberg; France: Sébillot France I 244, III 291; India: *Thompson-Balys; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 247 No. 29; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis I 108.
D735.p: An enchanted person or animal is restored to human form when someone kisses it.

D735.1.r: *Type 402, 425, 433A, 440; Fb “kys”; Dickson 55 nn. 70, 72; Tobler 53; Zs. f. Vksk. XIV 245; Studien zur vgl. Littgsch. II 360, 472 n. 4.—English: Child V 486 s.v. “kiss”; Chile: Pino Saavedra 404f.; India: Cowell Jataka V 141; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 303; Africa (Kaffir): Theal 38.
D735.1.p: A beast is freed from its animal shape when a woman (or a man) kisses it.

D735.2.r: Tobler 69; **M. Waehler Die weisse Frau (Erfurt 1931); *Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 928.—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 298 No. 3, 307 No. 24, 314 No. 103, 322 No. 93, 325 No. 3, 329 No. 32; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3592.
D735.2.p: A woman in animal form is freed only after a man kisses her three times, each time she has become a different frightening animal.

D735.3.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 262 n. 2 (Demophon and Phyllis).
D735.3.p: A person enchanted into a tree is freed when the lover embraces the tree.

D735.4.p: An enchanted animal is freed when a person endures its embraces without showing fear.

D735.4.1.p: A girl frees her animal husband by letting him embrace her without fear.

D735.4.2.r: Africa (Suto): Hoffman Zs. f. Eingeborenen-Spr. XXII 172 No. 11.
D735.4.2.p: A son frees his animal father by accepting his caresses without fear.

D741.p: A monster is freed from its spell when a prince promises to marry the monster's mother, whom the prince mistakenly assumes is also a monster.

D741.1.r: Type 708. Cf. Hupa: Goddard UCal I 147.
D741.1.p: A monster is freed from its spell when his mother acknowledges him as her son.

D741.2.p: A monstrous child is freed from its enchantment when it is baptized.

D742.p: An enchanted person is freed when someone promises to marry them.

D743.p: A woman in the form of a bear is freed from her enchantment when a man has sexual intercourse with her.

D745.p: Enchanted animals are freed when they are fed.

D750.p: An enchantment is broken through the loyalty or faithfulness of other people.

D753.r: Type 518; Irish myth: Cross; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *422; Prussian: Plenzat 21; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 308*; Hungarian: Honti FFC LXXXI No. 4011.
D753.p: An enchantment is lifted when someone completes the tasks set for them.

D753.1.p: Enchanted brothers are freed when someone sews shirts for them.

D753.2.p: A spell is broken when the enchanted person is freed by a jug of tears that someone weeps over them, as a task of faithfulness. The enchanted one is restored when the jug is filled with tears.

D753.3.p: A spell is broken when someone carries out instructions they were given in a dream, and that completion frees the enchanted person.

D753.4.p: A spell is broken when someone climbs a mountain made of glass, completing the task that frees the enchanted person.

D754.p: A transformed or enchanted person is freed when someone faithfully serves them while they are in that changed form.

D755.p: A spouse who has been enchanted or away for a long time is freed when the faithful partner remains loyal and true to them.

D757.r: *Types 403, 450; *MacCulloch Childhood 45; Hartland Science 242.—Greek: Fox 122 (Thetis); English: Child V 499 s.v. “transformation, successive”; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 326.—See also, in general, references to D610.
D757.p: A spell is broken when someone keeps hold of the enchanted person through a series of changes into different forms, without letting go.

D758.p: A spell is broken when someone keeps silent for a set period of time, so the enchanted person is freed.

D758.1.r: *Type 400; cf. Type 307; *BP II 330; *Fb “tie” III 792a; Hartland Science 246.
D758.1.p: A spell is broken when someone stays silent for three nights, even under threat of punishment.

D758.2.p: A spell is broken when someone stays silent for a year or longer.

D759.p: A miscellaneous group of spells broken by the loyalty or faithfulness of other people, not covered by the more specific categories.

D759.1.r: Hartland Science 240; Tobler Epiphanie der Seele 74.
D759.1.p: A spell is broken when the disenchanter takes the key from the mouth of a woman who is in serpent form, at midnight, using their own mouth to do so. The note says three keys must be taken this way.

D759.2.p: A bird-shaped enchanted creature is freed when the queen squirts her own milk into the bird's beak.

D759.3.p: A spell is broken when a naked young woman, alone, makes a frightening midnight journey. The note says she must go on St. John's night between midnight and one o'clock, climb the castle walls, and enter the treasure chamber.

D759.4.p: A spell is broken if twelve men refuse to leave the castle for a year.

D759.5.p: A spell is broken when someone follows an enchanted woman through a lake and reaches the castle beneath the water.

D759.6.p: A spell is broken when maidens walk in procession carrying lighted candles.

D759.7.p: A spell is broken when a maiden sits at the head of the bed of an enchanted king on the morning of St. John's day.

D759.8.p: A snake is freed from its enchantment when it is allowed to wrap itself three times around a person's neck.

D759.9.p: Someone fails to break a spell on a sleeping princess because they do not watch her long enough.

D759.10.p: Three soldiers enter an enchanted manor and lose the power to free the princesses because curiosity overcomes them. The note says seven seven-year-old boys later break the spell and save the princess.

D760.p: A spell or enchantment is broken by some miscellaneous means that does not fit a more specific category of disenchantment.

D762.r: *Type 403, 450; Cosquin 166f., 170.—Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 61 No. 445A; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *422A; Russian: Andrejev No. *400B.
D762.p: An enchanted person who has fallen into a magic sleep is woken by the right person, and the enchantment ends. If the sleeper has not woken after the enchanted person appears three times, the enchantment must last.

D762.1.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanted person is made to speak.

D762.2.p: A person under magic sleep is wakened by a suitable agent, which ends the enchantment.

D763.r: Chauvin VI 88 No. 252.—Irish myth: Cross; Eskimo (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 28, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 325.
D763.p: The enchantment is broken by destroying the enchanter who cast it.

D763.1.r: Fb “løse” II 517a.—Penobscot (European borrowing): Speck JAFL XXVIII 58 No. 4; India: Thompson-Balys.
D763.1.p: The enchantment is broken when the one who cast it is killed and the person eats his heart.

D763.2.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanter is defeated in a one-on-one fight.

D764.p: An enchantment is broken when the enchanted person eats or drinks something specific.

D764.1.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanted person drinks the milk of a queen who has borne two sons.

D764.2.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanted person bites a certain twig.

D764.3.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanted person eats a certain salmon.

D764.4.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanted person eats an apple.

D764.5.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanted person eats whale meat.

D764.6.r: German: Grimm No. 122; Apulejus Golden Ass.
D764.6.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanted person eats a certain plant.

D764.7.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanted person refuses food for three days.

D764.8.p: The enchantment is broken when the enchanted person eats the head of a serpent.

D765.p: An enchantment is undone by reversing it, so that the magic is removed by an opposite action.

D765.1.p: The enchantment is ended by removing whatever caused it.

D765.1.1.p: The enchantment is ended by taking an enchanting pill out of the mouth.

D765.1.1.1.p: The enchantment is ended by taking a ring from under a dead girl's tongue, which frees her lover from loving her.

D765.1.2.r: (Cf. D582.)—Fb “løse” II 517a.—Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 59, 62 Nos. 435, 449; Missouri-French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.
D765.1.2.p: A spell is broken by removing the enchanting pin or thorn that was causing it.

D765.2.p: A spell is broken by untying the knot that was used to enchant someone.

D766.p: A spell is broken by using a liquid of some kind.

D766.1.r: Type 433B; Taylor Washington Univ. Studies IV (2) (1917) 176 n. 8; Wimberly 388; Child I 308, 338 n., II 505, III 505, V 39f.—India: *Thompson-Balys.
D766.1.p: A spell is broken by bathing or immersing the enchanted person in water.

D766.1.1.p: A spell is broken by bathing in water while a command is spoken over it.

D766.1.2.p: A spell is broken simply by touching water.

D766.1.3.p: A spell is broken by pouring water into the enchanted person's ear.

D766.2.r: (Cf. D712.4, D712.4.1).—*Type 516; *Rösch FFC LXXVII 138; *Fb “blod” IV 46b, 47a; Child I 337 n.; Penzer I 97; Wesselski Mönchslatein 148 No. 119.—Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 53 No. 400A*; India: *Thompson-Balys.
D766.2.p: A spell is broken by applying blood to the enchanted person or creature.

D766.2.1.p: A spell is broken by rubbing the enchanted one with pig's blood.

D766.3.p: A spell is broken by tears shed over or on the enchanted person.

D766.4.r: Wimberly 372; Type 433B and 507 (Danish forms); India: Thompson-Balys.
D766.4.p: A spell is broken by bathing the enchanted person in milk.

D771.p: A spell is broken by using some magic object.

D771.1.p: A spell is broken by burning a magic hair.

D771.2.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 219 No. 73; Greek Odyssey 10 line 394.
D771.2.p: A spell is broken by rubbing the enchanted one with a magic grease or ointment.

D771.3.p: A spell is broken by sprinkling or using a magic powder.

D771.4.p: A spell is broken by waving or using a magic wand.

D771.5.p: A spell is broken by drinking from a golden vessel.

D771.6.p: A spell is broken by taking a medicine.

D771.7.p: A spell is broken by using a rosary or scapular, a devotional object worn or held.

D771.8.p: A spell is broken, and the enchanted person transformed back, by means of a magic sword.

D771.9.p: A transformed person is restored to human form when consecrated rice is sprinkled on them.

D771.10.p: A transformed person is restored to human form by means of a ring.

D771.11.p: A transformed person is restored to human form by means of a flower.

D771.12.p: A transformed person is restored to human form by using a crystal ball.

D772.p: A transformed person is restored to human form when someone calls them by name.

D772.1.p: A transformed person is restored to human form when someone recognizes them.

D775.p: A transformed creature is restored to human form when it is fed, but only if the feeding is done contrary to the commands given for it.

D777.p: A transformed creature is restored to human form when a handkerchief is placed between its horns.

D777.1.p: A transformed creature is restored to human form when it is covered with a cloth.

D778.r: Chauvin V 236 No. 134; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 105.
D778.p: A transformed person is restored to human form when someone blows on them.

D778.1.p: A berry restores its enchanted state to normal when someone blows on it.

D778.2.p: A transformed person is restored to human form when medicine is blown onto them.

D781.p: A transformed person is restored to human form through the prayer or mass of the Pope.

D781.1.p: A transformed person is restored to human form by a blessing.

D782.r: Kittredge Gawain 205f., 216f.—Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 70 No. 535; Irish myth: Cross; German: Grimm No. 49, 56, 60, 76, 96.
D782.p: A transformed person is restored to human form through physical contact with someone or something.

D782.1.p: A transformed person is restored to human form when touched by a holy man.

D782.2.p: A transformed person is restored to human form when touching the earth.

D783.p: A transformed person is restored to human form when they are found after being lost.

D784.p: A transformed person is restored to human form when a fire is lit.

D785.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 330.
D785.p: A transformed person is restored to human form as the result of a contest of magic.

D785.1.p: A spell is broken when the hero wins a series of contests against seven demons.

D786.p: An enchantment is undone by playing music.

D786.1.r: Eskimo (Greenland): Holm 63; Africa (Swazi): Bourhill and Drake 212ff. No. 18.
D786.1.p: An enchantment is undone by singing a song.

D787.p: An enchantment is undone by drawing a circle around the enchanted person or thing.

D788.p: An enchantment is undone by making the sign of the cross.

D789.p: An enchantment is undone by some other means not listed under the more specific headings.

D789.1.p: An enchantment is undone by covering the enchanted person with the clothing of the one who frees them.

D789.2.p: An enchantment is undone by breaking a lamp.

D789.3.p: An enchantment is undone when the enchanted person sees their old home.

D789.3.1.p: A frog-woman is disenchanted when she sees water.

D789.4.p: An enchantment is undone when the enchanted person breaks a taboo.

D789.5.p: An enchantment is undone by throwing golden objects into water.

D789.6.r: South Africa: Bourhill and Drake 237ff. No. 20.
D789.6.p: An enchantment is undone by repeating a magic formula.

D789.6.1.p: An enchantment is undone by speaking the proper words.

D789.7.p: An enchantment is undone by shaking a certain tree.

D789.8.p: An enchanted castle, town, or its inhabitants is freed by digging it out of the ground.

D789.9.p: A girl frees her tiger-husband from enchantment by putting a garland around his neck and sprinkling sand and water over him.

D789.10.p: An enchantment is undone by ringing a bell.

D790.p: The conditions or circumstances that must accompany a disenchantment, such as timing or who performs it.

D791.r: For many of these combinations see Hartland Science 240, 244, 248.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3593.
D791.p: A disenchantment can happen only under one particular combination of time, place, and person.

D791.1.p: A spell is broken only when a specified length of time has passed. The enchantment ends automatically once that time is up.

D791.1.1.p: The enchantment ends when seven years have passed.

D791.1.2.p: The enchantment ends when a superhuman task is completed. The enchanted person appears in human form every seven years and adds one stitch to a smock; when the smock is finished, she will be freed.

D791.1.3.r: **Ranke Der Erlöser in der Wiege; Hartland Science 244f; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 80.
D791.1.3.p: The enchanted person can be freed by a child who is rocked in a cradle made from an oak sapling that has grown large.

D791.1.4.p: The enchantment ends when two hundred years have passed.

D791.1.5.p: The enchantment ends when nine hundred years have passed.

D791.1.6.p: The enchantment can end only at the close of seven hundred years.

D791.1.7.p: The enchantment ends at the crowing of the cock, which is at dawn.

D791.1.8.p: The enchantment ends at midnight, after an owl has hooted three times.

D791.2.p: The enchantment can be broken by only one particular person. No one else can free the enchanted being.

D791.2.1.p: A girl under enchantment can be freed only by her lover.

D791.2.2.p: The enchantment can be broken by the enchanted person's wife.

D791.2.2.1.p: The enchantment will be broken if the girl is allowed to marry the transformed man.

D791.3.p: The enchantment cannot be broken because the required conditions were not met.

D791.4.p: The enchantment is broken when someone finds the key to the enchanted castle.

D792.p: A transformed mother is freed when her child calls her.

D793.p: A disenchantment is made permanent so the transformed person cannot be changed back again.

D793.1.p: The disenchantment is made permanent by holding on to a hair of the transformed creature.

D793.2.p: The disenchantment is made permanent by burning the cast-off skin of the transformed creature.

D794.p: An enchanted person draws the attention of someone who can rescue them.

D794.1.r: South Africa: Bourhill and Drake 237ff. No. 20.
D794.1.p: An enchanted person draws the attention of the one who will rescue them by dancing. The dancing signals to the rescuer that the person is under a spell.

D795.p: A maiden is freed from enchantment, then abandoned, and later found again.

D796.p: Gods or divine beings take on their own true form while asleep.

D797.p: A person is restored from enchantment in front of a judge, and this proves that a witness is telling the truth. The restoration convinces the judge of the witness's honesty.

D798.p: A person is disenchanted by being passed between another person's legs.

D799.p: Disenchantment is brought about by means not covered by the more specific motifs in this group.

D799.1.p: Children who have been enchanted for a long time become old when the enchantment is lifted.

D799.2.p: An enchanted valley is disenchanted and rises up to the level of the land around it.

D799.3.p: When a disenchanted person is freed, their attendants are freed from enchantment automatically.

D800.r: *Toldo Studien zur vgl. Littgsch. VIII 60ff.; *Siuts 89ff.; *Penzer I 25ff., V 3 n 1, IX 142; *Tibbals “Elements of Magic in the Romance of William of Palerne” MPh I (1903) 355 ff.; *Easter A Study of Magic Elements in the Romans d’Aventure (Dissertation, Baltimore 1906).
D800.p: A general heading for objects that have magical powers.

D801.p: A magic object is owned by a particular person or being, who controls its use.

D801.1.p: A magic object belongs to a witch, sorcerer, or evil dwarf.

D803.p: A magic object is made by a god or other deity.

D803.1.p: Magic objects are made by God on the sixth day of creation.

D804.p: An object becomes magical when an unspeakable or secret name is written on it.

D805.p: A magic object may be used only when there is extreme need.

D806.p: A magic object works only if its instructions for use are followed exactly.

D806.1.p: A magic object works only when struck on the ground once. A second blow makes it useless.

D806.2.p: A magic charm or formula used carelessly or at the wrong time brings death to its owner's wife, children, and the owner himself.

D810.r: *BP I 361; *Aarne JSFO XXVII 1—96.—Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
D810.p: A magic object is received as a present from someone else.

D811.r: *Toldo IX 451ff.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Örvar-Odds saga 138—41, Boberg; Finnish: Kalevala rune 36; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “baguette”; Greek: Fox 40, *Grote I 88.
D811.p: A magic object is given to someone as a gift from a god. The object comes from a divine source and carries supernatural power.

D811.1.p: A magic object is given to someone as a gift from a goddess. It is a divine gift, like other gifts from a god, but the giver is female.

D811.2.p: A magic object falls down from the sky or heaven to the person who receives it. It arrives unexpectedly from above as a divine gift.

D811.2.1.p: A magic needle and thread fall from heaven in answer to someone's prayer. The sewing tools are the supernatural gift granted for praying.

D812.p: A magic object is given to someone by a supernatural being other than a god. The category covers many kinds of spirits, creatures and beings.

D812.1.r: BP I 361.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 15f.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 25, 50.
D812.1.p: A magic object is received as a gift from a saint, a holy person who has been made holy after death or is especially holy.

D812.2.p: A magic object is received as a gift from a demigod, a being who is part divine and part mortal.

D812.3.r: *Aarne MSFO XXV 39.—Irish myth: Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “baguette”; Hindu: Penzer IX 45 n. 1.
D812.3.p: A magic object is received as a gift from the devil. The object is supernatural and comes from the devil.

D812.4.r: *Aarne MSFO XXV 39; *Chauvin V 78 No. 22 n. 1.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 25; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 47, 211.
D812.4.p: A magic object is received as a gift from a ghost, the spirit of a dead person who has returned.

D812.4.1.p: A magic object is received from a dead person in the lower world, the realm of the dead below the earth.

D812.4.2.p: A magic object is acquired as a reward for burying a dead person. The ghost or dead person repays the burial with a supernatural gift.

D812.5.p: A magic object is received as a gift from a genie, a supernatural spirit of the kind that grants wishes or powers.

D812.5.1.p: A magic object is received from demons that live in a temple, the spirits said to dwell within a sacred building.

D812.6.p: A magic object is received as a gift from a witch or wizard, a person with magical powers.

D812.7.p: A magic object is received as a gift from a dragon king, a ruler of the dragons or of the watery realm.

D812.8.r: (Cf. D825.)—Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Baum”; BP II 544.—Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 40; India: Thompson-Balys.
D812.8.p: A magic object is received from a lady who appears in a dream. The gift is given to the dreamer during sleep.

D812.8.1.p: A magic object is received from a giantess who appears in a dream. The gift is given to the dreamer during sleep.

D812.8.2.p: A magic object is received from a man who appears in a dream. The gift is given to the dreamer during sleep.

D812.9.p: A magic object is received as a gift from a wild man, a savage or hairy forest-dwelling figure.

D812.10.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D812.10.p: A magic object is received as a gift from an angel, a heavenly messenger of God.

D812.10.0.1.p: An angel shows the hero where a magic object can be found. The object is then given to him as a gift from the angel.

D812.11.p: A giant gives the hero a magic object as a gift.

D812.12.p: A dwarf gives the hero a magic object as a gift.

D812.12.1.p: A dwarf gives the hero a magic sword, appearing to him in a dream.

D812.13.p: A magician gives the hero magic objects as gifts.

D812.14.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 849, II 210, 656.
D812.14.p: An ascetic, a person living in strict religious self-denial, gives the hero a magic object.

D812.15.p: A maiden-spirit, a female supernatural being, gives the hero a magic object.

D813.r: *Type 510.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “baguette”; Missouri French: Carrière.
D813.p: A fairy gives the hero a magic object as a gift.

D813.1.p: A river-nymph, a water spirit, gives the hero a magic object.

D813.1.1.r: (Cf. D878.1.)—Irish myth: *Cross; English: Wells 50 (Le Morte Arthur); Indo-Chinese: Scott Indo-Chinese 303.
D813.1.1.p: The Lady of the Lake gives the hero a magic sword.

D813.1.2.p: A spirit of a lake gives the hero a magic cauldron.
