D1292.p: A magic bird's nest is a nest with supernatural power, used as a magic object in a tale.

D1293.p: A color is used as a magic object or has supernatural power in a tale.

D1293.1.r: Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 300 No. 6; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Gaster Oldest Stories 69; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1293.1.p: The color red has supernatural power in a tale.

D1293.2.p: The color green has supernatural power in a tale.

D1293.3.p: The color white has supernatural power in a tale.

D1293.4.p: The color black has supernatural power in a tale.

D1294.p: A magic footprint, a mark left on the ground that has supernatural power or effect.

D1295.p: Incense that has magical power, such as smoke that works enchantments or drives away evil.

D1296.p: A sacred relic that works as a magic object, bringing supernatural help or protection.

D1297.p: A dye with magical properties, for example one that changes appearance or effects a transformation when applied.

D1298.p: Firewood that has magic power, such as wood that burns with supernatural effect.

D1299.p: A catch-all heading for magic objects that do not fit the other categories listed.

D1299.1.p: A magic sign, symbol or insignia that has supernatural power.

D1299.2.p: A magic grave or tomb that has supernatural power.

D1299.3.p: A magic cross that has supernatural power.

D1299.4.p: Cotton wool that has magic power.

D1299.5.p: A pair of spectacles that has magic power, such as letting the wearer see things hidden or unseen.

D1300.p: A magic object that gives a person supernatural wisdom or changes them in mind through its power.

D1300.1.p: A magic hat that grants its wearer supernatural wisdom.

D1300.2.p: A magic cap that grants its wearer supernatural wisdom.

D1300.3.r: (Cf. D926.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 49, Boberg.
D1300.3.p: A magic well whose water gives supernatural wisdom to those who drink or use it.

D1300.3.1.p: Streams of wisdom flow out of a magic well, giving knowledge to whoever gets near it.

D1300.4.p: A magic stone that grants supernatural wisdom.

D1300.5.p: A magic staff that grants supernatural wisdom.

D1300.6.p: A magic charm or amulet that grants supernatural wisdom.

D1300.7.p: A fox's heart that, when eaten or possessed, grants supernatural wisdom.

D1301.p: A magic object gives a person the ability to understand the speech of animals.

D1301.1.p: A piece of magic turf taken from a church roof teaches the person to understand animal languages.

D1301.2.r: (Cf. D1041.)—**Scott Thumb; Panzer Sigfrid 281 s.v. “Vogelsprache”.—Icelandic: Völsungasaga 45, Boberg.
D1301.2.p: Drinking blood gives the drinker the ability to understand animal languages.

D1301.3.p: A marvelous ruby gives the holder the ability to understand birds' speech.

D1301.4.p: Eating the head of a bird teaches the eater to understand animal languages.

D1302.p: A magic object teaches the person how to work magic.

D1302.1.p: A magic axe teaches the person how to work magic.

D1305.p: A magic object gives the power to foretell the future.

D1305.1.p: A drop of water from Paradise gives the power to foretell the future.

D1310.p: A magic object gives the holder supernatural knowledge of hidden or distant things.

D1310.1.p: A magic seat gives the sitter complete, all-knowing wisdom.

D1310.2.p: A drop from a magic cauldron gives supernatural knowledge to whoever gets it.

D1310.3.r: (Cf. D1123.)—Icelandic: Boberg; English: Child IV 376—80, V 275f.
D1310.3.p: A ship that has intelligence and can think or act knowingly.

D1310.4.p: A magic object shows how a distant person is faring.

D1310.4.1.p: A magic ring shows how another person is faring.

D1310.4.2.p: A magic plant bears fruit to show that the heroine is ready to marry.

D1310.4.3.p: A barley plant droops when the prince is in trouble, showing his distress.

D1310.5.p: A magic staff gives the holder supernatural information.

D1310.6.p: A magic charm gives the holder knowledge.

D1310.7.p: The singing of a wave gives supernatural information to the hearer.

D1310.8.p: A magic divan (couch or sofa) that can talk and move about and gives the person sitting on it supernatural information.

D1310.9.p: Magic water that gives the one who drinks or uses it supernatural knowledge.

D1310.10.p: A magic fruit that gives the one who eats it supernatural knowledge.

D1310.10.1.p: A magic apple that gives the one who eats it supernatural knowledge.

D1310.10.2.p: A magic fig that gives the one who eats it supernatural knowledge.

D1310.10.3.p: A magic grape that gives the one who eats it supernatural knowledge.

D1310.11.p: A magic nut that gives the one who eats it supernatural knowledge.

D1311.p: A magic object used to foretell the future or learn hidden things by divination.

D1311.1.p: A magic harp that, when struck, gives a divine answer or foretelling.

D1311.2.r: (Cf. D1163, D1323.1.)—*Type 709; *Böklen Sneewittchenstudien 70 (Leipzig, 1915); *MacCulloch Childhood 34ff.; *BP I 463; *Cox Cinderella 483.—Africa (Angola): Chatelain 29.
D1311.2.p: A magic mirror that answers questions put to it.

D1311.3.p: A fountain that serves as an oracle, giving answers or predictions.

D1311.3.1.p: A spring whose water gives omens or signs of what is to come.

D1311.3.1.1.p: Foretelling the future by looking into or observing water.

D1311.4.r: (Cf. D950.)—Irish: Plummer cliii, *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
D1311.4.p: A tree that serves as an oracle, giving answers or predictions.

D1311.4.0.1.r: (Cf. D953, D1254.2, D1311.15, D1314.2.)—Irish myth: Cross; Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 86; Tacitus Germania Ch. 10.
D1311.4.0.1.p: A magic twig from an oracular tree that gives divine answers or foretellings.

D1311.4.0.1.1.p: Seeing magic twigs lets a person know in advance what will happen during the day.

D1311.4.0.2.p: Two trees falling reveal the Savior's will about whether friends should be separated.

D1311.4.1.p: A tree is called upon to judge a dispute as an arbiter.

D1311.4.1.1.p: Ash (also called quicken or rowan) was used by druids for divination.

D1311.4.1.2.p: Hazel was used by druids for divination.

D1311.4.2.p: A talking tree gives prophecies or foretells the future when consulted.

D1311.5.r: (Cf. D1271.)—Norwegian: Dasent Popular Tales from the Norse (New York, 1888) 261.
D1311.5.p: A flame or fire that, when questioned, gives supernatural answers about the future or hidden matters.

D1311.6.p: Foretelling the future by observing the heavenly bodies such as the sun, moon, stars or clouds.

D1311.6.0.1.p: Telling the future by looking through or at an astrolabe, an instrument for measuring the positions of stars.

D1311.6.1.r: Africa (Tonga): Junod 266ff., (Swahili): Baker FL XXXVII 299f. No. 16.
D1311.6.1.p: The moon or stars, when asked, give answers to questions.

D1311.6.2.p: A magic cloud that answers questions put to it.

D1311.6.3.p: The sun, when asked, gives answers to questions.

D1311.6.4.r: (Cf. D1291.2.)—Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 828.
D1311.6.4.p: Foretelling events by reading the stars.

D1311.7.p: A statue or image that gives supernatural answers or prophecies when consulted.

D1311.7.1.p: An artificial head, made by man, that gives oracular answers.

D1311.7.2.p: A brass lion statue that gives oracular answers or prophecies.

D1311.8.r: (Cf. D992, D1610.5, M118.)—*Dickson 201 n. 97; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 46.
D1311.8.p: Telling the future by using a head or skull, which is consulted for answers.

D1311.8.1.p: A dog's head is used to foretell the future or answer questions.

D1311.8.2.p: A severed head, when consulted, foretells that a fight will take place.

D1311.9.r: (Cf. D985.1.)—Sulka of New Britain: Dixon 132 and 132 n. 2.
D1311.9.p: A coconut shell that answers yes-or-no questions: it sinks for yes and floats for no.

D1311.10.p: Telling the future by examining a part of an animal's body.

D1311.10.1.p: Foretelling the future by examining the shoulder-bone of a sheep.

D1311.10.2.p: Foretelling the future by examining the gall and liver of a pig.

D1311.11.p: A river that gives oracular answers or prophecies.

D1311.11.1.r: *Fb “tid” III 789b; *Lizbarski Am Urds-Brunnen IV 56.—England: Baughman; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 54 No. 460; Netherlands: Sinninghe FFC CXXXII 52 No. 1; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3495; Livonian: Loorits in FFC LXVI 45 No. 44f.; Estonian: Aarne in FFC XXV 136 No. 95.
D1311.11.1.p: A river announces that the time has come but not the man, and a man is thereby led to drown himself.

D1311.12.p: A bell that rings or sounds on its own to give supernatural answers or predictions.

D1311.12.1.p: A bell that sounds on its own to show which man has been chosen as pope.

D1311.13.p: A plant that is used to foretell the future or reveal hidden knowledge.

D1311.13.1.p: The mandrake plant is used as a magic device that foretells future events.

D1311.13.2.p: Common weeds are used to tell the future or learn hidden things.

D1311.14.p: A sacred or magic book is opened at random, and the passage the reader lands on is taken as a prophecy or answer.

D1311.15.p: A magic rod or wand that is used to foretell things or locate hidden matters.

D1311.15.1.p: A druid uses a magic yew rod to find where a woman has been taken by fairies to a hidden underground home.

D1311.16.r: (Cf. D931.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 89.
D1311.16.p: A stone that gives supernatural answers or signs when consulted.

D1311.16.0.1.p: A saint's blessing gives a stone the power to give oracular answers.

D1311.16.1.p: The number of screams from a stone reveals how many kings will descend from the man standing on it.

D1311.17.p: A magic weapon is used to foretell the outcome of events.

D1311.17.1.p: A magic spear gives a sign that its owner will win the battle.

D1311.17.2.p: A magic arrow is used to foretell the future.

D1311.17.3.p: A lance rings when struck against a shield, except when its owner is going to be defeated, in which case it stays silent.

D1311.18.p: A magic ring that gives supernatural answers or predictions.

D1311.19.p: Answers or omens are read from water, such as from its movements or reflections.

D1311.20.p: Pubic hair is used as a magic object that gives oracular answers.

D1311.21.p: A cup is used to foretell the future or reveal hidden things.

D1311.22.p: Answers or omens are read from the sound of the wind.

D1311.23.p: A magic chessboard is used to foretell the future or reveal hidden knowledge.

D1312.r: *Huet 94.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 297 n. 86b.; Africa (Bankon): Ittman 97.
D1312.p: A magic object gives advice or counsel to the person who owns or consults it.

D1312.1.p: A part of the body speaks and gives advice to its owner.

D1312.1.1.p: Excrement speaks and gives advice to the person it belongs to.

D1312.2.p: A magic bone speaks and gives advice to its owner.

D1312.3.p: A blade of grass that can speak gives advice.

D1312.4.p: A magic book gives advice to the person who consults it.

D1313.r: *BP I 434.—Irish myth: Cross; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 297 n. 86c.
D1313.p: A magic object shows the traveler which way to go.

D1313.1.r: Rolls ahead. (Cf. D1256.)—Type 425; Tegethoff 43; *Chauvin V 87 No. 27 n. 2, VII 98 No. 375 n. 3; *Kittredge Gawain 170 n. 2.—Irish myth: Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “boule”; India: Thompson-Balys; U.S. (Ozarks): Randolph Who Blowed Up the Church House (New York, 1953) 59.
D1313.1.p: A magic ball rolls ahead or otherwise shows the traveler the road to follow.

D1313.1.1.r: Rolls ahead. (Cf. D1184.1)—*Köhler-Bolte I 407; BP I 434; Fb “nøgle”.
D1313.1.1.p: A magic ball of thread unrolls and shows the traveler the road to take.

D1313.1.2.r: (Cf. D1031.2.) BP III 458f.; Hdwb. d. Märch. I 335a.
D1313.1.2.p: A magic cake rolls along and shows the traveler which road to take.

D1313.2.p: A hat is thrown into the air and the direction it falls shows the road to take.

D1313.3.p: A copper statue of a horseman turns and points out the correct road for travelers when its hand is struck.

D1313.4.p: A blinded trickster is guided by trees, which tell him where he is by answering when he asks their names.

D1313.5.p: A magic stick points out the road the traveler should follow.

D1313.5.1.p: A saint's staff serves as a skilled navigator guiding a ship at sea.

D1313.5.2.p: A reed is used as a means of finding direction.

D1313.6.p: A magic apple shows the traveler which road to take.

D1313.7.p: A magic flute shows the traveler which road to follow.

D1313.8.p: A magic knife with two edges points the right direction and bends downward when the way is wrong.

D1313.9.p: A charm used as medicine shows the traveler which direction to take.

D1313.10.p: A magic feather shows the traveler which road to follow.

D1313.11.p: A magic fountain shows a saint the road by moving out of its place.

D1313.12.r: Rolls ahead. (Cf. D1031.2.)—*Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Ariadnefaden” n. 12.
D1313.12.p: A magic cake shows the traveler which road to take.

D1313.13.p: A magic shoe shows the traveler which road to follow.

D1313.14.p: A magic thornbush shows the traveler which road to take.

D1313.15.p: A magic wheel rolls or turns to show the traveler which road to take.

D1313.16.p: A magic pillar of fire shows the traveler which direction to go.

D1314.r: Irish myth: Cross; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 70f. Nos 598—604; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Werner 197.
D1314.p: A magic object reveals the place a person desires to find or reach.

D1314.0.1.p: A magic object reveals the place where a person has been killed.

D1314.1.p: A magic arrow shows the place a person desires to find.

D1314.1.1.p: A magic arrow is shot to choose where to spend the night.

D1314.1.2.p: A magic arrow is shot to choose where to build a city.

D1314.1.3.r: Köhler-Bolte I 419, 554.—English: Child II 499; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Dixon 75f. n. 65.
D1314.1.3.p: A magic arrow is shot to choose where to look for a bride.

D1314.1.4.p: A magic arrow shows the place where a church is to be built.

D1314.1.5.p: An arrow is shot to choose the place of burial.

D1314.1.6.p: An arrow shot into the air lands in and reveals an iron pit.

D1314.1.7.p: An arrow is shot to learn the direction from which an attacking army is coming.

D1314.2.r: (Cf. D954, D1254, D1254.2.)—*Barrett and Besterman The Divining Rod (London 1926); Encyc. Religion and Ethics II 832a; Fb “finkelrut”, “skat”, “pilegren”; *Norlind Skattsägner 28.—Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 86; Eng., U.S.; *Baughman; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 77 No. 650.
D1314.2.p: A magic wand or twig locates hidden treasure.

D1314.2.1.r: S. A. Indian (Inca): Alexander Lat. Am. 249.
D1314.2.1.p: A divining rod sinks down at the place where a tribe is to settle.

D1314.2.2.p: A divining rod, a forked twig, magically shows where underground water lies.

D1314.2.3.p: A divining rod, a forked twig, points to the house where a thief lives.

D1314.2.4.p: A divining rod, a forked twig, points to the spot where an unmarried mother drowned her child.

D1314.2.5.p: A saint's staff turns into a tree, showing where a building should be put.

D1314.2.6.r: S. A. Indian (Inca): Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 317.
D1314.2.6.p: A golden staff stuck into the ground marks the spot where a city should be built.

D1314.3.p: A saint's bachall, a crozier or staff, uncovers gold in the ground.

D1314.4.p: A bell stays silent until it reaches the place where a saint is destined to settle.

D1314.4.0.1.p: A saint's bell lands at the place where a monastery is to be founded.

D1314.4.1.p: A bell rings to show where a well is located.

D1314.5.p: A hand-of-glory, a magic severed hand, shows where treasure is hidden.

D1314.6.p: A loaf of bread set floating on water stops directly above a drowned man's body.

D1314.7.r: (Cf. D965, D975.)—*Norlind Skattsägner 19ff.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3646.
D1314.7.p: A magic plant or flower shows where treasure lies hidden.

D1314.7.1.p: A mandrake, a magic root, shows where treasure lies hidden.

D1314.8.p: Jewels help the seeker find treasure.

D1314.9.p: A magic cloth leads its owner to lost horses.

D1314.10.p: A pillar of fire guides a person, for example to a church.

D1314.11.p: Seat-pillars thrown into the sea, together with a god's image, show where to settle.

D1314.12.p: A coffin lands at the place where the dead man is to be buried, and his son is to settle there.

D1314.12.1.p: A rope breaks when it reaches the proper burial place.

D1314.13.p: A star shows where a newborn hero is located.

D1314.13.1.p: A star in the sky shows the place where a newborn hero can be found, as the Star of Bethlehem did for the newborn child. A magic object points the way to the desired location.

D1314.14.p: Four impoverished men each receive a magic ball, and the balls show them where to dig.

D1314.15.p: A dried root, when planted, sprouts, and the spot where it grows shows a holy man where to build his dwelling.

D1315.p: A magic object helps find someone who has gone missing.

D1315.1.r: (Cf. D1314.1.ff.) S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 147.
D1315.1.p: A magic arrow flies to or points out where a lost person is, leading the searcher to them.

D1316.p: A magic object reveals the truth about a matter or person.

D1316.1.p: A magic stone reveals the truth when consulted.

D1316.2.r: (Cf. D1162.1.) India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 43ff. (Version B.)
D1316.2.p: A magic lamp lights up when someone speaks falsehood, showing that they are lying.

D1316.3.p: Spittle that can speak reveals the truth.

D1316.4.p: A magic ring lets its owner learn what another person is secretly thinking.

D1316.4.1.p: A magic ring shows the real character of the person wearing or possessing it, revealing their true nature.

D1316.4.2.p: Magic spectacles let the wearer read other people's thoughts.

D1316.5.r: *Köhler-Bolte I 383 n. 1, 511, 587; Sébillot RTP I 327, VII 356; *Zs. d. deutschen morgenland. Gesel. XL 549; Crooke FL XXII 183; *BP IV 147 n. 7 (Celtic): *Basset 1001 Contes II 258; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1316.5.p: A king whispers a secret into a hole in the ground, and a magic reed or tree growing from that hole later tells the secret aloud, betraying it.

D1316.5.1.p: A voice comes out of a tree and reveals the truth.

D1316.6.p: A magic goblet or cup shows whether a statement is true or false.

D1316.7.p: A magic sod of turf tells the truth: it turns its grassy side down for a lie and up for the truth.

D1316.8.p: A magic collar tests a speaker: it squeezes the throat (or hand or foot) when a lie is told, and falls to the ground when the truth is spoken.

D1316.9.p: A magic letter brought from an apostle ensures that the wearer will speak only the truth.

D1316.10.p: A pig is cooked, as if by magic, when a true story is told.

D1316.11.p: A sword turns against its owner when he speaks an untruth.

D1316.12.p: A magic root, when water is poured over it, reveals the truth about a matter.

D1316.13.p: A magic bird's tongue, used as a magic object, reveals the truth.

D1317.p: A magic object gives a warning when someone is in danger.

D1317.0.1.r: (Cf. D1317.4.)—*Penzer I 110, IV 228 n. 1, IX 143; Dickson 228 n.
D1317.0.1.p: A magic object gives warning by detecting poison in food or drink.

D1317.1.p: A person's buttocks serve as a magic watcher that warns of danger.

D1317.2.p: A magic gall-bladder gives warning of danger.

D1317.3.p: Magic swallow-skin gives warning of danger.

D1317.4.p: A magic bracelet warns when poison is present.

D1317.4.1.p: A voice in the wall that always tells the truth warns against poisoned food.

D1317.5.r: (Cf. D1076.)—Type 425; Tegethoff 34f.—Icelandic: *Boberg; English: Wells II (Horn Childe and Maiden Rimnild).
D1317.5.p: A magic ring gives a warning of danger.

D1317.5.1.r: (Cf. D1076, D1317.4, D1317.0.1.)—Kittredge Witchcraft III, 440 n. 58.
D1317.5.1.p: A magic ring warns its wearer when poison is present.

D1317.5.2.p: A magic ring wakes its wearer in the morning.

D1317.6.p: A magic sword gives a warning of danger.

D1317.6.1.p: A sword bursts in a son's hand when he is about to kill his father, warning him in time.

D1317.7.r: (Cf. D1213.)—French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 73; cf. Types 327A, 328.—Thompson River: Teit JAFL XXIX 320 No. 11.
D1317.7.p: A magic bell sounds an alarm to warn of danger.

D1317.8.p: Magic dice warn their master, a thief, when it is time to seek safety.

D1317.9.p: A statue gives a warning of danger.

D1317.9.1.p: A brass or copper statue at the city gates blows a trumpet when a stranger approaches.

D1317.10.p: A wagon refuses to move because a ghost is sitting in it, giving warning of the danger.

D1317.11.p: A bedstead warns its occupant of the danger of a snake.

D1317.12.r: (Cf. D931.) Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 300.
D1317.12.p: A magic stone warns its owner of danger, usually by changing in some visible way.

D1317.12.1.p: A magic stone bleeds for three days before a church is robbed, giving advance warning of the plundering.

D1317.13.p: A magic shield roars loudly when its bearer is about to be harmed, warning him.

D1317.14.p: Human bones give a warning when danger is near.

D1317.15.p: A golden cock on a tent crows or moves to warn of danger.

D1317.16.p: A magic spear gives a warning when danger is coming.

D1317.17.p: A knife sings as a warning that someone is trying to cheat or deceive its owner.

D1317.18.p: A magic drinking horn gives a warning, often of poison or danger in the drink.

D1317.19.p: A cloak gives a warning of danger to the person wearing it.

D1317.20.p: A tree gives a warning when danger threatens someone nearby.

D1317.21.p: The pillars of a house give a warning of danger.

D1317.22.r: (Cf. D1242.) Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen II 317, 321, III 300, Holm 45, Rink 147.
D1317.22.p: Water rages and churns when a would-be murderer's boat passes over it, exposing the plot.

D1318.p: A magic object reveals who is guilty of a crime or wrongdoing.

D1318.0.1.p: A magic object singles out the guilty man from among several suspects.

D1318.1.p: A stone reveals that a person is guilty.

D1318.1.1.p: A stone bursts open as a sign that a judgment against someone was unjust.

D1318.2.p: A dead fish reveals that a person is guilty.

D1318.2.1.r: The fish reveals that he has laughed at the foolishness of the judge who, while he punishes minor offences severely, is unable to see the capital crimes in his own household. (Cf. D1281.) *Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 216.—India: Thompson-Balys, *Penzer I 46ff., VII 254, IX 142.—Cf. Child I 241, II 501b, IV 452a, V 288b.
D1318.2.1.p: A severe sentence is passed for a small offence, and as the convicted man is led away, a dried fish is heard to laugh, showing the judgment was unjust.

D1318.3.p: Charms show that a person is guilty.

D1318.4.p: A magic seed shows that a person is guilty.

D1318.5.r: (Cf. D1003.) Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Blut”; Icelandic: Boberg.
D1318.5.p: Blood acts as a supernatural test that shows whether a person is guilty or innocent of a crime.

D1318.5.1.p: When a murderer touches the victim, blood flows from the murderer's finger, exposing him as the killer.

D1318.5.2.r: **Christensen (C. V.) Baareprøven (1900); Fb “blod” IV 47a; Knudsen (H.) En Baareprøve (Danske Studier 1932 69ff.); Von Künssberg Jahrb. f. historische Volksk. I (1925) 94, 120; Jobbé-Duval Essais de folklore juridique@2 (Paris, 1920); English: Child II 143, 146, 148, 153, IV 468a, *Baughman; North Carolina: Brown Coll. I 639; Jewish: Neuman.
D1318.5.2.p: A corpse starts bleeding when the murderer touches it, showing who did the killing.

D1318.5.3.p: Each drop of blood from an innocent person turns into a burning candle, proving the person's innocence.

D1318.5.4.r: Frazer Old Testament I 101; Fb “blod” IV 47ab; Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Blut”.
D1318.5.4.p: Blood speaks and reveals that a murder took place, exposing the killing.

D1318.5.5.p: Blood drops out of a stone to show that a girl is innocent of the accusation against her.

D1318.5.6.p: Blood bubbles up at the place where a murder was committed, marking the scene of the crime.

D1318.6.p: Divining bones, used for magical divination, reveal who is guilty of a crime.

D1318.7.p: Flesh, often of a dead or slain body, reveals who is guilty of a crime.

D1318.7.0.1.p: Flesh speaks and reveals that a murder took place.

D1318.7.1.p: The flesh of an animal reveals who is guilty of a crime, usually a theft.

D1318.7.1.1.p: Meat from a stolen animal will not cook and instead turns putrid, exposing the thief who ate or handled it.

D1318.7.1.2.p: Food gets stuck in the thief's throat, betraying him as the one who stole.

D1318.8.p: A magical cloth reveals who is guilty of a crime.

D1318.8.1.p: A magic cloth calls out and tells who is wearing it, exposing the thief who has it on.

D1318.9.p: A ring reveals guilt, showing a person's wrongdoing through the ring's supernatural behavior.

D1318.9.1.p: A ring breaks apart when its wearer's lover is found to be unfaithful.

D1318.10.p: A ship reveals guilt by behaving strangely in response to a guilty person aboard.

D1318.10.1.r: *BP IV 196f.; Fb “skib” III 242b.—English: Child V 484 s.v. “Jonah”; U. S.: Baughman.
D1318.10.1.p: A ship refuses to move while a guilty man is on board, exposing him.

D1318.11.p: A light, such as a supernatural glow, shows that a person is guilty.

D1318.11.1.p: A light shining over the place where a murder was committed reveals the guilt of the killer.

D1318.12.p: Magic vessels, such as pots or cups, reveal guilt by behaving strangely when a guilty person is near or involved.

D1318.12.1.p: Magic vessels burst open when someone has disobeyed, exposing the disobedience.

D1318.12.1.1.p: A poet uses a spell so that the ale vessels burst when a request for ale is refused, revealing the refusal.

D1318.13.p: A magic cauldron boils or reacts to show who is guilty.

D1318.14.p: A sack of gold holds on to any hand that is thrust into it, so a thief is caught.

D1318.15.p: A mill refuses to grind wheat that was stolen, so the theft is revealed.

D1318.16.p: The earth speaks and reveals that a murder has been committed.

D1318.17.p: A river rises up to drown people who tell lies.

D1318.18.p: Apples growing from a tree under which a murder took place have red centers, revealing the crime.

D1318.19.p: Manna, the miraculous food, reveals guilt, showing who has done wrong.

D1322.p: A magic object gives warning of an approaching death.

D1322.1.p: A saw used for making coffins makes sounds that announce a death.

D1322.1.1.r: (Cf. D1209.4.) North Carolina: Brown Collection I 640.
D1322.1.1.p: A hammer in a coffin maker's shop makes a noise to announce a death.

D1322.1.2.p: Boards for making coffins move by themselves, announcing a death.

D1322.2.r: (Cf. D1162.) North Carolina: Brown Collection I 641.
D1322.2.p: A light moving toward the cemetery is a sign that someone will die.

D1323.p: A magic object gives the power to see distant or hidden things.

D1323.1.r: Type 425; Tegethoff 32; **Róheim Spiegelzauber; *Liebrecht 85, 88; *BP III 366ff.; *Kittredge Witchcraft 503 n. 1; MacCulloch Childhood 36f.; *Chauvin VIII 191 No. 228; *Handwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 547—565; Fb “spejl” III 481a; *Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 202f.; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 232.—England, U.S., Wales: *Baughman; Irish: Beal XXI 323; Icelandic: *Boberg; Chinese: Werner 244, 331; Japanese: Anesaki 325; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 111 No. 39; S. A. Indian (Aztec): Alexander Lat. Am. 62; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 61 No. 12, (Vai): Ellis 200 No. 18, (Mpongwe): Nassau 15 No. 1.
D1323.1.p: A magic mirror lets its owner see distant or hidden things.

D1323.1.1.p: A magic mirror shows the face of whoever is about to die.

D1323.2.p: A magic vase lets its owner see distant or hidden things.

D1323.3.p: A magic window or pane that gives clairvoyance, letting the viewer see distant or hidden things. Thompson's note says there are twelve of them, each more powerful than the next.

D1323.4.p: A magic globe or sphere that shows everything happening on earth when its owner looks at the part of the globe where the events are.

D1323.4.1.p: A named magic sphere (Salvatio Romae) that shows a picture of the land, and through a magic bell reveals an uprising breaking out in any province.

D1323.5.p: A magic salve or ointment that, when applied, gives the user the power to see things at a distance or hidden from ordinary sight.

D1323.6.p: A magic soap that gives the user the power of clairvoyance, seeing things beyond ordinary sight.

D1323.7.r: Placed on head in order to see witches. (Cf. D934.)—Fb “græstørv”; *De Vries Acta Philologica Scandinavica III 106ff.
D1323.7.p: A piece of turf taken from a church roof that gives clairvoyance to the one who has it.

D1323.8.r: Placed in pocket in order to see witches. (Cf. D1278, G250.)—Fb. “kirkegaardsmuld”.
D1323.8.p: Soil from a churchyard, the ground around graves, that gives the holder the power of clairvoyance.

D1323.9.p: A magic tube that gives clairvoyance, letting the user see distant or hidden things by looking through it.

D1323.10.p: A hat that gives its wearer clairvoyance, the power to see distant or hidden things.

D1323.11.r: (Cf. D991.)—Modoc: Curtin Myths of the Modocs (Boston, 1912) 32.
D1323.11.p: A hair, presumably one that has magic properties, gives the one who has it the power of clairvoyance.

D1323.12.r: Marquesas: Handy 109, 118; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 528; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/420).
D1323.12.p: A person gains clairvoyance by looking into an object filled with water, seeing distant or hidden things in the water.

D1323.12.1.p: A woman whose lover is away looks into a spring each day; if she sees his shadow in the water, it means he is about to marry someone else.

D1323.13.p: A magic powder that gives the user clairvoyance, the power to see distant or hidden things.

D1323.14.p: A four-leaf clover that gives its holder clairvoyance, the power to see distant or hidden things.

D1323.15.p: A magic telescope that gives clairvoyance and shows distant events.

D1323.16.p: A magic feather that gives its holder clairvoyance, the power to see distant or hidden things.

D1323.17.p: A magic girdle, or belt, that gives its wearer clairvoyance, the power to see distant or hidden things.

D1323.18.p: A person gains clairvoyance through prayer, receiving the power to see distant or hidden things.

D1323.19.p: A lamp, by its flame, gives the person who looks into it a vision of God, the Most High.

D1324.p: A magic object that shows the rise and fall of the tides.

D1324.1.p: A magic bag swells full when the tide is high and becomes empty when the tide goes out, so it reveals the state of the tide.

D1324.1.1.p: A magic tub drips when the tide is high and stays watertight when the tide is low, serving as a tide indicator.

D1324.2.p: A magic bundle of sticks drips water to signal that the tide is rising.

D1325.p: A magic object reveals what will happen in the future of a person or family.

D1325.1.p: A magic book in which the destiny of a family is written can be read to learn what will happen to it.

D1326.p: A magic object delivers a verdict or judgment on a matter, acting as a supernatural judge.

D1326.1.p: Magic slippers signal whether a court's decision is approved or disapproved.

D1327.p: A magic object shows where fish or game animals can be found.

D1327.1.r: (Cf. D1092.) S. A. Indian (Mataco): Métraux MAFLS XL 132.
D1327.1.p: A magic arrow points the way to fish.

D1327.2.r: (Cf. D1268.) Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 494.
D1327.2.p: A magic doll is consulted to learn where to go hunting.

D1329.p: A miscellaneous magic object gives supernatural information that does not fit other categories.

D1329.1.p: Putting one's head under a saint's cloak reveals what rewards await in heaven.

D1330.p: A magic object causes a physical change in a person's body or condition.

D1331.p: A magic object alters a person's eyesight.

D1331.1.p: An object gives the person who possesses or uses it the power of magic sight, letting them see what ordinary people cannot.

D1331.1.1.r: (Cf. D971.2.) England, Wales: *Baughman; English: Child V 59, 286a.
D1331.1.1.p: By sowing hempseed one acquires magic sight.

D1331.1.2.p: A medicine gives the one who takes it magic sight.

D1331.1.3.p: A fan gives the one who uses it magic sight.

D1331.1.4.p: A stone gives the one who holds it magic sight.

D1331.1.5.p: A jewel gives the one who wears or holds it magic sight.

D1331.1.5.1.p: A sapphire (jewel) gives its owner magical sight, letting them see things ordinarily hidden or far away.

D1331.2.p: A magic object makes a person blind.

D1331.2.1.p: A magic spike blinds people by throwing out a light so strong it destroys their sight.

D1331.2.2.p: A magic salve or ointment causes blindness when applied or seen.

D1331.2.2.1.p: A magic salve from the underworld, the realm of the dead, causes blindness.

D1331.2.3.p: The Virgin Mary's shift (undergarment or robe) used as a battle banner blinds the opposing army.

D1331.2.5.p: Merely seeing a magic wheel causes blindness.

D1331.2.7.p: Dog's urine makes a tiger blind.

D1331.2.8.p: A magic storm blinds enemy troops.

D1331.3.p: A magic object both gives supernatural sight and causes blindness.

D1331.3.1.r: (Cf. D1244, D1323.5, D1331.2.2.) Put on left eye causes one to see all treasure of earth; on the right, makes blind. Chauvin V 146 No. 72.
D1331.3.1.p: A magic salve both gives supernatural sight and causes blindness.

D1331.3.2.p: A magic powder both gives supernatural sight and causes blindness.

D1331.3.3.p: Magic antimony (a dark eye cosmetic) rubbed on the hero's eyes lets him make distant or near things appear as close or far as he wishes.

D1331.4.p: A magic object makes the viewer's sight shift, so that things appear displaced or changed in where they are seen.

D1332.p: A magic object affects a person's hearing.

D1332.1.p: A magic object makes a person deaf.

D1332.1.1.p: A magic stone makes a person deaf.

D1332.1.2.p: The sound of a magic wheel makes a person deaf.

D1335.p: An object gives its holder magical strength.

D1335.1.r: (Cf. D1030.)—Fb “mad” II 525a, “styrke” III 630a.—Norse: Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 11; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 70 n. 2; Chinese: Graham; N. A. Indian (Thompson River): Hill-Tout BAAS LXIX 540.
D1335.1.p: A magic food gives the one who eats it supernatural strength.

D1335.1.1.p: A magic grain of rice gives the eater supernatural strength.

D1335.1.2.p: Eating the heart of an enemy gives the eater magical strength.

D1335.1.3.p: Eating the flesh of fighting animals gives the eater magical strength.

D1335.1.4.p: Manna, the miraculous food, gives magical strength.

D1335.2.r: (Cf. D1040.)—*Fb “styrke”.—Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII xxxiii, Boberg*; Korean: Zong in-Sob 167 No. 72.
D1335.2.p: A magic drink gives the one who drinks it supernatural strength.

D1335.2.1.r: (Cf. D1041.)—Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Blut”.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Finnish: Holmberg Finno-Ugric 5.

D1335.2.3.r: (Cf. D1043.)—Irish myth: Cross; Hindu: Keith 134; India: Thompson-Balys.

D1335.3.p: A magic iron glove gives its wearer strength.

D1335.4.r: (Cf. D1057.)—*Type 590; *Fb “bælte” IV 84a; A. Haberlandt Gurtel als Heiltum in Volkskunde (Otto Lauffer zum 60. Geburtstage [1934] 83—96); Von der Hagen Gesammtabenteuer I 455ff.—Icelandic: *Boberg.—N. A. Indian (Chippewyan [European borrowing]): Thompson CColl II 392, (Micmac): Rand 274, 369, (Passamaquoddy): Leland 31.
D1335.4.p: A magic belt gives its wearer strength.

D1335.5.p: A magic ring gives its wearer strength.

D1335.5.1.p: A magic ring gives its wearer remarkable sexual potency.

D1335.5.2.p: Solomon's power to rule his kingdom depends on a ring, and he drops it in water and loses it.

D1335.6.p: A magic dagger gives its holder strength.

D1335.7.p: A magic flask gives strength to whoever drinks from it.

D1335.8.r: (Cf. D1171.2.)—Norwegian: Dasent 281.—S. A. Indian (Kwakiutl): Boas and Hunt JE III 104 (certain wash-basin); cf. Haida: Swanton JE X 365.
D1335.8.p: Bathing in a magic cauldron gives the bather strength.

D1335.9.p: A magic axe that gives its holder supernatural strength.

D1335.10.p: A magic medicine or charm that gives its user supernatural strength.

D1335.11.p: A magic powder that gives its user supernatural strength.

D1335.12.p: A magic song that gives its singer or hearer supernatural strength.

D1335.13.p: A magic hammer that gives its holder supernatural strength.

D1335.14.p: A magic staff that strengthens the person who carries it.

D1335.15.p: A magic apple that gives strength to whoever eats it.

D1335.16.p: A picture or image of a lion that gives its owner supernatural strength.

D1335.17.p: A garment that gives whoever wears it supernatural strength.

D1336.p: A magic object that makes a person weak or drains their strength.

D1336.1.p: A magic sword that makes its victim or holder weak.

D1336.2.p: Magic food that makes whoever eats it weak.

D1336.2.1.p: A magic apple that makes whoever eats it weak.

D1336.3.p: Magic music that makes listeners weak.

D1336.4.p: A magic shield that makes its victim weak.

D1336.5.p: A saint's bell that makes those who hear it weak.

D1336.6.p: Magic fire that makes those near it weak.

D1336.7.p: A magic drink that makes whoever drinks it weak.

D1336.8.p: A magic spell that makes its victim weak.

D1336.9.p: Spells cast by druids or poets that bind or hold a person fast.

D1336.10.p: A magic bow is taken from its owner, and as a result the owner loses all his strength.

D1337.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Japanese: Ikeda.
D1337.p: A magic object changes a person's appearance, making them either beautiful or ugly.

D1337.1.p: A magic object makes a person beautiful.

D1337.1.1.p: A charm gives its wearer or user magical beauty.

D1337.1.2.r: (Cf. D1242.1.)—Fb “livets vand” II 439b.—Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1337.1.2.p: Magic water makes a person beautiful.

D1337.1.3.p: Magic milk makes a person beautiful; in one version, milk touching an ugly girl turns her beautiful.

D1337.1.3.1.p: Washing hair in buffalo milk makes it grow unusually long.

D1337.1.4.p: Bathing in a magic cauldron makes a person beautiful.

D1337.1.5.r: (Cf. D1084.)—Also gives ugliness at will. Icelandic: Ritterhaus 227f. No. 54.
D1337.1.5.p: A magic spear makes a person beautiful.

D1337.1.6.p: A person is made beautiful by being touched with a saint's spittle.

D1337.1.7.p: A magic needle turns a plain room into a beautiful one.

D1337.1.8.p: A magic liquid makes a person beautiful.

D1337.1.8.1.p: Rose water gives magical beauty to whoever uses it.

D1337.1.9.p: A magic wand makes a person beautiful.

D1337.1.10.p: A magic apple makes a person beautiful.

D1337.1.11.p: Playing a magic flute makes a person beautiful.

D1337.1.12.p: A magic jewel makes its wearer beautiful.

D1337.2.p: A magic object makes a person ugly.

D1337.2.1.p: Magic leaves turn a white bird black.

D1337.2.2.p: Magic herbs make a person hideous.

D1337.2.3.p: A magic object made of dragon's breath makes a person hideously ugly.

D1337.2.4.p: Magic water makes a person ugly.

D1337.2.5.p: A magic skin makes the person wearing it look ugly.

D1338.p: A magic object makes a person young again.

D1338.0.1.p: A magic object slows down aging so the person stays young longer.

D1338.1.p: A magic drink makes a person young again.

D1338.1.1.r: (Cf. D925, D926, D927, D1341.1.) Water from certain fountain rejuvenates.—**Hopkins JAOS XXVI 1—67, 411—415; Penzer Ocean IV 145; DeCock Studien 16ff.; *Fb “ungdom” III 979b.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “fontaine”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 11; U.S.: *Baughman; Greek: Rohde Der griechische Roman 222; Japanese: Ikeda.—Alexander Lat. Am. 20 n. 6, 349.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 284 n. 50a.
D1338.1.1.p: A fountain whose water restores youth to anyone who drinks or bathes in it.

D1338.1.1.1.p: A magic lake that makes people young again.

D1338.1.2.r: (Cf. D1242.1.)—Type 551; *BP II 394ff.; *Wünsche Die Sagen vom Lebensbaum und Lebenswasser (Leipzig, 1905); *Dh II 154; *Chauvin VI 73f. Nos. 239, 202.
D1338.1.2.p: Water that restores youth when drunk.

D1338.1.3.p: Magic blood that makes a person young again.

D1338.2.r: (Cf. D965.)—*Chauvin VI 74 No. 239.—Babylonian: Gilgamesh-epos XI 282ff. (eaten by serpent); Gaster Oldest Stories 51.
D1338.2.p: A person is made young again by a plant.

D1338.2.1.p: A person is made young again by drinking or using the juice of a magic plant.

D1338.2.2.p: A magic root that gives eternal youth.

D1338.3.r: (Cf. D981.)—*Chauvin VI 74 No. 239; BP II 147.—India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer VI 216.
D1338.3.p: A person is made young again by eating a fruit.

D1338.3.1.p: A person is made young again by eating apples, specifically golden apples of youth.

D1338.3.2.p: A magic peach makes the eater immune to aging.

D1338.3.3.p: A person is made young again by eating the fruit of a magic tree.

D1338.3.3.1.p: Eating the fruit of a magic tree adds a year to a person's life.

D1338.4.p: A person is made young again by bathing in magic milk.

D1338.5.p: A magic ring restores a person to youth, making an old person young again.

D1338.6.p: A person is made young again by being put through a magic mill, which grinds away age.

D1338.7.r: Fb “ungdom” III 979b; Hartland Science 196f.—Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 181, *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
D1338.7.p: A land where people are kept from growing old, so its inhabitants stay young.

D1338.8.p: A magic oil rubbed on a person makes them young again.

D1338.9.p: Magic honey restores a person to youth when they eat or are anointed with it.

D1338.10.p: A magic tub or bath restores an old person to youth when they enter it.

D1338.11.p: Magic manure dust restores a person to youth.

D1338.12.p: A magic feather restores a person to youth.

D1338.13.p: Magic rice restores a person to youth when eaten or used.

D1341.p: A magic object causes a person to become old suddenly.

D1341.0.1.p: A magic well turns a person's hair gray.

D1341.1.p: A magic fountain makes a person grow old.

D1341.2.p: A magic cloak makes the person who wears it old.

D1341.3.p: A magic ointment, when applied, makes a person old.

D1341.4.p: A magic feather brings old age to a person by supernatural means.

D1342.p: A magic object gives a person good health.

D1342.1.p: A magic ring gives the wearer good health.

D1342.2.p: A magic apple gives a person good health.

D1342.3.p: Magic wood gives a person good health.

D1342.4.p: A magic wand gives a person good health.

D1342.5.p: An amulet that keeps its wearer healthy and free from sickness.

D1343.p: A magic object that gives its possessor a special skill or ability.

D1343.1.p: Magic oars that give the rower skill, so the boat moves well no matter who uses them.

D1344.p: A magic object that makes its owner impossible to wound or kill.

D1344.1.r: (Cf. D1076.)—*Kittredge Witchcraft 111, 440 n. 52; *Fb “ring” III 60b.—English: Child I 189f., Wells 9 (King Horn), II (Horn Childe and Maiden Rimnild); Icelandic: Boberg.
D1344.1.p: A magic ring that makes the wearer invulnerable to injury.

D1344.2.p: A magic drug or potion that makes the person who takes it invulnerable.

D1344.2.1.p: A magic drug that makes the drinker immune to fire and iron, so neither flame nor iron weapons can harm them.

D1344.3.p: An amulet that makes the wearer invulnerable.

D1344.4.r: (Cf. D1273.)—De Cock Studien 161; Irish myth: Cross.
D1344.4.p: A written charm or magic inscription that makes the bearer invulnerable.

D1344.5.r: (Cf. D1244.)—Greek: Roscher Lexikon I 24 s.v. “Achilleus”; Boberg.
D1344.5.p: A magic ointment or salve that, rubbed on the body, makes the person invulnerable.

D1344.6.p: A tunic once worn by a saint that makes whoever wears it invulnerable.

D1344.7.p: A girdle or belt once worn by a saint that makes the wearer invulnerable.

D1344.8.p: A hood or cowl once worn by a saint that makes the wearer invulnerable.

D1344.8.1.r: Eskimo (Greenland): Holm 17, Rasmussen II 70, III 304, Rink 344.
D1344.8.1.p: An ordinary hood that makes the wearer invulnerable.

D1344.9.r: (Cf. D1052.)—Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen II 210, III 105, 117, 153.
D1344.9.p: A magic garment that makes the wearer invulnerable.

D1344.9.1.r: (Cf. D1056.)—*Fb “skjorte” III 268a; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 1712; Icelandic: *Boberg; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 187.
D1344.9.1.p: A magic shirt that gives the wearer invulnerability.

D1344.9.2.p: Magic trousers that make the wearer invulnerable.

D1344.10.p: A magic mandrake root that gives its possessor invulnerability.

D1344.11.p: A magic sword that gives its wielder invulnerability.

D1344.12.p: Blood smeared over the body makes the person invulnerable.

D1344.13.p: A magic golden helmet makes whoever wears it impossible to wound or kill.

D1345.p: A magic object that makes the one who has it live a very long life.

D1345.1.p: Water from a serpent gives the one who drinks it a very long life.

D1345.2.p: A magic statue of a dragon gives the one who owns or touches it a very long life.

D1346.p: A magic object that makes the one who has it live forever.

D1346.1.r: (Cf. D1040.)—Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 31, 54; Greek: Grote I 219; Jewish: Neuman; Hindu: Keith 41, Penzer III 253f.; Chinese: Giles 316.
D1346.1.p: A magic drink that makes the one who drinks it immortal.

D1346.1.1.p: The water of life is destroyed so that no one can become immortal, since living forever would become wearisome.

D1346.1.2.p: A nectar that grants immortality to whoever drinks it.

D1346.2.p: A fountain whose water grants immortality to those who drink or bathe in it.

D1346.3.r: (Cf. D1030.)—**G. Dumézil Le festin d’Immortalité (Paris, 1924)—Irish myth: *Cross.
D1346.3.p: A food that makes the one who eats it immortal.

D1346.3.1.p: A magic honey that makes the one who eats it immortal.

D1346.4.r: (Cf. D950.)—Jewish: Neuman; Persian: Carnoy 281; S. A. Indian (Tiatinagua): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 449.
D1346.4.p: A tree whose fruit or parts grant immortality.

D1346.5.r: (Cf. D965.)—Babylonian: Spence 158, 160, 178; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 215.
D1346.5.p: A plant that grants immortality to whoever uses it.

D1346.6.r: (Cf. D981.)—Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer VI 216.
D1346.6.p: A fruit that makes the one who eats it immortal.

D1346.6.1.p: A magic peach that makes the one who eats it immortal.

D1346.6.2.p: An apple that makes the one who eats it immortal.

D1346.7.p: A pill that makes the one who swallows it immortal.

D1346.8.p: A magic ointment that makes the one who is anointed with it immortal; the body is burned at night and anointed with it by day.

D1346.8.1.p: An oil that makes the one who is anointed with it immortal.

D1346.9.p: A magic sword that makes the one who has it immortal.

D1346.10.p: Magic water, when sprinkled on a person, makes them immortal and unable to die.

D1346.11.p: A medicine given to someone makes them immortal and unable to die.

D1346.12.p: Incense, when burned or used, makes a person immortal.

D1346.13.p: Eating filth, such as dirt or excrement, makes a person immortal.

D1346.14.p: A magic cup, when drunk from, makes the drinker immortal.

D1347.p: A magic object causes a person or animal to become fertile and able to bear offspring.

D1347.1.p: A magic apple makes a person fertile and able to have children.

D1347.2.p: Blood is used as a cure for a woman who cannot conceive.

D1347.3.p: A magic medicine turns a sterile person into one who can have children.

D1347.3.1.p: Magic pills ensure that a woman gives birth to twin sons.

D1347.4.p: A magic statue makes a person fertile and able to have children.

D1347.5.r: (Cf. D1032.1.)—Jewish: Neuman; S. A. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 169.
D1347.5.p: Eating a magic fish causes a person to become fertile.

D1347.6.p: Eating a hare's stomach causes a person to become fertile.

D1349.p: A magic object produces various other physical changes in people or things.

D1349.1.p: A magic object makes a person immune to hunger and thirst.

D1349.1.2.p: A magic perfume makes the wearer immune to hunger and thirst.

D1349.1.3.p: Magic milk makes the drinker immune to hunger and thirst.

D1349.1.4.p: A magic belt makes the wearer immune to hunger.

D1349.1.5.p: Two magic sweets: one quenches thirst and the other satisfies hunger.

D1349.1.6.p: A very small amount of food, through magic, leaves a person fully satisfied and free from hunger and thirst.

D1349.1.6.1.p: Licking a single drop of blood from a magic object satisfies hunger.

D1349.2.p: A magic object makes its possessor immune to aging, so they do not grow old.

D1349.2.1.p: Eating a magic peach makes a person immune to old age.

D1349.2.2.p: Washing oneself in a magic bowl makes a person immune to old age.

D1349.2.3.p: Eating a magic apple makes a person immune to old age.

D1349.3.p: A magic stone turns ordinary water into wine.

D1349.4.p: A magic jewel makes whoever owns it grow fat.

D1350.p: A magic object changes a person's temperament or character.

D1351.p: A magic object makes a person calm and peaceful.

D1351.1.p: A saint's staff (bachall) makes a person peaceful.

D1351.2.p: A magic branch brings peace, so that fighting stops when it is shaken.

D1351.3.p: A magic veil turns enmity between people into peaceful feelings.

D1351.4.p: A charm makes the inhabitants of a city become cowardly and fearful.

D1352.p: A magic object has an effect on a person before they are born, influencing their nature while still in the womb.

D1352.1.p: A magic net has an effect on a person before they are born.

D1353.p: A magic object makes a person foolish.

D1353.1.p: Magic rain makes everyone it falls on act foolishly.

D1354.p: A magic object makes a person kind and gentle.

D1355.p: A magic object that produces love in whoever it affects.

D1355.0.1.p: A magic spear causes the person it touches or is aimed at to become lovesick, pining with desire.

D1355.1.p: Music that has the magical power to make a listener fall in love.

D1355.1.1.p: A song with the magical power to make the hearer fall in love.

D1355.1.2.r: (Cf. D1224.)—English: Child I 47; N. A. Indian (Arikara): Dorsey CI XVII 85 No. 25, 90 No. 27.
D1355.1.2.p: A magic pipe whose music makes the listener fall in love.

D1355.1.3.p: A magic horn whose sound makes the hearer fall in love.

D1355.2.p: A magic drink or potion that causes a person to fall in love with the one who gives it.

D1355.2.1.p: Water blessed by a saint that acts as a love potion when drunk or used.

D1355.2.1.1.p: Baptismal water, used in baptism, that works as a love potion.

D1355.2.1.2.p: Magic water that arouses sexual desire in the person who drinks or is touched by it.

D1355.2.2.p: Blood used as a love potion, causing the drinker to fall in love.

D1355.2.2.1.p: The blood of a wounded centaur used as a love potion.

D1355.2.3.p: Semen placed in a love potion to make the drinker fall in love.

D1355.3.r: (Cf. D1274.)—Kittredge Witchcraft 30, 111, 382 n. 52, 440 nn. 61—70 passim.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; *English: Child I 57; India: *Thompson-Balys, Penzer I 137f.; Am. Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 198 No. 34.
D1355.3.p: A charm or spell, often performed with objects, meant to draw a desired lover to the person who works it.

D1355.3.1.p: A love charm made from seed mixed with blood.

D1355.3.2.p: A love charm in which an animal figure pierced with pins is used to win a lover.

D1355.3.3.p: A love charm in which fruit pierced with pins is used to win a lover.

D1355.3.4.p: Entrails of a live pigeon hung above the house door bring the desired lover to the spot.

D1355.3.5.p: Boiling a lock of the lover's hair draws him to his sweetheart.

D1355.3.6.p: A burning candle stuck with pins makes the lover come to the one who lit it.

D1355.3.7.p: A person burns salt while saying a charm to bring the lover to the spot.

D1355.3.8.p: A person burns dragonsblood (a resin from a plant) and recites a charm so that a lover is drawn to the spot.

D1355.4.r: (Cf. D1076.)—*Kittredge Witchcraft 109, 436ff. nn. 38—48 passim; Fb “ring” III 60b.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
D1355.4.p: A magic ring causes the person who receives or wears it to fall in love.

D1355.5.r: (Cf. D991.)—Wesselski Märchen 196; Frazer Golden Bough III 270.—N. A. Indian (Thompson River): Teit MAFLS VI 73 No. 23, (Shuswap): Teit JE II 708 No. 34 (in the last two named references, the hair is a woman’s pubic hair); India: Thompson-Balys.

D1355.6.p: Soil from a churchyard grave produces love; a girl takes three handfuls and passes it over a churn.

D1355.7.r: (Cf. D981.1.)—*Fb “æble” III 1135a.—English: Child I 364; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
D1355.7.p: An apple causes love in the person who eats it or is given it.

D1355.8.p: An olive branch keeps a husband faithful, and the wife is to beat him with it.

D1355.9.p: A magic belt causes love in the person who wears it or is involved with it.

D1355.10.p: Consecrated bread (blessed bread used in religious rites) produces love in the person who eats or is given it.

D1355.10.1.p: Consecrated bread is kept in the mouth and then fed to a toad, and this produces love.

D1355.11.r: (Cf. D1050.)—Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 274.
D1355.11.p: Magic clothing causes love in the person who wears it or is given it.

D1355.11.1.r: (Cf. D1065.4.)—N. A. Indian (Arapaho): Dorsey and Kroeber FM V 15 No. 6.
D1355.11.1.p: Magic moccasins (soft leather shoes) cause love.

D1355.12.p: Magic nuts, when eaten, cause love.

D1355.13.p: A love-spot is a mark on the body that makes a man irresistible to any woman who sees it.

D1355.13.1.p: A charm placed on the cheeks of an old woman (hag) causes love.

D1355.14.p: Eating a magic fruit arouses sexual desire.

D1355.17.p: A bath in herbs causes love in the person who bathes.

D1355.18.p: A love charm made of spoken words causes love.

D1355.18.1.p: Word charms woven into clothing cause love in the wearer.

D1355.19.p: Magic writings are used to make a person fall in love. The writings act as a love-producing magic object.

D1355.20.p: A green stone makes women fall in love with whoever possesses it.

D1355.21.p: Magic grass makes a girl fall in love with whoever she lies down with, when she sleeps on it.

D1355.21.1.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 28.
D1355.21.1.p: A love charm is made from a tuber, which is a type of magic grass that produces love when a girl sleeps on it.

D1355.22.p: A magic plant that causes love in whoever comes in contact with it or uses it.

D1355.23.p: A magic feather that produces love in the person it is used on.

D1358.2.p: A magic spell makes the person who is affected by it courageous.

D1358.3.p: A magic crystal makes its owner courageous.

D1359.2.p: A magic object makes a person feel grief and mourn.

D1359.3.p: A magic object makes a person feel joy.

D1359.3.1.2.p: A magic musical branch soothes those who listen to it.

D1359.3.1.3.p: Grief is driven away by the sound of a bell attached to a magic fairy dog.

D1359.3.2.p: Eating a magic pig brings happiness.

D1359.3.3.p: The fruit of a magic tree is exhilarating, lifting the spirits of whoever eats it.

D1359.3.4.p: A stone blessed by a saint drives away sorrow.

D1359.4.p: A magic food makes a person drunk and then sober again.

D1359.5.p: A magic sign ensures that warriors will not flee from battle.

D1359.6.p: A magic object destroys a person's pride.

D1500.1.10.4.p: Grain that has been consecrated is used as a remedy for illness.

D1500.1.11.p: A magic drink heals the person who drinks it.

D1500.1.12.1.p: A magic statue of a brazen serpent cures disease.

D1500.1.13.p: Something that belonged to a saint, such as a personal item, cures disease.

D1500.1.13.1.p: A saint's girdle, or belt, works as a magic cure for illness.

D1500.1.13.2.p: A saint's cowl (hooded garment) has magical power to cure illness when used or touched.

D1500.1.13.3.p: A saint's bell has the power to cure disease.

D1500.1.13.4.r: (Cf. D1277.) *Loomis White Magic 105; Irish: Plummer clxxv, Cross.
D1500.1.13.4.p: A saint's bachall (a staff or crozier) serves as a healing remedy.

D1500.1.14.p: A saint's mallet has the power to cure disease.

D1500.1.15.p: A magic ring has the power to heal illness.

D1500.1.15.2.p: A ring made from a coffin hinge works as a cure for illness.

D1500.1.16.p: A magic bottle has the power to heal illness.

D1500.1.17.p: A magic weapon has the power to cure disease.

D1500.1.17.1.p: A magic sword has the power to cure disease.

D1500.1.18.3.p: Holy water serves as a remedy for illness.

D1500.1.18.4.p: A lake with magical power to heal illness.

D1500.1.18.5.p: Water collected from a bullaun (a hollowed-out stone basin) serves as a remedy for illness.

D1500.1.18.6.p: A river with magical power to heal illness.

D1500.1.19.r: (Cf. D1244.) Type 611; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1500.1.19.p: A magic salve or ointment that heals illness.

D1500.1.19.1.p: A magic salve, rubbed on, instantly restores feet that have been cut off and reattaches them to the body.

D1500.1.19.2.p: A healing oil obtained from saints or from sacred places cures illness.

D1500.1.20.p: A magic powder that cures disease.

D1500.1.21.p: A magic wand that heals sickness when waved or used.

D1500.1.22.p: A magic book whose contents cure disease.

D1500.1.23.r: (Cf. D1273.) Kittredge Witchcraft 31f., 387f. nn. 75; Icelandic: *Boberg; Irish myth: *Cross; England, Wales, U.S.: *Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1500.1.23.p: A magic charm or spell that cures disease when recited or used.

D1500.1.24.p: A magic song that cures illness when sung.

D1500.1.26.p: Pieces of a gallows (gibbet) used as a cure for illness.

D1500.1.32.p: A magic comb that cures illness.

D1500.1.33.4.p: The hide of a sheep or goat serves as a cure for illness.

D1500.1.34.p: Magic writings have the power to heal illness.

D1500.1.35.r: (Cf. D1056.1.) S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 182.

D1500.1.36.p: A person's sweat is used as medicine.

D1500.1.38.p: A magic mountain has the power to heal illness.

D1500.2.p: A magic object protects a person from getting sick.

D1500.2.1.r: (Cf. D1213, V221.) Irish: Plummer clxxvi, Cross.
D1500.2.1.p: A saint's bell protects against disease.

D1500.2.2.r: (Cf. D1273.) Kittredge Witchcraft 40, *396 n. 145, 146; England: Baughman.
D1500.2.2.p: A charm protects a person against sickness.

D1500.2.3.p: A magic picture protects against disease.

D1500.2.5.p: Eating a magic pig prevents disease.

D1500.2.6.p: A magic girdle protects its wearer from disease.

D1500.2.7.p: A magic tree bears fruit that protects against disease.

D1500.2.8.p: Eating a snake's liver prevents disease.

D1500.3.2.p: A disease is transferred into a saint's bell, which holds the illness.

D1500.4.2.p: A magic breath causes disease in those who receive it.

D1500.4.3.1.p: A magic tank, or water container, causes disease.

D1500.4.5.p: Gloves thrown after a ship cause disease.

D1500.4.7.p: A magic bed causes disease in whoever lies on it.

D1501.p: A magic object helps a woman during pregnancy and childbirth.

D1501.1.r: (Cf. D1273.) Kittredge Witchcraft 32, 388 n. 89; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1501.1.p: Charms keep a woman from being barren or from miscarrying.

D1501.1.1.p: Druids use mistletoe to prevent a woman from being barren.

D1501.2.r: (Cf. D1273.) Kittredge Witchcraft 32, 388 n. 88; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 296, *Boberg.
D1501.2.p: Charms make childbirth easy and painless.

D1501.3.p: A magic plant makes childbirth easy.

D1501.7.p: Certain leaves help a woman in childbirth.

D1501.8.p: A medicine causes a woman to bear twins.

D1502.2.2.p: A charm is used to cure toothache.

D1502.2.3.p: A magic object cures scrofula, a tuberculosis-like swelling of the neck glands.

D1502.2.3.1.r: (Cf. D1278.) Kittredge Witchcraft 461 n. 22; England: Baughman.

D1503.p: A magic object has the power to heal wounds.

D1503.2.p: Magic pigskin heals wounds when applied.

D1503.17.p: A pair of magic gloves heals a wound.

D1505.1.p: A magic herb or herbs, when applied, restores a person's sight.

D1506.1.p: Spittle restores hearing to the deaf.

D1512.p: A magic object cures ulcers or sores.

D1514.p: A magic object relieves pain or suffering.

D1514.2.p: A magic girdle, or belt, relieves pain.

D1514.3.p: A charm is used to cure pain.

D1518.4.1.p: A magic plant heals a broken bone.
