D1658.1.4.r: (Cf. D1146.) Type 480; *Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 63 (to Gonzenbach No. 13).
D1658.1.4.p: Doors that keep slamming are grateful when they are fastened shut.

D1658.1.5.r: (Cf. D950, D1610.2.0.1.) *Type 480, 510; *BP I 208ff., 227; Fb “træ” III 867b; Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Baum”.
D1658.1.5.p: An apple tree that is grateful when someone shakes it.

D1658.1.5.1.p: A tree that is grateful when its boughs are trimmed.

D1658.1.5.2.p: A tree is grateful to someone who pours milk on its roots, and repays the kindness. Under apple-tree tales, the tree is grateful for being shaken, so this is a variant where the favor is milk.

D1658.1.6.p: A river is grateful to someone who gives it color, and repays the kindness.

D1658.2.p: Heading for the different types of objects that show gratitude by repaying kindness, such as a stove, carpets, or a plant.

D1658.2.1.p: A stove that is grateful to the person who treats it well and repays that kindness.

D1658.2.2.p: Carpets that are grateful to whoever treats them kindly and repay that kindness.

D1658.2.3.p: A plant that is grateful to the person who cares for it and repays that kindness.

D1658.3.p: Heading for the kinds of help that grateful objects give the people who were kind to them.

D1658.3.1.p: A grateful object gives advice to the person it is repaying.

D1658.3.2.p: A grateful object helps its helper choose the correct casket from several.

D1658.3.3.p: A grateful object gives gifts to a helper who has been kind to it.

D1658.3.4.p: A grateful object helps a person who is fleeing or escaping from pursuers.

D1661.p: A magic object that is destroyed cannot be replaced or made again.

D1661.1.p: A talking statue that is destroyed cannot be replaced for thirty thousand years.

D1662.p: A magic object is activated simply by being stroked or rubbed.

D1662.1.r: (Cf. D1076.) *Type 560; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “bague”; India: *Thompson-Balys.
D1662.1.p: A magic ring that works when it is stroked or rubbed.

D1662.1.1.p: A magic ring that works when the sun's rays flash on its gem.

D1662.2.p: A magic lamp that works when it is stroked or rubbed.

D1662.3.r: (Cf. D1070.) French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule.
D1662.3.p: A magic diamond that works when it is pressed.

D1663.p: A magic object that works in opposite ways depending on how it is used.

D1663.1.r: (Cf. D1254.1, D1402.10.) MacCulloch Childhood 205; N. A. Indian (Bella Coola): Boas JE I 54, (Chilcotin): Farrand JE II 44 No. 30.
D1663.1.p: Magic wands that have opposite powers: one end kills and the other end brings back to life.

D1663.1.1.p: A magic club can both kill and bring back to life, depending on which end is used. It is a wand that works in opposite ways.

D1663.2.p: A magic ointment heals the left cheek but does nothing for the right cheek. The same remedy works in opposite ways on the two sides.

D1663.3.p: A magic well has two sides: on one it kills, and on the other it protects against disease.

D1663.4.p: Two magic fountains have opposite effects: one poisons and one cures. The poisoning water tastes sweet and comes from a bronze vessel, while the curing water tastes bitter and comes from an iron vessel.

D1663.5.p: A magic well rises or sinks to show whether a person will live a long or short life.

D1663.6.p: A magic tree gives money to the good brother and poisonous animals to the bad brother.

D1664.r: (Cf. D961.) *BP II 232; Köhler-Bolte I 215f.—N. A. Indian (Tsimshian): Boas RBAE XXXI 182.
D1664.p: A magic garden blooms in winter, so it has flowers even in the cold season when no ordinary garden would.

D1665.r: (Cf. D1030, D1359.4.) Irish: Plummer clxxxv, *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 824, 930.
D1665.p: Food tastes like whatever delicacy one wishes for, though it is really something plainer.

D1665.1.p: A magic drink tastes like whatever alcoholic liquor one desires.

D1665.2.p: A magic cow gives milk that tastes of honey, intoxicating wine, and the satisfaction of good food.

D1665.3.p: A magic fruit can taste like any flavor one wishes for.

D1665.4.p: Manna, the miraculous food, tastes bitter to non-Jews (gentiles).

D1666.r: (Cf. D1081, D1564.7, F833.) Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 65, Cross.
D1666.p: A magic sword strikes a blow but leaves no wound or mark behind it.

D1667.p: A magic garden grows to full maturity at once, instead of slowly over time.

D1667.1.p: A magic tree instantly produces leaves, flowers, and fruit all at the same time.

D1667.2.p: Magic acorns grow into full-sized oaks immediately.

D1667.3.p: A magic rice plant produces a million-fold harvest and ripens in a single night.

D1667.4.p: A garden that has not bloomed for twelve years blooms again as soon as a girl steps into it.

D1668.p: A magic tree always bears fruit, never going without.

D1671.p: Silver in a chain becomes brighter or grows larger when put in fire.

D1672.p: A fire that cannot be put out by any ordinary means. It keeps burning indefinitely as a magic property of an object or place.

D1672.0.1.r: (Cf. D1271.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
D1672.0.1.p: A magic fire that keeps burning for seven years without going out.

D1672.1.p: A flaming shield that cannot be quenched or extinguished.

D1672.2.p: A bush that burns itself without being consumed by the fire.

D1673.p: A magic staff or stick that sprouts leaves and flowers, growing into something living.

D1673.1.p: A tree grows from a stick that a saint has used and then thrown away.

D1674.r: (Cf. D1080, V220.) *Loomis White Magic 105; Irish: Plummer clxxxv, *Cross.
D1674.p: Iron that has been blessed by a saint cannot wound anyone.

D1675.p: A garden wall that no one can jump over, no matter how skilled.

D1676.p: A mill that will not grind grain on Sunday, stopping of its own accord.

D1676.1.p: Manna, the miraculous food, does not fall on the Sabbath day.

D1677.p: A mill stops working when a saint is mistreated.

D1678.p: A magic book that, once used, forces the person who used it to do evil.

D1681.p: A charm or spell that fails to work if it is not spoken exactly right.

D1682.p: A magic jewel so heavy that it outweighs many heavy objects placed against it on a scale.

D1683.p: A hearth that an angel has cleaned always stays free of ashes.

D1684.p: A dye that a saint has blessed colors animals and trees.

D1685.p: The buried body of a saint performs signs and miracles.

D1686.p: A magic object goes away and comes back when given a set formula of command.

D1687.p: An object becomes magically heavy, too heavy to move.

D1688.p: A marvelous post that wears away at the top rather than rotting from the bottom.

D1691.p: A magic power that makes a heavy object weigh so little it can be carried or lifted easily.

D1691.1.p: A holy person carries an enormous load with ease because of the magic suspension of its weight.

D1692.p: A magic cloak (and sometimes a shirt) that automatically fits anyone, whatever their size.

D1693.p: A magic rod that swallows up other rods, so that they disappear into it.

D1694.r: (See D2086.1.) Icelandic: Göngu-Hrólfs saga 354, Bósa saga p. lxvi, *Boberg.
D1694.p: A magic sword that cannot be made dull by any magic, so it stays sharp.

D1700.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft passim; Fb “kunst” II 331; Penzer VIII 36ff., 46ff., 79, 100n.; E. E. Evans-Prichard Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande (Oxford, 1937); M. Summers Witchcraft and Black Magic (London, 1946); *Arne Runeberg Witches, Demons and Fertility Magic (Helsinki, 1947); *E. M. Butler Ritual Magic (Cambridge, Eng., 1949); Loomis White Magic; *Tibbals Elements of Magic in the Romance of William of Palerne (MPh I (1903) 355ff.); *Easter A Study of Magic Elements in the Romans d’Aventure (Dissertation, Baltimore 1906).—Estonian: *Loorits Grundzüge; Japanese: Anesaki 274.
D1700.p: A general heading for supernatural powers that people, beings or objects may possess or display.

D1710.r: (Cf. D800.) Hdwb. d. Märchens II “Gegenzauber”; Irish myth: *Cross.
D1710.p: General heading for who possesses magic powers and how those powers are held or used.

D1711.r: (Cf. D1721.) *Type 325; Dickson 121 n. 64; *Finnur Jónsson “Um galdra, seieth, seiethmenn og völur,” thyjár ritgjörethir (København, 1892) 5—28; *Seligmann 6f.; *Penzer IV 39 n. 1, 46ff.; *Fb “klog mand” II 187; Malone PMLA XLIII 400.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 299, *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 57ff. Nos. 128—159; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 50ff. Nos. 90—119; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 162.
D1711.p: A person who has magic powers and works magic; a magician or sorcerer.

D1711.0.1.p: A young person learning magic under a master magician.

D1711.0.2.p: A magician keeps his magic power hidden in a tumor or growth on his back.

D1711.0.3.p: The ways in which a person can become a magician.

D1711.1.p: A figure from the Bible is portrayed as a magician.

D1711.1.1.r: **G. Weil Biblische Legenden der Musselmänner (Frankfurt, 1845); *C. C. MacCown Journal of the Palestine Oriental Society II (1922) 1—24; **C. Singer Salomosagen in Deutschland (Zs. f. deutsches Altertum XXXV (1891) 177ff.); *E. A. W. Budge The Queen of Sheba (London, 1922); *M. D. Conway Solomon and Solomonic Literature (Chicago, 1900); St. John D. Seymour Tales of King Solomon (Oxford, 1924); *H. A. Winkler Salomo und die Karina: eine orientalische Legende von der Bezwingung einer Kindbettdämonin (Stuttgart, 1931); *Fb “Salomon” III 146b; Jewish: Neuman.
D1711.1.1.p: King Solomon is portrayed as the greatest master of magicians.

D1711.1.2.p: Esau is portrayed as a magician.

D1711.1.3.p: Balaam is portrayed as the master of magicians.

D1711.2.r: **D. Comparetti Virgilio nel medio evo@2 (Florence, 1896) (Eng. trans. by E. F. M. Benecke, London, 1895); *Chauvin VIII 188ff. No. 228; *Penzer I 24 n. 1; *C. G. Leland Unpublished Legends of Virgil (London, 1899); *Otto Söhring Romanische Forschungen XII (1900) 580ff.; *Hertel Verzauberte Oertlichkeiten; J. D. Bruce MPh X (1913) 511ff.; **John W. Spargo Virgil the Necromancer (Cambridge, Mass., 1934).
D1711.2.p: The Roman poet Virgil is portrayed as a magician.

D1711.3.p: The sun is portrayed as a magician.

D1711.4.p: A druid is portrayed as a magician.

D1711.5.p: A fairy is portrayed as a magician.

D1711.6.p: A god or demigod is portrayed as a magician.

D1711.6.1.r: Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 45ff., 296; Herrmann Saxo Gr. II 239ff., *Boberg.
D1711.6.1.p: The Norse god Odin is portrayed as a magician who possesses magic powers.

D1711.6.2.p: The god of healing, Aesculapius, is portrayed as a magician who possesses magic powers.

D1711.7.p: A king is portrayed as a magician who possesses magic powers.

D1711.7.1.p: A pharaoh, the ruler of ancient Egypt, is portrayed as a magician with magic powers.

D1711.8.p: A man of great physical strength is portrayed as a magician who possesses magic powers.

D1711.9.p: People with dark hair and a bowed (hooked) nose are portrayed as magicians who possess magic powers.

D1711.10.p: The people of a certain place are portrayed as magicians who possess magic powers.

D1711.10.1.p: The Finns are portrayed as magicians who possess magic powers.

D1711.10.2.p: The people of Gestrikland, a province in Sweden, are portrayed as magicians who possess magic powers.

D1711.10.3.p: The Egyptians are portrayed as magicians who possess magic powers.

D1711.10.4.p: The people of Palmyra, an ancient city in Syria, are portrayed as magicians who possess magic powers.

D1711.10.5.p: The Ammonites, an ancient people, are portrayed as magicians who possess magic powers.

D1711.10.6.p: The Amalekites, an ancient people, are portrayed as magicians who possess magic powers.

D1711.11.p: A whole family is portrayed as having magic powers, with magic passed down among its members.

D1711.11.1.p: The family of Balaam, a seer in the Bible, is portrayed as a family of magicians.

D1711.12.p: People who arrive on a ship carrying sickness are accused of being magicians who caused the illness.

D1711.13.p: Reptile-men cure snake bites and can call together snakes or mice and lead them away anywhere.

D1712.r: (Cf. M301.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 383ff. nn. 61, 62; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 299, *Boberg; England: Baughman; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 138 No. 104; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 48; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 349; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 254; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 57 No. 2, 139 No. 13, (Congo): Weeks 202 No. 1.
D1712.p: A soothsayer, a person who foretells the future or reveals hidden things through divination or an oracle, possesses magic powers.

D1712.0.1.p: A soothsayer who is also a magician, using astrology to foretell events.

D1712.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3667; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1712.1.p: A soothsayer who foretells the future or finds hidden things by using various methods of divination.

D1712.2.p: A blind man is gifted with the power to foretell the future or reveal hidden things, acting as a soothsayer.

D1712.3.p: A person has the magic ability to interpret dreams and explain what they mean.

D1713.r: (Cf. P426.2.) **Loomis White Magic; *Plummer passim; Dickson 121 n. 66; Penzer VI 201ff., VII 73, 113f.; *Barry JAFL XXVIII 195; **Toldo Studien zur vgl. Littgsch. I-IX passim; Günter; Irish: *Cross, Beal. XXI 328, O’Suilleabhain 85; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys (D1711.14, D1711.16.); Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 210, 286. See V220 for cross-references concerning magic powers of saints.
D1713.p: A hermit, saint, or yogi has magic power, which comes from his holy and ascetic way of life.

D1714.p: A person who is free of sin has magic power.

D1714.1.p: A chaste woman has magic power, which comes from her purity.

D1714.1.1.p: A chaste maiden praying is rescued when she vanishes from the embrace of a man trying to rape her.

D1715.r: *Type 960; BP II 531; Krappe Science 216—217.—Icelandic: Völsunga saga ch. 33 (31).
D1715.p: The words a dying man speaks have magic power and come true.

D1715.1.p: A dying person's last wish comes true by magic, for example by the person being reborn in a new form.

D1715.2.p: A dying peasant summons a greedy bishop to his funeral by magic words, and the bishop dies on hearing the message.

D1715.3.p: A dying man orders a cloud to carry a message to his wife.

D1716.p: A person who is infirm or disabled has magic power.

D1716.1.p: A person who is an idiot or fool has magic power.

D1716.2.p: A lame person has magic power.

D1716.3.p: A sterile (infertile) woman has magic power.

D1717.1.p: A monstrous child has magic power.

D1718.p: Magic power is held in a particular object or place rather than in the person.

D1718.1.p: Magic power is held in a stick and in water.

D1719.p: Miscellaneous cases of how magic powers are possessed.

D1719.1.r: (Cf. H1573.3.) Type 325.—Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 327 n. 182; Eskimo (Greenland): Thalbitzer 7, Rasmussen II 334; S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 139, (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII 3 484.
D1719.1.p: Two magicians compete to see who has the greater magic power.

D1719.1.1.p: A magic contest in which a druid and a saint try to outdo each other with their powers.

D1719.1.2.p: A magic contest in which a druid and a fairy being try to outdo each other with their powers.

D1719.1.3.p: A magic contest between a magician and a giant: the magician makes a dog's tail crooked, the giant straightens it, and this back-and-forth goes on endlessly.

D1719.1.4.p: A contest in which a carpenter and his son each race wooden horses they have made.

D1719.2.r: (Cf. F567.) Dickson 120 n. 62; *Handwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 968f.
D1719.2.p: A wild man possesses magical wisdom or knowledge.

D1719.3.p: A member of a superhuman race has magic power.

D1719.4.p: A companion with extraordinary qualities has magical wisdom or knowledge.

D1719.6.p: The holy cross has magic power.

D1719.8.p: A man has magic servants who plow his fields for him; each day he swallows them and keeps their existence secret.

D1719.9.p: Someone's magic power works only at a certain time.

D1719.9.1.p: Someone's magic power works only at night.

D1719.9.2.p: Someone's magic power works only at Passover.

D1719.10.p: Someone's magic power works only under certain conditions.

D1719.10.1.p: Someone's magic power works only while the magician's feet are touching the ground.

D1719.11.p: The world has only a limited supply of magic.

D1719.11.1.p: Only ten measures of magic were allotted to the world.

D1720.r: (Cf. D810.) Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 461, Rasmussen II 222, III 111.
D1720.p: How a person comes to acquire magic powers.

D1720.1.r: Fb “ønske” III 1179a; Irish myth: Cross; Italian: Rotunda, Basile Pentamerone I No. 3; India: *Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 453, Holm 25.
D1720.1.p: A man is given the power to make wishes come true.

D1720.1.1.p: The devil grants a man the power of wishing, so that whatever he wishes for comes to pass.

D1720.2.p: A man receives a divine 'possession' that makes him a diviner, someone able to foretell or reveal hidden things.

D1721.r: *Type 325; *Chauvin II 151 No. 11; *Fb. “sorte skole” III 469a.—Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 49, 296; English: Wells 43 (Arthour and Merlin); Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 49 No. 87; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 383.
D1721.p: A person acquires magic power by receiving it from a magician.

D1721.0.1.r: (Cf. D1052.) N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 131 No. 20.
D1721.0.1.p: A person gains magic power simply by putting on a magician's clothes.

D1721.0.2.p: A person secretly obtains magic power from the friends of a magician, without the magician giving it directly.

D1721.1.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 45, 399 n. 175; Dickson 213 n. 145.—Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 47 No. 325*A.
D1721.1.p: A person acquires magic power from the devil.

D1721.1.1.p: A person learns magic arts in hell, usually from the devil or his servants.

D1721.1.2.p: A person acquires magic power from a demon.

D1721.1.3.p: A spirit gives a man the power to exorcise, that is, drive out, the spirit from any person it has possessed.

D1721.1.4.p: A person acquires magic power from a rakshasi, a female demon or ogress of Indian lore.

D1721.2.p: A person gains magic power by eating fish that have fed on the flesh of a dead magician.

D1721.3.p: A magician blows magic into the ears of his disciples to pass on his power to them.

D1721.4.p: A magician's disciples gain magic power by drinking the magician's urine.

D1721.5.p: A magician's disciples gain magic power by eating magic iron.

D1721.6.p: A magician's disciples acquire magic powers through study and learning rather than by any other means.

D1722.r: (Cf. D1713, V223.4.1.) Irish: Plummer clxxxv, Cross.
D1722.p: A person gains magic power from a saint.

D1722.1.p: A person gains magic power from a prophet.

D1723.r: Type 403; Irish myth: Cross; Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 251; Italian: Basile Pentamerone. I No. 3, Rotunda.
D1723.p: A person gains magic power from a fairy.

D1724.r: Death as godfather. (Cf. D1725.1.) *Type 332; *BP I 377ff.—Italian Novella: Rotunda.
D1724.p: A person gains magic power from Death personified.

D1725.p: A person obtains magic power from angels.

D1725.1.p: A person gains magical power from the Angel of Death. This is a way of acquiring supernatural abilities through an angel linked to death.

D1726.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Grote I 105; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1726.p: A person receives magical power from a god. The god grants the ability as a gift.

D1726.0.1.p: A person learns the art of foretelling the future from a god. The knowledge of divination comes directly from the deity.

D1726.1.p: A person receives magical power from a celestial maiden, a heavenly female being. She grants the power to the mortal.

D1726.2.p: A person receives magical power from a stone idol, a carved stone image of a deity. The power comes through the statue.

D1727.r: Icelandic: Bárdar saga Snæfellsáss ch. 2 (ed. Vigfússon 1860) 2, Boberg.
D1727.p: A person learns magic from a giant who raises them as a foster-child. The giant's magical knowledge passes to the foster child.

D1728.p: A person receives magical power from a superhuman race, a being of a kind beyond ordinary humans. The power is given by these beings.

D1731.r: Dickson 188; Jewish: Neuman; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 58; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 134.
D1731.p: A person receives magical power while dreaming. The ability comes to them in a dream.

D1731.1.r: (Cf. D1275.) See story of Caedmon in Bede’s Ecclesiastical History, as well as numerous biblical stories of “inspiration”; *Kittredge Witchcraft 222, 529 n. 89.—Pawnee: Dorsey CI LIX 241ff. Nos. 77—116 passim.
D1731.1.p: A person learns a song in a dream, and the song carries magical power. The knowledge comes through the dream.

D1731.2.p: A person sees wonders or marvels in a dream, which give them knowledge or power.

D1731.2.1.p: A person sees a fairy in a dream, and this vision brings them magical knowledge or power.

D1731.2.2.p: In a dream or vision, a person sees that all of nature is made of food. The vision reveals this strange truth.

D1731.3.p: A person dreams of a contest in which rocks are thrown, and the dream gives them magical power or knowledge.

D1732.p: A person gains magical power through meditation, quiet contemplation focused on a spiritual goal.

D1733.p: Certain actions or deeds cause a person to gain magical power. The power is acquired by performing these acts.

D1733.1.p: A person gains magical power by jumping into fire.

D1733.2.p: A person gains magical power by crawling through the ear of a magic horse.

D1733.3.p: A person gains magical power through ascetic practices, which are severe self-denial and bodily discipline.

D1733.3.1.r: (Cf. G224.16, P623.) Kittredge Witchcraft 128, 450f. nn. 26—27 passim; Irish myth: *Cross; England: Baughman.
D1733.3.1.p: A person gains magical power by fasting, going without food.

D1733.3.1.1.p: Oracular twigs, used for divination, only work if the person using them has fasted beforehand.

D1733.4.p: A person gains magic power simply by sitting in a particular seat or chair.

D1733.5.p: A person acquires magic power by fainting or falling into a swoon.

D1733.6.p: A person acquires magic power by singing magic songs.

D1734.p: A person gains magic power by rubbing something, such as an object or charm.

D1734.1.p: A person gains magic power by rubbing a talisman or charm.

D1735.p: A person acquires magic power by swallowing something.

D1735.1.p: A person gains magic power by swallowing a straw.

D1735.2.p: A person gains the ability to read or speak a language by swallowing written characters.

D1735.3.p: A person gains magic power by swallowing a magic drink.

D1735.4.p: A person gains magic knowledge and witchcraft by eating part of a dead man's body, specifically his father's corpse.

D1736.p: A person gains magic power as a reward for great piety or religious devotion.

D1736.1.p: A person gains magic power by making a sacrifice.

D1737.p: Magic power is passed down to a person by inheritance from a relative.

D1737.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 93.
D1737.1.p: A person inherits magic power from his or her mother.

D1738.p: A person gains magic power by studying magic arts.

D1739.p: A miscellaneous way of acquiring magic power that does not fit the other categories.

D1739.1.p: A person gains magic power by overhearing spirits talking.

D1739.2.p: A person gains magic power from a voice from heaven.

D1740.p: A person loses the magic power they had.

D1741.p: A person's magic powers are taken away or lost.

D1741.1.p: A magic power is lost while the magic-user is asleep.

D1741.2.p: A magic power is lost when the magic-user loses blood.

D1741.2.1.r: (Cf. G271.4.4., G273.6.) Kittredge Witchcraft 47, *399f. nn. 190, 191; *Fb “blod” IV 47b.
D1741.2.1.p: Drawing a witch's blood cancels her spells.

D1741.3.p: A magic spell is broken when the enchanted person keeps silent under punishment.

D1741.4.p: Magic powers stop working when the person using or affected by them does not believe in them.

D1741.5.p: A magic-user loses his or her power by being frightened.

D1741.6.p: Magic power is lost as a result of incest.

D1741.7.p: A saint causes a magic-user to lose his or her magic power.

D1741.8.p: A sorcerer loses his magic power when his teeth are knocked out.

D1741.9.p: A conjurer loses his magic power after eating magic food.

D1745.p: A magic power is made ineffective, so it has no effect.

D1745.1.p: A magic power does not work on men born on a certain day.

D1745.2.p: Magic power is made ineffective by pious deeds.

D1749.p: Miscellaneous other ways in which magic power is lost.

D1749.1.p: A sorceress loses her magic power when one of her transformed husbands seizes and swallows her.

D1749.2.p: A woman loses her magic power when she loses her simplicity and humility.

D1750.p: Other characteristics of how magic power behaves or is possessed.

D1751.p: Magic power passes from one body to another.

D1760.p: Ways of acquiring or producing magic power.

D1761.r: **Riklin Wuncherfüllung und Symbolik in Märchen. (1908); *Fb “ønske” III 1178a.—Irish myth: *Cross; German: Grimm Nos. 50, 76; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Seneca: Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 122 No. 19; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 151.
D1761.p: Magic results are produced simply by wishing for them.

D1761.0.1.p: A wisher receives unlimited wishes, so whatever is asked for is granted without end.

D1761.0.2.r: *Types 750A, 1173*, 1951*; *BP II 491; *Loomis White Magic 124, 130; Irish myth: Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1761.0.2.p: Wishes are granted, but only a fixed number of them come true.

D1761.0.2.1.p: A man is allowed as many wishes as he can say in a single breath, so the trick is to repeat them all before breathing out.

D1761.0.2.2.p: Only one wish is granted, so the wisher must choose carefully.

D1761.1.p: A wish is made by means of the stars, which carry it or grant it.

D1761.1.1.p: A wish is made upon seeing a shooting star, which makes it come true.

D1765.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Babylonian: Spence 76f.; Jewish: Neuman, Genesis 1:3, etc.
D1765.p: Magic results are produced simply by giving a command, such as ordering something to happen.

D1766.r: (Cf. G224.5, V70.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 145, 465f. nn. 56, 57, 74, 75, 76—87 passim; England: Baughman.
D1766.p: Magic results are produced through a religious rite or ceremony.

D1766.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys; Norse: Boberg.
D1766.1.p: Magic results are produced when someone prays.

D1766.1.1.p: A magic fountain of water appears in answer to someone's prayer.

D1766.1.2.p: Through a nun's prayers, the Virgin Mary shows her the infant Jesus.

D1766.1.3.p: A garment comes into being in answer to prayer.

D1766.1.4.p: Pain is relieved or ended by prayer.

D1766.1.5.p: Through a saint's prayer, a sea or pool is filled with sand so people can cross on foot without getting wet.

D1766.1.6.p: A mouse prays to the gods about her children, and her prayer is granted.

D1766.1.7.p: A saint's prayer causes a prison door to open.

D1766.1.8.p: Food is produced in answer to prayer.

D1766.2.r: Irish: O’Suilleabhain 89, Beal XXI 329; Jewish: Neuman.
D1766.2.p: Magic results are produced through sacrifices offered in a religious way.

D1766.2.1.p: Magic results follow when sacrifices are made at trees or wells.

D1766.2.2.p: Magic power is gained by sacrificing a rooster (cock).

D1766.2.3.p: A person gains magic power by shedding blood as part of a religious sacrifice.

D1766.3.p: Magic power is obtained by baptizing an animal in a religious ceremony.

D1766.4.p: Magic power is obtained by giving an animal a Christian name in a religious ceremony.

D1766.4.1.p: A cock that has been christened gains magic power.

D1766.5.p: Magic results are produced by saying a Christian mass.

D1766.5.1.p: A mass is said together with other magic in order to curse someone.

D1766.5.2.p: Magic objects are made while a mass is being said.

D1766.6.p: Making the sign of the cross produces a magic result.

D1766.6.1.p: A fountain of water springs up when the sign of the cross is made.

D1766.6.2.p: Making the sign of the cross over a sword or knife gives it magic powers.

D1766.6.3.p: Making the sign of the cross enables a person to tell a marvelous story.

D1766.6.4.p: Making the sign of the cross over beer protects the drinker against poison.

D1766.6.5.p: A venomous dog is killed by the sign of the cross.

D1766.7.p: Magic results are produced by speaking a powerful name.

D1766.7.1.p: Magic results are produced by invoking a god's name.

D1766.7.1.1.r: (Cf. D1385.) Fb “lygtemand” II 473 b.—Irish: O’Suilleabhain 31f., 66, Beal XXI 310, 325; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
D1766.7.1.1.p: Evil spirits are driven away by invoking a god's name.

D1766.7.2.p: Using a hero's name magically causes water to appear.

D1766.7.3.p: Magic results are produced by invoking a saint's name.

D1766.8.p: Magic results are produced by fasting.

D1766.8.1.p: Fasting is part of a magic ritual.

D1766.9.p: Magic is produced when a person sings a hymn as part of a religious ceremony.

D1766.10.p: Magic is produced when a person worships a god or goddess.

D1773.p: Magic is produced when a person laughs.

D1773.1.p: Laughing causes flowers to give off their scent, a magical effect.

D1774.p: Magic is produced when a person speaks, usually by uttering particular words.

D1775.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Japanese: Ikeda; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 201.
D1775.p: Magic is produced when a person licks something.

D1776.r: Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (Koryak): Jochelson JE VI 170.
D1776.p: Magic is produced when a person spits.

D1777.p: Magic is produced simply by the power of thinking or willing something.

D1778.p: Magic is produced when a person touches the earth or ground.

D1781.p: Magic is produced when a person sings.

D1782.r: *Frazer Golden Bough XII 481 s.v. “Sympathetic magic”; *Andree Ethnographische 8ff.—Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Hindu: Penzer III 38, VI 24 n., 133, IX 27 n. 1; N. A. Indian (Blackfoot): Wissler and Duvall PaAM II 128, (Maliseet): Mechling GSCan IV 100 No. 29, (Arapaho): Dorsey and Kroeber FM V 271 No. 120, (Pawnee): Dorsey CI LIX 160 No. 43, (Micmac): Parsons JAFL XXXVIII 78 No. 11, Rand 370 No. 71, (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 186 No. 35, 457 No. 94, 659 No. 127.
D1782.p: Sympathetic magic: a desired result is brought about by imitating it, on the principle that like produces like.

D1782.1.p: A magical result is obtained by acting out or imitating the action one wants to happen.

D1782.1.1.p: A person opens their mouth, and by imitation a door is made to open wider.

D1782.2.p: A wound is cured by treating the object that caused the wound, rather than the wound itself.

D1782.3.p: A magical result is produced by untying knots.

D1782.3.1.p: When a fakir loses his sandals, his magic power is destroyed.

D1782.3.2.p: By untying knots, a horse is enabled to return home.

D1783.p: Reverse magic: a result is obtained by performing the opposite of the desired result.

D1783.1.r: (Cf. D1273.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 167, 485 nn. 31—33; Penzer VI 149 n. 1, 150ff.
D1783.1.p: A spell is undone by saying its formula backward, which reverses the work it did.

D1783.2.p: Leprosy is cured by drinking from the opposite end of a horn from the one that caused the disease.

D1783.3.r: The slower, the shorter. N. A. Indian (Plains Cree): Skinner JAFL XXIX 356 No. 3.
D1783.3.p: A magic power over a monster or wizard is gained by doing the opposite of what one is told; the farther one walks, the longer the trail left behind, as a reversed kind of magic.

D1783.4.p: A hero gains power over a monster, wizard, or king by doing the exact opposite of the command given.

D1783.5.p: Magic is turned back against those who worked it, leaving them confused so that they kill themselves.

D1784.p: Magic power is produced by breathing.

D1785.r: Influence at a distance. Koryak: *Jochelson JE VI 380.
D1785.p: A person gains the magical ability to read or send thoughts to another at a distance.

D1786.r: *Fb “korsvej” II 277f; *Frazer Golden Bough XII 232 s.v. “cross roads”; *Penzer III 37f.; Finnish: Kalevala rune 8.
D1786.p: Magic power is obtained at a crossroads.

D1787.p: Magic power is produced by burning something.

D1788.p: Magic power is produced by bathing.

D1788.1.p: Magic power is produced by touching water.

D1791.r: (Cf. G224.8, D1272.) *Fb “rundt” III 96b; Frazer Golden Bough X 233ff.; *Penzer X 109 s.v. “circumambulation”; Cowell Jataka index s.v. “rightwise”; Cosquin Études 356ff.; *Saintyves Essais 196ff.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
D1791.p: Magic power is produced by walking around a person or object in a circle.

D1791.1.p: Walking in a circle sunwise (clockwise, to the right) brings good luck.

D1791.1.1.p: A druid walks around someone to the right, sunwise, to honor them or bring good luck.

D1791.2.p: Walking in a circle against the sun (to the left, withershins) brings bad luck.

D1791.2.1.p: A druid walks around someone withershins, against the sun, to bring them ill luck.

D1792.p: Magic power is produced by a curse.

D1792.1.p: A saint's curse splits rocks apart.

D1792.2.p: A curse is laid on wells, causing magical effects.

D1792.3.p: A curse is laid on stones, causing magical effects.

D1793.p: Magic power is produced by eating or drinking something.

D1793.1.p: A person acquires the qualities of an animal by eating it.

D1794.p: Someone gains magic power simply by being kissed.

D1795.r: *Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 477 s.v. “durchkriechen”; *Lowy Zs. f. Vksk. XXXVII—XXXVIII 85.
D1795.p: Magic power is gained by crawling, running, or pulling oneself through a hole.

D1796.p: Magic power comes from a maiden walking naked in public.

D1796.1.p: A person's nudity itself is believed to have magical force.

D1799.p: Magic power is gained through various other actions not covered by more specific headings.

D1799.1.r: (Cf. D1081, D1610.9, V1.8.) Irish myth: Cross.
D1799.1.p: Magic power is gained by washing or cleansing oneself.

D1799.2.p: Magic power is produced by clapping the hands together.

D1799.3.p: Magic power is produced by carrying out a particular ritual.

D1799.4.p: Magic power is transmitted or gained by touching someone or something.

D1799.5.p: Magic power is gained by chewing something.

D1799.6.p: Magic power results from doing good deeds.

D1810.r: (Cf. D1310.) India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 456, Rasmussen I 78, III 123, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 244, (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 490.
D1810.p: A being or person has magical knowledge, the ability to know things beyond ordinary understanding.

D1810.0.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Norse: De la Saussaye 280, Boberg; Greek: Aeschylus Prometheus Bound line 167, Grote I 6; Jewish: Neuman.
D1810.0.1.p: A god knows everything; his knowledge is unlimited.

D1810.0.2.r: (Cf. D1711, D1814.1.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; English: Wells 42 (Arthour and Merlin); India: Thompson-Balys.
D1810.0.2.p: A magician has the ability to know hidden things.

D1810.0.2.1.p: A magician knows about and rebukes someone's secret lending of money at interest.

D1810.0.3.p: Saints and holy men have supernatural knowledge.

D1810.0.3.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
D1810.0.3.1.p: A saint sees through a cheat or trickery by his supernatural insight.

D1810.0.3.2.p: A holy man finds something lost or someone missing by supernatural means.

D1810.0.5.r: Irish myth: Cross; England, U.S., Wales: *Baughman.

D1810.0.6.p: An angel has magical knowledge, so that whoever has this power knows things ordinary people cannot know.

D1810.0.7.p: A superman, a being of extraordinary powers, possesses magical knowledge.

D1810.0.8.p: A druid, a priest of the ancient Celtic religion, possesses magical knowledge.

D1810.0.8.1.p: The druid's special magical knowledge is figured as "keys of wisdom", the means by which he unlocks hidden truths.

D1810.0.9.p: The Pope possesses magical knowledge, so that he knows things beyond ordinary understanding.

D1810.0.10.p: King Solomon possesses magical knowledge or wisdom far beyond what ordinary people have.

D1810.0.11.p: A poet has magical knowledge, so that he knows things hidden from others.

D1810.0.12.p: Magical knowledge reveals what offense a culprit has committed against a god.

D1810.0.13.p: Magical knowledge reveals who a stranger really is.

D1810.1.p: Someone gains magical knowledge from the queen of the otherworld, the fairy realm.

D1810.2.p: Someone gains magical knowledge from the devil.

D1810.3.r: (Cf. D1009.2, D1811.1.1.) **Scott Thumb; Irish myth: Cross; English: Baughman.
D1810.3.p: Magical knowledge is obtained by touching a special "knowledge tooth" with the thumb.

D1810.3.1.p: The future is revealed through the "knowledge tooth".

D1810.4.p: Someone acquires magical knowledge by being taught by a magician.

D1810.5.p: Someone gains magical knowledge from an angel.

D1810.6.p: Magical knowledge is gained by bathing in holy water.

D1810.7.p: Magical knowledge is gained by making the sign of the cross.

D1810.8.r: (Cf. D1812.3.3, D1812.5.1.2, D1813.1, D1814.2, D1817.2.1, D1819.2.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic. Þiðriks saga II 393—95 (n.), *Boberg.
D1810.8.p: Magical knowledge is received in a dream.

D1810.8.1.p: The truth is revealed to someone in a vision.

D1810.8.2.p: Information is received through a dream.

D1810.8.2.1.p: A dream reveals where a kidnapped girl is being kept hidden.

D1810.8.2.2.p: Someone dreams the exact spot where a drowned body lies.

D1810.8.2.3.p: A dream makes a murder known to someone who did not otherwise learn of it.

D1810.8.2.4.p: A dream tells a person that someone far away, who was in danger, is safe.

D1810.8.2.5.p: A raja is told in a dream that a stranger he plans to destroy is actually his own son.

D1810.8.3.p: A dream gives a warning about something bad that is going to happen.

D1810.8.3.1.p: A warning received in a dream comes true as the dream said.

D1810.8.3.1.1.p: A dream warns that someone will become ill or be hurt, and that illness or injury then occurs.

D1810.8.3.2.p: A dream warns of danger that is about to happen soon, and the warning lets the person avoid it.

D1810.8.4.p: Someone finds the answer to a difficult problem in a dream.

D1810.9.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 297—98 (Odin); India: Thompson-Balys.
D1810.9.p: Magical knowledge or wisdom is granted by God.

D1810.10.p: Magical knowledge or wisdom is granted by a goddess.

D1810.11.p: Magical knowledge or wisdom is obtained from a mythical ancestor.

D1810.12.r: (See E721.9.) Icelandic: Hrólfs saga Kraka II, Boberg.
D1810.12.p: Magical knowledge is obtained from guardian spirits.

D1810.13.r: Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 46, 298, 299—300, 311, Herrmann Saxo II 98—99.
D1810.13.p: Magical knowledge is obtained from the dead.

D1811.p: Magical wisdom or knowledge in general.

D1811.0.1.p: Adam is said to have mastered seventy-two kinds of wisdom.

D1811.1.p: Magical wisdom is gained by eating or drinking something.

D1811.1.1.p: A man cooks a magic animal and burns his thumb; when he puts the thumb in his mouth he gains magical knowledge.

D1811.1.1.1.p: The thumb of knowledge is obtained by catching a thumb in a fairy's door.

D1811.1.2.r: (Cf. D1242.1, D1300.3, V134.) Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
D1811.1.2.p: A person gains magical wisdom or knowledge by drinking from a well.

D1811.2.p: A person receives magical wisdom or knowledge from a supernatural being.

D1811.2.1.p: Divine inspiration gives a person the ability to write sacred books.

D1812.r: (Cf. D1311.) Icelandic: *Boberg; English: Child III 418—422; Greek: Grote I 216, 249, 307; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Ferguson 135.—N. A. Indian (Micmac): Parsons JAFL XXXVIII 75 No. 10.
D1812.p: A person has the magic power to foretell future events.

D1812.0.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; England: *Baughman; Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “mort”; Greek: Aeschylus Agamemnon line 1260; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1812.0.1.p: A person knows in advance when they will die.

D1812.0.1.1.p: A person's cheek is bitten or twitches as a sign that death is near.

D1812.0.1.2.p: A person knows in advance how they will die.

D1812.0.2.p: Holy people know in advance when guests are coming.

D1812.0.2.1.p: A holy person knows in advance when unwelcome guests are coming.

D1812.0.2.2.p: A hero knows in advance when guests are coming.

D1812.0.2.3.p: A fakir (wandering holy man) knows in advance when guests are coming.

D1812.0.3.p: A person knows in advance that they will be wounded in battle.

D1812.0.4.p: A person foresees that their son or sons will be unhappy.

D1812.0.5.p: A person has magic knowledge of what will happen to them after death.

D1812.1.p: The power of prophecy is given to a person as a gift.

D1812.1.1.p: A person receives the power of prophecy from a fairy.

D1812.1.2.p: A person receives the power of prophecy from God.

D1812.2.p: The power of prophecy is brought on deliberately by a person.

D1812.2.1.p: A person gains the power of prophecy by crawling backward around a grave.

D1812.2.2.p: A person gains the power of prophecy by conjuring, that is, by calling up spirits with magic words or rites.

D1812.2.3.p: A person gains the power to foretell the future by accidentally drinking water from a magic fountain.

D1812.2.4.p: A dying man gains or shows the power to foretell the future.

D1812.3.p: Various ways in which a person can learn what will happen in the future.

D1812.3.1.p: A person learns the future by sitting on a animal hide.

D1812.3.2.p: A person tells the future by cutting sand.

D1812.3.3.r: (Cf. D1810.8, D1812.5.1.2, D1813.1.) *Type 725; *BP I 324; *Fb “sove” III 472b; *Hartland FLJ IV 321; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 182, 183, 287, 328, 466, 826—830; *Gaster Exempla Nos. 215, 216, 218, 219, 242; Loomis White Magic; Alphabet Nos. 266, 305; Child V 477 s.v. “dreams”; *Encyc. Religion and Ethics s.v. “Dreams and sleep”; Loomis White Magic 17f.; Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 334, 347.—Irish myth: *Cross; Norse: Sofus Larsen Antik og Nordisk Drømmetro (Aarbøger for Nordisk Oldkyndighed 1917, 37ff.), G. D. Kelchner Dreams in Old Norse Literature and Their Affinities in Folklore (Cambridge, England, 1935); Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 311—12, *Boberg; England, Scotland, Wales, U.S.: *Baughman; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 46 n. 1 (Hecuba); Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 276, Graham.—S. D1812.3.3.p: The future is revealed to a person in a dream.

D1812.3.3.0.1.p: A druid explains the meaning of a prophetic dream.

D1812.3.3.0.2.p: Poets are the ones who interpret dreams.

D1812.3.3.0.3.p: A dream interpreter changes or corrects the meaning of a dream.

D1812.3.3.1.p: Dreams are most true when they come at daybreak.

D1812.3.3.2.p: A dream that foretells the future is brought on by sleeping in an unusual place or position.

D1812.3.3.3.p: A prophetic dream is brought on by a magic chant or spell.

D1812.3.3.4.p: A prophetic dream stops being valid after one year.

D1812.3.3.5.p: A prophetic dream is symbolic, its meaning hidden in images that stand for other things.

D1812.3.3.5.1.p: A symbolic dream shows ripe and unripe ears of grain and fat and lean cattle, which stand for coming years of plenty and famine.

D1812.3.3.6.p: A prophetic dream is brought on by eating the meat of a bull.

D1812.3.3.7.p: In a vision, Eve sees Cain drink Abel's blood.

D1812.3.3.8.p: A pregnant woman dreams about what will become of her unborn child.

D1812.3.3.9.p: A person sees their future husband or wife in a dream.

D1812.3.3.10.p: A dream is interpreted by taking its meaning as the opposite of what it shows.

D1812.3.3.11.p: A person sees in a dream that someone else will die, and the dream reveals the future death.

D1812.4.r: Irish myth: Cross; England, U.S.: *Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 88; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 68, 227, (Zulu): Callaway 194.
D1812.4.p: A person somehow knows the future by an inner sense or foreboding, without outside signs.

D1812.4.1.p: A woman cries out when she first sees a man whom the child she carries is destined to kill.

D1812.5.r: *Fb “varsel”; *Kittredge Witchcraft 398 n. 170; Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 110, Beal XXI 334; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys, Cowell Jataka index s.v. “Omens”.
D1812.5.p: A person learns what will happen from omens, which are signs in nature or events taken as messages about the future.

D1812.5.0.1.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 44, 398 n. 170; *Pease Classical Philology VI (1911) 429ff; *Tylor Primitive Culture (First Am. ed.) I 97ff.; Knowlson Popular Superstitions (1910) 175ff.; Schweizer Volkskunde (1912) 20f.; Encyc. Rel. Ethics IX 398f.; Penzer III 303ff.; Gessler Bull. bib. et péd. du Musée belge XXX (1926) 193ff.; Saintyves L’Eternuement et le Baillement (Paris, 1921) 148; *Fb “nyse” II 704; Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “niesen” VI 1076ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1812.5.0.1.p: A sneeze is taken as a sign that tells what will happen in the future.

D1812.5.0.2.p: The way birds fly is read as a sign of what will happen.

D1812.5.0.3.r: *Fb “ild” II 13a.; Virgil Aeneid II 680, V 525, VII 74; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1812.5.0.3.p: The way a fire behaves is read as an omen of future events.

D1812.5.0.4.r: N. A. Indian: Kroeber JAFL XXI 224.
D1812.5.0.4.p: The direction, shape or behavior of rising smoke is taken as a sign of the future.

D1812.5.0.4.1.p: A person foretells the future by reading rising smoke.

D1812.5.0.5.p: Diviners called haruspices foretell the future by examining the liver of a sacrificed animal.

D1812.5.0.6.p: Objects are thrown into water to foretell the future: if they float or swim the omen is bad, and if they sink the omen is good.

D1812.5.0.7.p: The future is foretold from the first person or thing one meets.

D1812.5.0.7.1.p: Whoever is first to eat a certain feast will be the first to disobey the king or the like.

D1812.5.0.7.2.p: A saint declares that the first man to come to a certain place will be his successor, and a young cleric arrives first and is chosen.

D1812.5.0.7.3.p: Predictions are made from which day of the week the first day of the year falls on.

D1812.5.0.8.p: The outcome of a fight between animals is taken as a sign of the future.

D1812.5.0.8.1.p: Omens are read from the way an animal moves.

D1812.5.0.9.p: The howling of a dog is taken as an omen of what will happen.

D1812.5.0.10.p: The shapes or movements of clouds are read as signs of the future.

D1812.5.0.11.p: The sound of a voice heard is taken as a sign that tells what will happen.

D1812.5.0.12.p: A person learns what will happen by hearing the sound of chariot wheels, which is read as an omen.

D1812.5.0.13.p: A magical occurrence is taken as a sign of what is to come.

D1812.5.0.14.r: (Cf. D1293.1, D1293.2, D1317.12.) Irish myth: Cross.
D1812.5.0.14.p: A stone that changes color from red to green is read as a lucky sign.

D1812.5.0.15.p: Future events are foretold from signs in the weather.

D1812.5.0.15.1.r: Icelandic: Egils saga einhenda, ed. Lagerholm 47.
D1812.5.0.15.1.p: Future events are foretold by reading the wind.

D1812.5.0.16.p: The coming year's fortunes are predicted from the winds that blow on January 1.

D1812.5.0.17.p: Which son will be born first is foretold by choosing between roads.

D1812.5.1.r: *Penzer III 46, 86, X 251 s.v. “Omen, evil.”; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1812.5.1.p: Events are foretold as bad luck from unfavorable omens.

D1812.5.1.1.r: *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 69; *Penzer II 39 n. 2.—Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 185 n. 1, 232 n. 2.
D1812.5.1.1.p: An unusual marvel or monstrous birth is taken as a sign of evil to come.

D1812.5.1.1.1.p: Tears of blood are taken as a sign of coming evil.

D1812.5.1.1.2.p: Two drops of blood found in a book mean that two people will be killed.

D1812.5.1.1.3.p: Blood seen in a dream is a sign that someone will be killed.

D1812.5.1.1.4.p: A wave of blood is taken as a sign of death.

D1812.5.1.1.5.p: Drops of blood foretell a massacre or slaughter.

D1812.5.1.1.6.p: A woman seen washing bloody armor, chariot cushions, or a human limb at a ford is a sign of coming disaster in battle.

D1812.5.1.2.r: (Cf. D1810.8, D1812.3.3, D1813.1.) Dickson 74, 225.—Irish myth: *Cross; English: Wells 9 (King Horn), 31 (Geoffrey’s life of Arthur), 33 (Layamon’s Brut), 48 (Lancelot of the Laik), 89 (The Sege of Melayne), 92 (The Song of Roland), 122 (The King of Tars); Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 233, *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1812.5.1.2.p: A bad dream is taken as a warning of misfortune.

D1812.5.1.2.1.p: A vision seen is taken as an evil omen.

D1812.5.1.3.p: Breaking a mirror is taken as a sign of bad luck to come.

D1812.5.1.4.p: An eclipse is taken as a sign of evil to come.

D1812.5.1.5.p: The moon gives a sign of coming misfortune.

D1812.5.1.5.1.p: A new moon with an old moon held in its arm (the faint outline of the old moon visible) foretells a storm.

D1812.5.1.5.2.p: A red or pale moon is taken as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.6.p: The stars are read as signs that predict the future, and their appearance can signal bad fortune.

D1812.5.1.6.1.p: The star Sirius, the Dog Star, is taken as a sign of bad luck.

D1812.5.1.7.p: Meeting certain people or animals by chance is taken as a warning of bad luck.

D1812.5.1.7.1.p: Being greeted by someone before dawn is a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.8.p: If two bridal processions meet on the way, it is a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.9.p: Seeing a mermaid is a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.10.p: Seeing a ghostly phantom ship is taken as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.11.p: Red, gray, or similarly colored clouds are taken as evil omens.

D1812.5.1.12.p: The behavior of animals is read as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.12.1.p: A dog howling is taken as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.12.2.p: The calls of certain birds are taken as evil omens.

D1812.5.1.12.3.p: A spider dropping onto a person's back is an ill omen.

D1812.5.1.12.4.p: Mice gnawing at clothes are taken as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.13.p: Hearing fairy music is taken as an evil omen.

D1812.5.1.14.p: A holy man falling from his horse is taken as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.15.p: A hailstorm is taken as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.16.p: A dried-up riverbed is taken as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.16.1.p: A dried-up riverbed is taken as a sign that someone will soon die.

D1812.5.1.17.r: (Cf. D1812.5.1.1.6.) Irish myth: *Cross; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 678f.
D1812.5.1.17.p: A spectre (ghostly apparition) is taken as a sign of coming evil.

D1812.5.1.17.1.p: A host of spirits seen fighting in the air is read as a sign of coming evil.

D1812.5.1.17.2.p: The sound of clashing shields heard in the heavens is taken as a sign of coming evil.

D1812.5.1.17.3.p: A roaring sound like shields is heard and taken as a sign of coming evil.

D1812.5.1.18.p: Snow falling on a house is taken as a sign that someone in it will soon die.

D1812.5.1.19.p: An outbreak of plague is read as a sign of bad fortune to come.

D1812.5.1.20.p: A tree withering or dying is taken as a sign of bad fortune.

D1812.5.1.21.p: Forgetting to take the leashes when going hunting with hounds is taken as a sign of bad luck.

D1812.5.1.22.p: Seeing something unusual or strange on the road home is taken as a sign of bad luck.

D1812.5.1.23.p: A man killed by accident when a ship is pushed into the sea is read as an evil omen.

D1812.5.1.24.p: The roaring of waves is taken as a sign of danger to the king.

D1812.5.1.25.p: Shields falling down are taken as a sign of coming evil.

D1812.5.1.26.p: Book satchels falling down are taken as a sign of coming evil.

D1812.5.1.27.p: The croaking of a raven is taken as a sign of bad fortune.

D1812.5.1.27.1.p: The hooting of an owl is taken as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.28.p: A stirrup leather breaking is taken as a sign of bad fortune.

D1812.5.1.29.p: A scavenger carrying a load of wood is seen as an evil omen.

D1812.5.1.30.p: A particular place is regarded as a bad omen.

D1812.5.1.31.p: Stubbing one's toe is taken as a sign of bad luck.

D1812.5.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys, *Penzer I 116, IV 122 n. 1, 171 n. 1.
D1812.5.2.p: Signs read as foretelling good fortune rather than bad.

D1812.5.2.1.p: The throbbing of the right eye is taken as a sign of good fortune to come.

D1812.5.2.2.p: Meeting a certain person or animal on the way is read as a sign that things will go well.

D1812.5.2.2.1.p: Meeting an old woman carrying a pot of freshly drawn water is a lucky sign.

D1812.5.2.3.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 45, 398 n. 172; *Frazer Pausanias III 417 (lightning on the right).
D1812.5.2.3.p: Hearing thunder as one sets out on a journey is taken as a good sign.

D1812.5.2.4.p: Seeing a bird of prey catch its quarry is read as a lucky sign.

D1812.5.2.5.p: Hearing a bird's cry is taken as a favorable sign.

D1812.5.2.5.1.p: Hearing the cuckoo call is taken as a good sign.

D1812.5.2.5.2.p: Hearing a heron's cry is taken as a good sign.

D1812.5.2.6.p: A shooting star is taken as a sign of good fortune.

D1812.5.2.7.p: A roaring wave is taken as a sign that good luck is coming.

D1812.5.2.8.p: Something that happens when the foundation of a building is laid is read as a favorable omen.

D1812.5.2.9.p: A king who finds a golden bow and arrow (or spindle) learns that an heir will be born to him.

D1812.5.2.10.p: Seeing a black dog is taken as a good omen.

D1812.5.2.11.p: A spider dropping onto one's front is taken as a good sign.

D1812.6.p: A person loses the ability to foretell the future.

D1812.6.1.p: A prophet loses the power of prophecy when, on request, he spits into the mouth of the man who taught him.

D1813.r: Irish: Plummer clxx, *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1813.p: A person has magical knowledge of things happening in a distant place.

D1813.0.1.p: A bear knows when a person has looked at its track.

D1813.0.2.p: A fairy knows how mortals are faring in their lives.

D1813.0.3.r: (Cf. D1812.0.4, D1812.5.1.1.4.) Icelandic: Hrólfs saga Kraka ch. 14, Boberg.
D1813.0.3.p: A father senses through magic or intuition that his son is in danger.

D1813.0.3.1.p: A father senses from far away that his son has died or is in danger, through magical knowledge.

D1813.1.r: (Cf. D1810.8, D1812.3.3, D1812.5.1.2.) India: Thompson-Balys; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
D1813.1.p: A dream reveals to the dreamer what is happening in a distant place.

D1813.1.1.r: English: Wells 138 (The Earl of Toulous); Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1813.1.1.p: A dream warns an emperor that his wife is being unfaithful to him.

D1813.1.2.p: A dream warns a king that he has made a mistake in a judgment.

D1813.1.3.p: A dream warns a king that his kingdom is in danger.

D1813.1.4.p: A dream reveals to the dreamer that his brother has died.

D1813.1.5.p: A dream reveals to a girl that her lover has died.

D1813.1.6.p: A dream shows that other people are in danger.

D1813.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Hrolfs saga Kraka ch. 2, Boberg.
D1813.2.p: Magic reveals where pursuers are chasing a person who is fleeing.

D1813.3.p: A magical tooth called a knowledge tooth reveals events happening in a distant place.

D1813.4.r: Icelandic: Hrólfs saga Kraka ch. 1; Egils saga einhenda ch. IX 8 p. 44, *Boberg.
D1813.4.p: Magic reveals the route taken by fugitives who are escaping.

D1814.p: A magical source gives advice or knowledge that helps the person who receives it.

D1814.1.r: (Cf. D1711, D1810.0.2, D1817.) Irish myth: *Cross; English: Wells 39 (Nennius Historia Britonum); Greek: Grote I 249.
D1814.1.p: A magician, fortune-teller, or similar figure gives advice through magical knowledge.

D1814.1.1.p: A wizard shows a man a likeness of a rooster that will win a cockfight.

D1814.2.r: (Cf. D1810.8.) Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys. Icelandic: *Boberg.
D1814.2.p: Advice comes to a person in a dream.

D1814.3.p: Advice comes from God or the gods.

D1815.r: Irish myth: *Cross; English: Child III 418—422; Ward II 676 No. 68; Jewish: Neuman.
D1815.p: Through magic, a person gains knowledge of strange or unknown languages.

D1815.0.1.p: A person receives the gift of understanding languages from ghosts.

D1815.1.p: A person knows the language spoken by ghosts.

D1815.2.p: Through magic, a person understands the language of animals.

D1815.3.p: Through magic, a person understands the language of demons.

D1815.4.p: A person magically understands the speech of trees, hearing what they say to one another.

D1815.5.p: A person magically understands the language of plants and vegetables.

D1815.6.p: A person magically understands the language spoken in valleys, such as the sounds or messages carried there.

D1816.p: Someone uses magic to find a place they are seeking.

D1816.1.r: (Cf. D925, D925.1, D1731.) Irish: Plummer cl, Cross.
D1816.1.p: A person learns in a dream where a fountain is located.

D1816.2.p: A lost object is found through magic.

D1816.2.1.p: A lost object is found by throwing a spade at a ghost; wherever the spade sticks, the lost object will be found.

D1816.3.p: The location of a fort is discovered by reading in a book.

D1816.4.p: The place where a buried object or body lies is revealed by magic.

D1816.4.1.p: The place where the corpse of a drowned person lies is found by magic.

D1816.5.p: A druid uses divination to learn where a missing person is.

D1816.5.1.p: A druid uses magic to discover where his abducted wife has been taken.

D1816.6.p: Magic is used to find the right place for building a church.

D1817.p: Magic is used to find out who committed a crime.

D1817.0.1.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 190ff., 505 nn. 28, 29—53; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
D1817.0.1.p: Magic is used to detect a theft and the thief.

D1817.0.1.1.p: A witch or wizard magically reveals the name of the thief.

D1817.0.1.2.p: A wizard magically tells where the stolen property is hidden or kept.

D1817.0.1.3.p: A wizard uses magic to force a thief to give back the stolen property.

D1817.0.1.3.1.p: A wizard uses magic to force a thief to bring the stolen property personally to its owner.

D1817.0.1.4.p: A wizard magically shows the form, shadow, or picture of the thief.

D1817.0.1.5.p: A wizard finds out who the thieves are by putting a leaf from the Bible under the doorstep; the guilty ones stumble over it when they step across the threshold.

D1817.0.1.6.p: A wizard identifies a thief by going into a trance and seeing who did it.

D1817.0.2.p: Magic is used to discover that poison has been used.

D1817.0.3.p: Magic is used to discover that a murder has been committed, or who did it.

D1817.0.4.p: Magic is used to uncover a secret plot or conspiracy.

D1817.0.5.p: Magic is used to reveal that someone has committed a sin.

D1817.1.p: Druids use their magical knowledge to find out about crimes.

D1817.2.p: Saints use their magical powers to find out about crimes.

D1817.2.1.p: A saint learns of someone's sin through a dream.

D1817.2.2.p: By magic, a saint forces a thief to give back stolen goods.

D1817.3.p: A crime is detected through a magical tooth that gives knowledge.

D1818.p: A magic cure or remedy is learned through magic.

D1819.p: Miscellaneous cases of gaining knowledge through magic.

D1819.1.p: Someone uses magic to know what another person is thinking.

D1819.1.1.p: A chief uses magic to read the thoughts of a visitor.

D1819.2.p: A deception is revealed to someone in a dream.

D1819.3.p: Through magic knowledge, a man is able to identify a headless body.

D1819.4.p: A person learns to read by magic rather than by study.

D1819.4.1.p: A man is able to read the baptismal service after washing in holy water.

D1819.4.2.p: Someone learns the alphabet by eating a cake on which the letters were written.

D1819.5.p: Through magic, the identity of a grave's occupant is revealed.

D1819.6.p: Through magic, the identity of singers is revealed.

D1819.7.p: A man magically tells a king a dream the king has forgotten himself.

D1819.8.p: Someone has magic knowledge of a calf that is not yet born.

D1820.r: (Cf. D1331.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 185ff.; 503ff.—Irish: Plummer clxxi; England, U.S.: Baughman; Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 102.
D1820.p: A person has magical power to see and hear things that are far off or hidden from ordinary people.

D1820.1.r: (Cf. D1810.0.3, V220.) *Toldo Studien I 347.—Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 109, 128, Beal XXI 334, 337.
D1820.1.p: Saints have magical power to see things that ordinary people cannot.

D1820.1.1.p: A blind holy man nevertheless has magical sight.

D1820.2.p: A saint gives a king the power to see things at great distances.

D1820.3.p: A saint blesses two brothers' eyes so that they can see heaven.

D1821.p: Ways in which a person can acquire magic sight.

D1821.1.r: *BP II 319, 518; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 204; Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 243; *Fb “se” III 175a.—Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 255, 283; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 297 No. 1, 298 No. 7, 302 No. 27, 309 No. 10.
D1821.1.p: A person gains magic sight by treading on another person's foot.

D1821.2.r: (Cf. D1810.3, D1811.1.1.) **Scott Thumb.—Irish myth: *Cross; Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 253.
D1821.2.p: A man gains magic sight by putting his burned thumb into his mouth after cooking a magic animal.

D1821.3.p: A person gains magic sight by looking at a certain place.

D1821.3.1.r: Jakob Grimm Kleinere Schriften VII 3; *Fb “øje” III 1168b, “se” III 174.—Icelandic: *Boberg; English: Child III 411, V 299b.
D1821.3.1.p: A person gains magic sight by looking under the arm.

D1821.3.2.p: A person gains magic sight by looking over the right shoulder.

D1821.3.3.p: A person gains magic sight by looking under his own legs.

D1821.3.4.p: A person gains magic sight by looking between a dog's ears.

D1821.3.5.r: (Cf. D1076.) Irish myth: *Cross; English: Child III 412.
D1821.3.5.p: A person gains magic sight by looking through a ring.

D1821.3.5.1.p: A person becomes able to see ghosts after looking through a hole in a coffin.

D1821.3.6.p: A person gains magic sight by looking through a keyhole.

D1821.3.7.p: A person gains magic sight by gazing at a shining or reflective object. The seer then sees things hidden from ordinary eyes.

D1821.3.7.1.r: Fb “vand” III 1001a; Kittredge Witchcraft 185ff., 504, 508 nn. 6, 47.—Chinese: Graham.
D1821.3.7.1.p: A person gains magic sight by looking into a glass of water, which lets them see things hidden from ordinary eyes.

D1821.3.7.2.p: A person gains magic sight by looking at the polished surface of a fingernail, which lets them see hidden things.

D1821.3.7.3.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 185ff., 503ff. nn. *1—3, 10—24, 35, 47.—England, U.S.: Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1821.3.7.3.p: A person gains clairvoyance, the power to see distant or hidden things, by gazing into a crystal ball.

D1821.3.7.4.p: A person gains magic sight by looking at the polished blade of a sword, which lets them see hidden things.

D1821.3.8.p: A person gains magic sight by reading or looking at the shoulder-blade bone of a sheep, which lets them see hidden things.

D1821.3.9.p: A person gains magic sight by looking into the hollow of their own hand, which lets them see hidden things.

D1821.3.10.p: A person gains magic sight by looking through a feather, which lets them see hidden things.

D1821.4.r: (Cf. D1244.) England: Lang English Fairy Tales 220.
D1821.4.p: A person gains magic sight by putting a special ointment into the eye, which lets them see hidden things.

D1821.5.p: A person gains magic sight by standing on a certain stone, which lets them see hidden things.

D1821.6.p: A child abandoned by its parents is given magic sight, which lets them see hidden things.

D1821.7.p: A deaf and mute man is able to see a soul being taken to heaven or hell.

D1821.8.p: A person who is possessed by the spirit of a dead person gains second sight.

D1821.9.p: A person gains magic sight by turning their clothes inside out.

D1821.10.p: A person gains magic sight by standing alone for three days.

D1821.11.p: A person gains magic sight as a gift from grateful animals that they had helped.

D1822.p: A person loses their magic sight.

D1822.1.p: A person's magic sight is removed or stopped by a spell or chant.

D1825.p: A general heading for the different kinds of magic sight.

D1825.1.r: Power to see future happenings. (Cf. D1812.) *Chauvin V 90 No. 28 n. 2; *Fb “synsk”, “spåkjælling”, “spåmand”, “gjenviser”; *RTP XXVII *145, 151, 284, 382.—Irish: Plummer clxx, *Cross; Scotland: Macdougall and Calder 183, 251, 255, 281; Icelandic: Snorra Edda Prol. V and Gylf. II, *Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 478 No. 103, (Plains Ojibwa): Skinner JAFL XXXII 300.
D1825.1.p: Second sight: the ability to see hidden, distant, or future events, or spirits, that ordinary people cannot see.

D1825.1.2.r: *Fb “kjæreste” II 153; Type 737*.—England, U.S.: *Baughman; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1825.1.2.p: A person has magical foresight that lets them see their future lover before meeting them.

D1825.2.r: (Cf. D1813.3, D1817.0.1, D1825.5.) *BP II 319; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 204.—Celtic: Hartland Science 197; England: Child III 412; England, Scotland, U.S.: *Baughman; Icelandic: *Boberg; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3507; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 91 No. 5.
D1825.2.p: A person has the magical power to see objects that are far away.

D1825.2.1.p: A person with magic sight from the otherworld can see ordinary earthly objects from there.

D1825.2.2.p: A person has the magic power to see an entire country at one glance.

D1825.3.r: Swiss. Jegerlehner Oberwallis 297f. Nos. 1, 7; Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 183, Lang English Fairy Tales 220; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3510.
D1825.3.p: A person has the magic power to see beings that are normally invisible.

D1825.3.1.r: *Type 332; *BP I 377 ff.—Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman.
D1825.3.1.p: A person with magic sight can see Death standing at the head or foot of a sick person's bed, and so predict how the illness will go.

D1825.3.2.p: A person sees angels hovering over good people and black stars over bad people.

D1825.3.3.p: A person has the magic ability to see another person's soul, or astral body.

D1825.3.3.1.p: A person with magic sight can see souls of the dead after they have died.

D1825.3.3.2.p: A person with magic sight can see a soul leaving the body.

D1825.3.4.p: A person has the magic ability to see heavenly beings.

D1825.3.4.1.p: A person has the magic ability to see an angel of God.

D1825.3.4.2.p: A person has the magic ability to see the messengers of Pluto, the god of the underworld.

D1825.4.p: A person has the magic power to see things that are hidden or concealed.

D1825.4.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 12 n. 3.
D1825.4.1.p: A person with magic sight can see things buried or hidden underground.

D1825.4.2.p: A person has the magic power to tell whether a girl is a virgin.

D1825.4.3.p: A person has the magic power to see where lost things are.

D1825.4.3.1.p: A prophet uses magic sight to find a lost child.

D1825.5.p: A person has the magic power to see how an absent person died or what happened to them when they were far away.

D1825.6.p: A person has the magic power to see who will die during the coming year.

D1825.7.p: A person gains magic sight that shows an event before it happens, so they see it in advance.

D1825.7.1.p: Someone sees a ghostly funeral procession in advance, well before the real funeral takes place.

D1825.8.p: A holy ascetic sees gold where ordinary people see scorpions, so the same objects look different to them through magic sight.

D1825.9.p: Witches are able to see things happening far away.

D1827.p: A general magic power to hear things that ordinary people cannot hear.

D1827.1.p: Magic hearing picks up noises that foretell someone's death.

D1827.1.1.p: On Halloween a person listens at the church door to hear the names of those who will die in the coming year.

D1827.1.2.p: A person hears sounds before a death, and the same sounds are later heard again at the death or funeral.

D1827.1.3.p: A noise gives warning that death is approaching.

D1827.1.4.p: Sounds are heard from far away at the moment of someone's death.

D1827.2.p: A person hears a call for help coming from a great distance.

D1830.r: (Cf. D1335.) Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 491.
D1830.p: A general magic power of great strength.

D1830.1.p: A man's strength is made equal to that of an angel.

D1831.r: (Cf. D991.) *Frazer Old Testament II 482ff., Jewish: *Neuman; *Frazer Golden Bough I 102, XI 158ff.; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 1258; *Wilken Verspreide Geschriften III 551ff.; *Fb “styrke” III 630a, “hår” IV 241b; Krappe “Samson” Revue Archéologique (1933) 195—211.—Greek: Fox 69 (Nisos), 77 (Pterelaos); Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 67 No. 508A*, Keller; N. A. Indian (Pawnee): Dorsey MAFLS VIII 113 No. 31; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 466.
D1831.p: A person's magic strength is located in their hair.

D1831.1.p: A female saint binds the devil using a single hair from her head.

D1831.2.p: A person's magic strength is located in their beard.

D1831.3.p: A person's magic strength is located in their semen.

D1832.r: (Cf. D1242.1.) *MacCulloch Childhood 70ff.—N. A. Indian (Tsimshian, Tlingit, Haida): Boas RBAE XXXI 729.
D1832.p: Magic strength is gained by bathing.

D1833.p: Magic strength is gained by touching the earth.

D1834.p: Magic strength comes from a helpful animal.

D1835.p: A general category of ways a person can gain magical strength by means other than the usual ones.

D1835.1.p: A person gains magical strength by looking at a necklace.

D1835.2.p: A horse is given magical strength by having its hair combed in one direction and then the opposite way.

D1835.3.p: Magical strength is transferred or gained by being stroked or touched.

D1835.4.r: French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule. (Cf. D1078.1.)
D1835.4.p: Wearing a blue ribbon gives a person magical strength.

D1835.5.p: Magical strength comes from singing songs.

D1835.6.p: Magical strength is obtained from a demon.

D1836.r: English: Wells 50 (Le Morte Arthur); Irish myth: *Cross.
D1836.p: A person's magical strength rises and falls over time, being greatest until noon and then declining afterward.

D1836.1.r: N. A. Indian (Teton): Dorsey Am. Anth. o.s. II (1889) 150.
D1836.1.p: A ghost's strength grows and shrinks depending on how high the fire burns.

D1836.2.p: Magical strength decreases when a being is in certain places.

D1837.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Scotch: Campbell Tales II 47; Icelandic: Boberg.
D1837.p: A general category of magical weakness, where a being's magic power is reduced or fails.

D1837.1.p: Magical power is weak only during a particular period of time.

D1837.1.1.p: Magical power is weakened for five days each year.

D1837.2.p: A magical weakness that can never be fully removed.

D1837.3.p: Magical weakness is caused by a curse from a fairy or goddess.

D1837.4.p: A snake loses its power when a pregnant woman crosses its path.

D1837.5.p: Magical power is weakened by eating food sent by the one who cast the magic.

D1840.r: **Otto Berthold Die Unverwundbarkeit in Sage und Aberglauben der Griechen (Giessen, 1911); cf. Zs. f. Vksk. XXI 415.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 312, *Boberg; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 150 n. 1; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 300 No. 5; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 287, 597.—Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 99, 417, Rasmussen II 260, III 105, 250; Teheulche (Patagonian): Alexander Lat. Am. 336; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 93, 233.
D1840.p: A general category of magical invulnerability, where a being cannot be harmed by ordinary means.

D1840.1.p: Saints are magically invulnerable and cannot be harmed.

D1840.1.1.p: A saint's magic invulnerability protects him so that he can pick up poisonous snakes with his bare hands without being bitten harmfully.

D1840.1.2.p: A saint is magically immune to poison and cannot be harmed by it.

D1840.1.2.1.p: Poisoned food or drink is rendered harmless when a saint blesses it.

D1840.1.3.p: St. Cecilia survives three blows from an executioner's sword and lives for three days after being beheaded.

D1840.2.p: Certain animals are magically invulnerable and cannot be killed or wounded in the usual way.

D1840.2.1.p: A cat that cannot be harmed or killed by ordinary means because of magic.

D1840.2.2.r: Chinese and Persian: Coyajee JPASB XXIV 182.
D1840.2.2.p: A stag that cannot be harmed or killed by ordinary means because of magic.

D1840.3.p: Ogres are magically invulnerable and cannot be harmed in the usual way.

D1841.p: A person is made invulnerable to harm from certain specific substances or things.

D1841.1.p: A man is proof against being harmed by iron, stone, or wood.

D1841.2.p: A man is unharmed by boiling water.

D1841.2.1.p: A saint is kept in boiling water for three days and shows no sign of pain or harm.

D1841.2.2.p: A saint is unhurt when bathed in boiling oil, pitch, or molten lead.

D1841.2.2.1.p: A saint is placed in boiling oil but is not injured.

D1841.3.r: (Cf. D1656.) Chauvin VI 189 No. 356; Crane Liber de Miraculis 88 No. 15; Günter Christliche Legende 234 s.v. “Feuer”; Cosquin Indiens 439ff.; Toldo Studien VI 298; Alphabet No. 308; *Loomis White Magic 114.—Jewish: *Neuman, Spence 51f., Gaster Rabbis 191 No. 28, 185 No. 28; Irish: *Cross, O’suilleabhain 71, Beal XXI 326; Spanish Exempla: Keller; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 311 n. 120.
D1841.3.p: A person or thing escapes burning through magic.

D1841.3.1.p: A magical animal cannot be burned.

D1841.3.2.p: A saint is not injured by fire.

D1841.3.2.1.p: A fiery furnace used to torture a saint fails to harm him.

D1841.3.2.2.p: A saint walks across glowing coals without being burned.

D1841.3.2.3.p: A saint carries red-hot iron in his bare hands without being burned.

D1841.3.2.3.1.p: A holy man carries red-hot iron in his bare hands and is not harmed by it, so the fire does not hurt him. He may use this to warm his guests.

D1841.3.2.4.p: Holy women carry glowing coals in their robes and the fire does not burn them.

D1841.3.3.p: A sacred book or manuscript cannot be burned; it survives fire untouched.

D1841.4.r: (Cf. D1524.1, D1540, D1551, D2125, D2151.) India: Thompson-Balys.
D1841.4.p: A person is magically kept dry and cannot be soaked by water or weather.

D1841.4.1.r: *Loomis White Magic 39; Irish: Plummer cxxxvii, *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 198.—Africa (Kaffir): Theal 76.
D1841.4.1.p: A person stays dry in the rain and is not soaked by it.

D1841.4.2.p: A person stays dry in snow and is not made wet by it.

D1841.4.3.p: A person walks on water without getting his feet or clothes wet.

D1841.4.3.1.p: Seas, lakes, and rivers part or pull back so that a holy man can walk through them without getting wet.

D1841.4.3.2.p: Stones thrown into the ocean stay dry instead of sinking or getting wet.

D1841.4.4.p: A saint or monk can make rain or snow avoid certain places simply by wishing it.

D1841.4.5.p: A wife's eyes are made immune to sea water by her whale husband, so salt water does not hurt them.

D1841.5.p: A person or animal cannot be harmed by weapons.

D1841.5.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Holm 26, Rink 335.
D1841.5.1.p: A man whom weapons cannot wound.

D1841.5.1.1.p: A person cannot be hurt by stones thrown at him.

D1841.5.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 262.
D1841.5.2.p: A magic animal cannot be wounded by weapons.

D1841.5.3.p: An axe cannot cut a man, no matter how hard he hits himself with it.

D1841.7.p: A magic animal cannot be harmed by hounds or dogs.

D1841.8.p: A man cannot be harmed by poison.

D1841.9.p: A person is made proof against harm from demons, so demons cannot hurt them.

D1845.p: A person's invulnerability (immunity to harm) lasts only for a set period of time.

D1845.1.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 109 n. 4, 110 n. 1.
D1845.1.p: A person is invulnerable, but only for the span of one day.

D1845.2.p: A person is invulnerable only while wearing certain clothes; without them they can be harmed.

D1846.p: A person comes to acquire invulnerability, becoming immune to harm, through some means.

D1846.1.r: (Cf. D1244.) Roscher Lexikon s.v. “Achilleus” I 24, *Grote I 218.
D1846.1.p: A person becomes invulnerable by being burned and then rubbed with magic ointments.

D1846.2.p: A many-headed monster grants a person invulnerability.

D1846.3.p: A magic horse makes its rider invulnerable.

D1846.4.r: *Von Sydow Sigurds Strid med Fåvne 27ff.; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *650A.
D1846.4.p: A person becomes invulnerable to harm by bathing in dragon's blood. The bath makes the body impossible to wound.

D1846.4.1.p: A person becomes invulnerable by bathing in dragon's blood.

D1846.5.p: A saint grants a person invulnerability.

D1846.5.1.p: A person becomes invulnerable by calling upon a saint.

D1846.5.2.p: A pious man living in a city makes a person invulnerable to harm.

D1846.6.p: A man is killed and then brought back to life as invulnerable.

D1847.p: A person loses invulnerability that they once had.

D1847.1.p: A man loses his invulnerability if he forgets his sweetheart.

D1850.r: (Cf. D1346.) Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1850.p: A person is made immortal, able to live forever and not die.

D1850.1.p: Immortality is worthless unless the person also remains forever young.

D1850.2.p: A woman is transformed into an immortal being.

D1851.p: Immortality is granted to a person by someone else.

D1851.1.r: Greek: Roscher Lexikon s.v. “Achilleus” I 24, Frazer Apollodorus II 69 n. 4, I 37 n. (burning and stripping off mortal flesh [Demophon]) *Carl-Martin Edsman Ignis Divinus: Le feu comme moyen de rajeunissement et d’immortalité (Publications of the New Society of Letters No. 34, Lund, 1949).
D1851.1.p: A person is made immortal through burning.

D1851.2.p: A person gains immortality by making a bargain with Death.

D1851.3.p: A saint grants a person immortality, so they will never die.

D1851.4.p: Christ grants a person immortality, so they will never die.

D1851.5.p: A god grants a person immortality, so they will never die.

D1853.p: A being who is immortal trades away its immortality to another, and so is allowed to die. In the note, a wounded centaur who cannot be cured gives his immortality to Prometheus and dies.

D1853.1.p: Immortality is traded for a arrangement in which the person dies on alternate days, living and dying in turns.

D1854.p: A giant cannot die as long as he keeps touching the land where he was born.

D1855.r: (Cf. D1345, D1857.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Icelandic: Boberg.
D1855.p: The moment of a person's death is put off to a later time.

D1855.1.p: A witch holds off a person's death, delaying it.
