D1855.2.r: Greek: Euripides Alcestis, *Grote I 108; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1855.2.p: Death can be put off if someone else is found to take their place as a substitute.

D1855.3.p: A saint holds off a person's death, delaying it.

D1855.4.p: Death can be put off if a man avoids breaking a taboo for forty days.

D1855.5.p: A person's life is extended for a thousand years by traveling for six months of each year.

D1855.6.p: A person's death is delayed for three generations.

D1856.r: Greek: Fox 53 (Amphiaraos); Hebrew: Genesis 5:24, 2 Kings 2:11; U.S.: Baughman.
D1856.p: A person passes into the next life without dying first.

D1856.1.p: A hero or saint is taken alive into Paradise or Heaven without dying.

D1856.1.1.p: Elijah and Enoch pass to the otherworld without dying, as told in the tale "The Two Sorrows of the Kingdom of Heaven."

D1856.2.p: Jesus Christ grants three Nephites a quasi-immortal state at the time of the resurrection.

D1857.p: A person has unusually long, magically sustained life.

D1857.1.p: An old woman has lived for ages, far beyond ordinary human years.

D1857.2.p: A fairy woman offers a warrior two hundred years of unfailing life and happiness in exchange for delaying a battle by one day.

D1860.r: BP I 86ff., 99ff., 165ff., 207ff. (Gr. Nos. 11, 13, 21, 24); *Loomis White Magic 80, 82; Cox Cinderella 481 n. 12 (most of references there given).—Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 335; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “beauté”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 17; Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 527.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 349 n. 259, (Zuñi): Parsons JAFL XXXI 244 No. 16; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 43 No. 6, (Hottentot): Bleek 76 No. 35.—See also all references to D732 and D733.
D1860.p: A general case of magic that makes a person or thing beautiful. The beautifying power is the central event, with no specific method given.

D1860.0.1.p: A fairy is made beautiful through magic.

D1862.p: A person is given lasting beauty by magic.

D1862.1.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 44.
D1862.1.p: A supernatural wife gives magic beauty to her husband.

D1862.2.p: A saint gives magic beauty to a person.

D1863.p: A person is made beautiful by being stroked or tapped with a magic object or hand.

D1864.p: A saint makes someone beautiful through prayer.

D1865.p: A person is made beautiful by being killed and then brought back to life.

D1865.1.r: *Type 531.—Italian Novella: Rotunda; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 503.
D1865.1.p: A person is made more beautiful by having the head cut off and a new head put on.

D1865.2.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 156 n. 2 (Pelops); N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 349 n. 258.
D1865.2.p: A person is made more beautiful by being boiled and then brought back to life.

D1865.2.1.p: A girl grows more beautiful as she is burned, while her brother, who loves her in an incestuous way, is turned to charcoal.

D1865.3.p: At death, the face of a pious girl becomes angelic and beautiful.

D1866.p: A general heading for other ways of making someone beautiful, apart from the listed methods.

D1866.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 70 No. 531; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: Dixon 216; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 159, 161; Tonga: Gifford 186; Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 388.
D1866.1.p: A person is made beautiful by taking a bath.

D1866.2.p: A person is made beautiful by having the skin removed.

D1866.3.p: A person is made beautiful by fasting.

D1867.p: A house or dwelling is made magically beautiful.

D1867.1.p: A poor hut is magically turned into a grand mansion.

D1868.p: An animal is made magically beautiful.

D1868.1.p: A worn-out, broken-down old horse magically becomes a magnificent riding horse.

D1870.r: (Cf. D1337, D1860, M400.) See references to following motifs: D732, D733, D621.3.—BP I 86ff., 99ff., 165ff., 207ff. (Gr. Nos. 11, 13, 21, 24); *Loomis White Magic 82; Cox Cinderella 481 n. 12. References to BP and to Cox concern motif Q2 (Kind and Unkind) which usually involves magic hideousness.—Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman.—S. A. Indian (Carajá): Métraux MAFLS XL 48, (Toba): ibid. 87; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 273.
D1870.p: A general motif for magic that leaves a person or thing permanently ugly or hideous. It covers the lasting magical qualities group as a whole.

D1871.p: A girl is turned into something hideous or ugly by magic.

D1872.p: A man is turned into something hideous or ugly by magic.

D1872.1.p: A handsome man is magically made ugly, often as a punishment or curse.

D1873.p: An object is magically made ugly or hideous.

D1873.1.p: A picture is magically made ugly or hideous.

D1880.r: Irish: Plummer clxxxiv, *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 180; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “vieille”, “rajeunissement”; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Hindu: Keith 31; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 960.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 284 n. 50; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 208, 238.
D1880.p: A general motif for magic that restores youth or makes a person young again.

D1881.p: A person magically makes himself or herself young again.

D1882.p: A supernatural being restores someone's youth.

D1883.r: (Cf. F167.9, F172.) Irish myth: Cross; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 424, 447.
D1883.p: A person is given or keeps youth that never fades or ends.

D1884.r: (Cf. D1885.1.) *Dh II 154; BP III 198 n. 3; Gaster Thespis 266, 300.
D1884.p: A person is cut into pieces and then restored to youth.

D1885.r: (Cf. D1865.) *Fb “ungdom” III 979ab.—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “rajeunissement”; Greek: Fox 114, Frazer Apollodorus I 121 n. 4.
D1885.p: A person is boiled and thereby made young again.

D1885.1.r: (Cf. D1884.) Girard de Rialle RTP I 74; *Fb “ungdom” III 979ab; Greek: Grote I 110.
D1885.1.p: A person is both dismembered and boiled to be made young again.

D1886.r: *Type 753; *BP III 198 (Gr. No. 147); *FB “ungdom” III 979; *Dh II 154, 162ff., 288; *Bolte Herrigs Archiv CII 241—266, CIV 355; Köhler-Bolte I 298; *Carl-Martin Edsman Ignis Divinus: Le feu comme moyen de rajeunissement et d’immortalité (Publications of the New Society of Letters No. 34, Lund 1949).—Icelandic: Ritterhaus 338; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “four”; German: Hartung Zs. f. Vksk. VII 89, Piger ibid. X 84; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 121 n. 4; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1886.p: A person is burned and thereby made young again.

D1886.1.p: A person is burned and the bones are thrown into a tub of milk, restoring youth.

D1887.p: A person is made young again by bathing.

D1889.p: Other, miscellaneous ways of becoming young again by magic that do not fit the earlier groups.

D1889.1.p: A person becomes young again by reading in a book.

D1889.2.p: A person is made young again simply by looking into a magic mirror.

D1889.3.p: A person is made young again by hearing the song of a pelican.

D1889.4.p: A person is made young again by smelling an apple.

D1889.5.p: A person travels to another world and has their digestive tract removed, which makes them young again.

D1889.6.r: Penzer IX 48 n.; Icelandic: *Boberg; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 227; Africa (Congo): Grenfell (Baluba) 814f., (Wachaga): Gutman 120.
D1889.6.p: A person becomes young again by shedding or changing their skin, as a snake does.

D1889.7.p: A person is made young again by being reborn, here after being eaten in fish form and born again.

D1889.8.p: A person is made young again by riding the surf of the sea.

D1889.9.p: A person is made young again by drinking from a magic horn.

D1889.10.p: A person is made young again through conjuring, that is, by performing magic spells.

D1889.11.p: A person is made young again by jumping over a cliff.

D1890.r: (Cf. D1857.) Fb “ungdom” III 979b; *Loomis White Magic 80; Penzer I 137.—Irish: Plummer clxxiv, *Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “vieux”; Estonian: Hartland Science 201; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 284 n. 50b.
D1890.p: A general heading for magic that makes a person age, or appear older, by supernatural means.

D1891.r: Icelandic: FSS 27, Boberg; Maori: Dixon 60; Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 80.
D1891.p: A person magically changes into an old man so that others will not recognize them.

D1895.p: A person is magically aged by bathing.

D1896.r: Fb “jord” II 46a; Hartland Science 197ff.—Irish myth: *Cross; England, Wales: Baughman.
D1896.p: A person is magically aged after returning from a journey to the otherworld, by touching the earth.

D1897.p: The youngest of the three Magi becomes the oldest, through the power of the Savior.

D1900.r: (Cf. D1355, D1825.1.2.) *Type 580; Kittredge Witchcraft 104ff nn. 1—22 passim; Malory Morte Darthur VIII 1; K. Reuschel “Die Sage vom Liebeszauber Karls des Grossen in dichterischen Behandlungen der Neuzeit” (Philolog. u. volkskundliche Arbeiten K. Vollmöller dargeboten, 1908, pp. 371ff.); Zs. f. Vksk. XIX 243; Crane Miraculis 389ff. No. 34.—India: Thompson-Balys; Penzer II 43; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 77; Cherokee: Mooney RBAE XIX 259 No. 12; Irish myth: *Cross.
D1900.p: A general heading for love that is produced by magic spells or charms.

D1900.0.1.p: Love that is made pure or cleansed through magic.

D1900.1.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 108 nn. 32—48 passim; Heptameron No. 1; England: Baughman.
D1900.1.p: A person gains the favor of a king or queen through magic.

D1901.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 30, 382 nn. 52—54.—England: Baughman; Icelandic: Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
D1901.p: Witches cause people to fall in love by magic.

D1903.r: (Cf. B500.) India: Thompson-Balys; Pawnee: Dorsey CI LIX 301 No. 83.
D1903.p: The power to induce love is given to a person by animals.

D1904.p: A man is given magical power that makes every woman fall in love with him, and the women smother him to death with their affection.

D1905.p: A general heading for the ways magic is used to make someone fall in love.

D1905.1.p: A girl's heart is magically taken out and fed to a man, which draws her to him.

D1905.2.p: An apple is cut in two and both halves are eaten by the pair as a love charm.

D1905.3.p: Love is brought about through a curse.

D1908.p: A general heading for cases where love is destroyed by magic.

D1908.1.p: A husband's love for his wife is magically changed into hatred.

D1910.r: Penzer I 12 n. 1; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
D1910.p: A general heading for magical powers of memory.

D1910.0.1.p: A book is written by a man who has a marvelous, magically perfect memory.

D1911.p: A person magically remembers everything he has ever learned.

D1920.p: A general heading for other lasting magical characteristics a person or thing may have.

D1921.r: Irish: Plummer clxxii, *Cross; England, U.S.: Baughman; Jewish: Neuman.
D1921.p: A person's voice has magical power to carry over great distances.

D1922.p: A person has magical power to hear very distant or faint sounds.

D1923.r: Fb “friskytte” I 373; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 2; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1923.p: A person has the magical power to hit whatever he aims at.

D1924.p: A person is magically unable to become tired.

D1925.p: A general heading for magic that makes a woman or animal able to bear children.

D1925.1.p: Barrenness is cured when the woman eats or drinks something magical.

D1925.2.p: Barrenness is cured when the woman bathes in a magical way.

D1925.4.p: Barrenness is cured when a saint blesses the woman.

D1926.p: A saint magically gives a person lasting skill at a craft, so their work is exceptionally good.

D1927.p: Someone's appetite is reduced by magic, so they barely want to eat.

D1931.p: Magic causes one person to feel hatred toward another.

D1932.p: Druids have the magic ability to pass through trees.

D1933.p: A magician lights an empty lamp just by breathing on it, and this power is used for telling the future.

D1935.p: Any work that the magic person touches gets done by itself, automatically.

D1936.p: A magical ability to run extremely fast.

D1936.1.p: A woman puts on a skin and becomes magically swift of foot.

D1960.r: *Type 410; *BP I 440, III 261; *Fb “sove” III 472b. Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 35(a), Beal XXI 312; Icelandic: Panzer Sigfrid 113ff., Krappe Scandinavian Studies X (1928) 14—25, *Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 11; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 236; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 144; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 428, Rasmussen I 310, 367, II 168, 197.
D1960.p: A person is put into a magic sleep.

D1960.1.r: **Huber Die Wanderlegende von den Siebenschläfern; Type 763*; *Chauvin VII 102 No. 376; *Hartland Science 173ff.; *Frazer Pausanias II 121; Alphabet No. 283; *Loomis White Magic 115.—Irish myth: *Cross; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 18 No. 163; Jewish: Neuman; N. A. Indian: cf. Thompson Tales 314 No. 143.
D1960.1.p: People fall into a magic sleep that lasts many years, then wake to find the world changed. The title's name refers to Rip Van Winkle.

D1960.1.1.p: A person who sleeps magically with great strength, one of the Seven Sleepers type of long sleeper.

D1960.2.r: *BP III 460; *Feilberg Danske Studier (1920) 97ff.; **Weltig Der Sagenkreis des Kyffhäusers (Bremen, 1891); *Wehrhan Die Sage 47ff.; *Hartland Science 170ff.; *Krappe “Die Sage vom König im Berge” (Mitt. d. schles. Gesell. f. Volkskunde XXX (1935) 76—102).—Celtic: MacCulloch Celtic 15, 180; England, Scotland, U.S.: *Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3595; Armenian: Ananikian 34; Jewish: Neuman; Persian: Carnoy 327; India: Thompson-Balys, Keith 173.
D1960.2.p: A king sleeps magically inside a mountain and will wake one day to help his people.

D1960.2.1.p: The sleeping king in the mountain will wake only when the shoes of his magic horse are worn thin. The horse goes around the castle every seven years.

D1960.3.p: A princess or other person sleeps by magic for a set length of time, such as a hundred years.

D1960.4.p: A magic sleep so deep it looks like death.

D1961.r: (Argus). *Frazer Apollodorus I 109 n. 4; Köhler-Bolte I 101; *Fb “øje” III 1166.
D1961.p: A watchman who never sleeps is magically put to sleep.

D1962.p: A method or means of putting someone into magic sleep.

D1962.1.p: A person is put into magic sleep by a curse.

D1962.2.r: *Type 300; Hartland Perseus III 211; *Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 62 (to Gonzenbach No. 9).—English: Child V 487 s.v. “lousing”; India: Thompson-Balys; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 2 No. 1a; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 326 n. 174; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 364; Africa (Thonga): Junod 226.
D1962.2.p: A person is put to sleep by picking lice from his head. The victim is an old person or an ogre.

D1962.3.r: *Cox Cinderella 498 n. 34; MacCulloch Childhood 31; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Dakota): Schoolcraft Hiawatha 184.
D1962.3.p: A person is put to sleep by having their hair combed or dressed while their head rests in another's lap.

D1962.3.1.p: A hero's hair is combed, which puts him into a magic sleep that lasts six months.

D1962.4.p: A character is put into a magic sleep by hypnotic suggestion, meaning words or a spoken charm alone induce the sleep.

D1962.4.1.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 322 n. 162, (Bella Coola): Boas JE I 98.
D1962.4.1.p: Someone is lulled to sleep by sleepy stories or songs, which act as a magic means of inducing sleep.

D1962.4.2.p: A crónán, a soothing song, is sung to lull children to sleep.

D1962.5.r: (Cf. B765, D1275.1.) Icelandic: Völsunga saga ch. 39 (37), Boberg.
D1962.5.p: Snakes are made to fall asleep by the music of a harp.

D1962.6.p: A character falls into magic sleep as a result of breaking a taboo, a forbidden act.

D1962.6.1.p: The hero is thrown into magic sleep when he opens a fruit too soon, before he is permitted to.

D1964.p: Magic sleep is induced by a particular person who has the power to put others to sleep.

D1964.1.p: A wild, savage elephant is lulled to sleep by a virgin maiden.

D1964.2.p: A rejected suitor, one whose courtship was refused, uses magic to put someone to sleep.

D1964.3.p: A person who has abducted someone puts the victim or others into magic sleep.

D1964.4.p: A druid, a priest of the ancient Celts, induces magic sleep in someone.

D1964.5.p: A saint induces magic sleep in someone.

D1964.6.r: Greek: Homer Iliad II 395, Odyssey XVIII 191.
D1964.6.p: A god or deity induces magic sleep in someone.

D1965.p: A guardian is magically put to sleep so that a girl can slip away to visit her lover.

D1965.1.p: A guardian is magically put to sleep so that a lover can visit the maiden.

D1967.p: A person in magic sleep is surrounded and protected by a ring of fire.

D1967.1.p: A person in magic sleep is surrounded and protected by a hedge.

D1971.r: *Types 303, 313; BP II 51, 273; Cox Cinderella 481.—Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 61 No 445A.
D1971.p: A husband or lover is put into magic sleep by a false bride, and he wakes only on the third night, the last chance to break the spell.

D1972.r: *Type 400; Chauvin V 145 No. 71 n. 1; *Fb “sove” III 472b; *Dickson 94 n. 78; Wesselski Mönchslatein 172 No. 138; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1972.p: A lover who is to meet his mistress magically oversleeps and misses the rendezvous; in the note, the lover is a husband.

D1973.p: A character falls into magic sleep in order to sleep off a period of enchantment, so that the enchantment ends.

D1975.r: (Cf. D1962.2.) *Type 300; *Hartland Perseus III 211.—French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 20; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1975.p: A hero who is about to face a dragon falls into a magical, deep sleep while waiting for the fight.

D1976.p: Things that happen to a person while they are under a magic sleep.

D1976.1.r: Dickson 223; Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: Homer Odyssey XVIII 121; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1976.1.p: A person under magic sleep is carried or moved to another place without waking.

D1976.2.p: A person under magic sleep meets the man or woman they will later marry.

D1978.p: The ways a person under magic sleep is woken up.

D1978.1.p: A magic sleep is broken when someone cuts off the sleeper's finger.

D1978.2.p: A magic sleep is broken when a tear falls onto the sleeper.

D1978.3.r: BP I 436; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XX 354; India: Thompson-Balys.
D1978.3.p: A magic sleep is broken when the enchanting instrument, such as a musical instrument, is taken away.

D1978.4.r: (Cf. D1971.) Cox Cinderella 481; Type 313; BP II 51, 273; Indonesia: DeVries’ list No. 176.
D1978.4.p: A hero is woken from magic sleep by his wife, who has bought the right to sleep in his bed from a false bride who had been lying beside him.

D1978.5.p: A magic sleep is broken when the sleeper is kissed.

D1980.r: *Type 306; *Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 214; *Chauvin VII 39 No. 212B, 103 No. 377; *Loomis White Magic 51; *Fb “usynlig”; Penzer VIII 36f.—Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 65, 208, *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 189; Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “invisibilité”; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys, Keith 152; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 49, 109f., 134 No. 92.—Africa (Zulu): Callavay 223, (Fang): Trilles 269.
D1980.p: Things or people are made magically unable to be seen.

D1981.p: Certain kinds of people are magically invisible.

D1981.2.r: (Cf. V229.8.) *Toldo IV 80; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Icelandic: Boberg.

D1982.1.p: A magic door can be seen only by men and is invisible to women.

D1982.2.p: A ship is made invisible by magic, so it cannot be seen.

D1982.3.p: A chariot is made invisible by magic, so it cannot be seen.

D1982.4.p: Food and drink appear and then vanish again in the otherworld, a place of spirits or fairies.

D1982.5.p: A boat is made invisible by magic, so it cannot be seen.

D1983.p: A person is given the power to become invisible.

D1983.1.r: (Cf. A180.) Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 127 (Paris).
D1983.1.p: A god gives a person the power of invisibility.

D1983.2.p: A fairy gives a person the power of invisibility.

D1985.p: The ways a person can acquire invisibility.

D1985.1.p: A person becomes invisible by having their skin cut or marked.

D1985.2.p: A person becomes invisible by reciting a magic formula backwards.

D2000.r: *Cox Cinderella 511; *Kittredge Witchcraft 55, 406 nn. 241, 242.—Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “oubli”; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 457, Rasmussen III 145.
D2000.p: Magic causes a person or creature to forget things.

D2003.r: (For details of the ways in which the memory is lost and regained see D2004 and D2006.—*Type 313C, 425; Tegethoff 50ff.; *BP I 442, II 56, 527, III 338, 406, 443 (Gr. Nos. 56, 67, 113, 186, 193, 198); Cox Cinderella 511; *Fb “brud” IV 65a; Jiriczek Der Vergessenheitstrank in der Niebelungensage (Zs. f. vgl. Littgsch. N. F. VII 49): Köhler-Bolte I 169.—English: Child I 461 and note; Icelandic: *Boberg; Korean: Zong in-Sob 25; American Indian (European borrowings): Thompson CColl II 343, 367—371 (Micmac, New Mexican Spanish, Thompson River, Chilcotin), (cf. Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 91 No. 5.
D2003.p: A young husband visiting his home breaks a taboo and forgets his wife; later she manages to make him remember her.

D2003.1.p: A husband is magically made to forget his wife.

D2004.p: The means by which magic forgetfulness is brought about.

D2004.1.r: *Cox Cinderella 512; Köhler-Bolte I 170.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
D2004.1.p: A curse causes a person to forget.

D2004.2.r: *Type 313; *Cox Cinderella 511 and practically all references given under D2003 (Forgotten Fiancée); *Fb “kys” II 349.—Italian Novella: Rotunda.
D2004.2.p: A kiss causes forgetfulness, so that the person kissed loses their memory.

D2004.2.1.p: A man is made to forget when a dog licks him.

D2004.3.p: A person is made to forget by eating something.

D2004.3.1.p: A person is made to forget by drinking something.

D2004.4.p: A person is made to forget by being spat upon or spat on something magic.

D2004.5.r: Type 1687*.—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “nom”; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *1687; Russian: Andrejev No. 1687*; India: Thompson—Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 303 n. 109g; Africa (Kaffir): Theal 114, (Ila, Rhodesia): Smith and Dale II 394 No. 18.
D2004.5.p: A name or magic formula is forgotten when a person stumbles or jumps.

D2004.5.1.p: A person is made to forget something simply by stumbling or tripping over a log.

D2004.6.p: A husband loses his memory of his wife when he takes off a shirt she gave him, through magic.

D2004.7.p: A person is made to forget things because of a sudden fright.

D2004.8.p: A person loses their memory through grief or prolonged mourning.

D2004.9.p: Forgetfulness is caused by visiting or being in a particular place.

D2004.9.1.p: The place of the Tower of Babel causes forgetfulness, as a specific instance of forgetting caused by a location.

D2004.10.p: The barking of brass or bronze dogs causes those who hear it to forget.

D2006.r: (Cf. D1360, D1910.) Irish: Plummer lxxx, Cross.
D2006.p: A magic event restores a person's lost memory.

D2006.1.p: A forgotten fiancée or wife restores her husband's memory through some magical or clever means.

D2006.1.1.r: *Type 313; Tegethoff 50; *BP II 231 n. 1; *Cosquin Lorraine II 28; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; Thompson River: Thompson CColl II 372 (European borrowing).
D2006.1.1.p: The forgotten fiancée wins back her forgetful husband's memory by magically delaying a rival lover, who tells the husband of the encounter. She sets up magic birds that keep falling from their roost, or the lover is stuck to a calf's tail, and the lover's account gets the husband's attention.

D2006.1.2.p: The forgotten fiancée works as a milkmaid and talks to a calf, and this reminds her husband of her.

D2006.1.3.r: *Type 313; Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 65; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2006.1.3.p: The forgotten fiancée uses magic doves that talk to each other, and this brings back her husband's memory.

D2006.1.4.r: *Types 313, 425; *BP II 234ff., 527 n. 2; Tegethoff 52f.—Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 165.
D2006.1.4.p: A forgotten fiancée buys her way into her husband's bed, and this reawakens his lost memory of her.

D2006.1.5.p: The forgotten fiancée magically stops the wedding carriage of the new bride, drawing her husband's attention and restoring his memory.

D2006.1.6.p: The forgotten fiancée is remembered through a doll that reminds the husband of her.

D2006.1.7.p: The forgotten fiancée is remembered through a bird that reminds the husband of her.

D2006.1.8.p: A piece of wood brings back a person's memory.

D2006.1.9.p: A forgotten wife is remembered when her husband sees her initials.

D2006.1.10.p: A forgotten wife gives food to a beggar, and this restores her husband's memory.

D2006.2.r: Hartland Science 200.—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 330 n. 193; *Thompson Star Husband; Melanesia: Codrington 365.
D2006.2.p: Seeing an old home again restores a person's memory and brings them back from the other world.

D2006.2.1.p: A human child of a sky-mother longs to visit their father on earth, and this longing brings back memory and draws them back to earth.

D2011.r: (Cf. F379.5.) Years spent in the other world or asleep seem as days because of magic forgetfulness. *Type 470; *Fb “tid” III 790a; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 561, 562; *Köhler-Bolte II 224ff., 406ff.; *Hartland Science 162ff.—Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 116, 119, 181f., *Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “temps”; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 101; Scottish: McKay Bealoideas III 138; English: Child V 290a; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *472; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 299, (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 459; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 314 n. 143.
D2011.p: Magic makes a person lose track of time, so that years pass in what feels like days.

D2011.1.r: **Hammerich Munken og Fuglen (København, 1933); *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 562; *Herbert III 67; Longfellow “The Golden Legend”; Hartland Science 188f.—Irish: Plummer clxxxvi, *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 104; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 472A*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 471*; Russian: Andrejev Ukazatel’ Skazochnik No. 471.
D2011.1.p: A person listening to a bird's song feels that years have passed only as moments.

D2011.1.1.p: A saint listening to music made by a bird's wing experiences a whole day as a single moment.

D2011.1.2.p: While a saint preaches, three days and three nights pass for his listeners as if they were one hour.

D2011.2.p: Two friars talking about Christ do not notice time passing from Shrovetide until the following Easter.

D2011.3.p: To the creator, years are no more than moments.

D2012.r: Hartland Science 226f.; Wesselski Märchen 255 No. 65; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXV (1933) 114f., Scandinavian Studies 19 (1947) 217—224; Irish myth: *Cross.
D2012.p: A person experiences the events of many years within a single moment.

D2012.1.r: *Chauvin VII 106 No. 94; Penzer VII 244ff.; Hartland Science 225ff.
D2012.1.p: A king dips his head under water in his bath and in that moment lives through many years of experience.

D2012.2.p: A wizard makes a man believe he has been away for twenty or forty years when only a short time has passed.

D2020.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “muet”; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 154.
D2020.p: A person is struck temporarily unable to speak because of magic.

D2021.p: The various ways by which magic muteness is brought about.

D2021.1.p: Muteness is laid on a person as a curse.

D2025.p: A person who has lost speech by magic regains it by magic means.

D2025.0.1.p: Magic removes a person's speech and later magic restores it.

D2025.1.p: A mute person's speech is magically restored when he is placed on the execution stake.

D2025.2.p: A mute person's speech is magically restored when a certain bird is caught.

D2025.3.p: A mute person's speech returns when a third person correctly guesses a secret transaction.

D2025.4.p: Muteness is magically cured when the person is astonished.

D2025.5.p: A mute person's speech is magically restored on Hallowe'en.

D2030.p: Other magical conditions that last only for a time.

D2031.r: *BP III 203; *Loomis White Magic 51; Irish myth: *Cross; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn VI (1900) 426ff., (1936) 193ff., Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 93, *Boberg.
D2031.p: A magical illusion: someone makes people or things seem to be something they are not, or makes an unreal scene appear real.

D2031.0.1.p: Holy men called saints create illusions that deceive people's senses.

D2031.0.2.p: Fairies create illusions that make people see or experience things that are not real.

D2031.0.3.p: A magic illusion disappears when someone makes the sign of the cross.

D2031.0.4.p: Druids, the priests of ancient Celtic peoples, create illusions.

D2031.0.5.r: Icelandic: Egils saga og Asm. 58, Boberg.
D2031.0.5.p: A giantess's punishment turns out to be only an illusion and does not really happen.

D2031.1.r: *BP III 203; Dickson 222 n. 18; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn VI (1900) 426ff; FSS 22—23, Boberg; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 137 No. 103; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 51 No. 99.
D2031.1.p: A magician tricks people into lifting their clothes to keep them dry, though there is no real river.

D2031.1.2.p: People swim in a river that is only imaginary, which seems to rise around them as they swim.

D2031.2.p: A piece of thread is made to look like a huge log, and a cock appears to be carrying it.

D2031.3.p: A hunted animal escapes by running through a river that exists only as an illusion.

D2031.4.p: An ugly person uses magic to make themselves appear beautiful to others.

D2031.4.1.p: A druid makes himself look ugly on one side of the body and beautiful on the other.

D2031.4.2.p: A magician takes on the forms of a swineherd, a dwarf, and a giant to seduce a queen, then later scorns her while appearing in those same forms.

D2031.4.3.p: A magician disguises himself as a beggar or an old man in order to free prisoners.

D2031.5.p: A man is magically made to believe he is a bishop, an archbishop, and the pope. When he keeps refusing to pay the magician, the magician shows him the truth.

D2031.6.p: A magic illusion is used to protect someone from pursuers.

D2031.6.1.p: A man is magically made to look to his pursuers like a woman carrying a baby.

D2031.6.2.p: A son is magically made to look to his pursuers like a spinning wheel, a buck, and a hog in turn.

D2031.6.3.p: A wife alone at home frightens robbers by making it seem that her husband is there.

D2031.6.4.p: Pursuers are confused in other ways by magic illusions.

D2031.7.p: A horse is magically disguised so that it looks like a tree trunk. The disguise hides it from those looking for it.

D2031.8.p: Through illusion, two opposing armies are each made to believe they have won the thing they were fighting over, so they stop fighting and separate.

D2031.9.p: A magician makes an enemy's last arrow look bent, so the enemy thinks it is useless and does not shoot it. This gives the magician's side time to kill him.

D2031.10.p: A spear is magically made to look like a harmless reed, so the victim does not guard against it and is treacherously killed.

D2031.11.r: Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn III (1895) 452—53, (1931) 310—11; Icelandic: Boberg.
D2031.11.p: An illusory fire is created that frightens men or stops them in their tracks, though the fire is not real.

D2031.12.p: Sea water is magically made to act like solid ground, so people can walk or stand on it.

D2031.13.p: A magic chariot or vehicle called a rath always seems far away and never comes close, no matter how far one travels toward it.

D2031.14.p: By illusion, mountains appear to be fighting or clashing with each other.

D2031.15.p: A goat appears to become two goats each time a man aims at it, so he cannot hit the real one.

D2031.16.p: A magical vision of food appears to tempt women who are fasting, trying to make them break their fast.

D2031.17.p: A storm is magically made to look like an island, so that observers mistake it for land.

D2031.18.p: A person is made to appear in several places at the same time through magic illusion.

D2032.p: Someone magically avoids becoming tired, so they can keep going without fatigue.

D2033.p: Thirst is magically made to disappear, so a person no longer feels thirsty.

D2034.p: Magic is used to make a child cry as a trick to force the child's mother to act, or to come to them.

D2035.p: Something or someone is magically made extremely heavy, so that it cannot be lifted or moved.

D2036.r: Greek: Homer Odyssey XV 66, Iliad III 139.
D2036.p: Magic causes a person to feel homesick, longing intensely for home.

D2038.p: An animal is magically made to grow larger than normal.

D2038.1.p: A centipede grows large by magic, big enough to kill a demon.

D2050.p: A person or object has a magic power that destroys or causes ruin.

D2060.r: (Cf. C920f., D1207.1, D1400, D2089.3.) Irish myth: Cross.
D2060.p: Someone is killed or physically hurt through magical power.

D2061.r: (Cf. D1402.) Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 115, 120.
D2061.p: A person is murdered by magical means rather than by ordinary force.

D2061.1.p: A list of the different ways magic can bring about a person's death.

D2061.1.1.r: (Cf. D1896.) Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer IV 232, 244; Chauvin V 16 n. 2, 293.
D2061.1.1.p: A person is magically burned until nothing is left but ash.

D2061.1.1.1.p: A person is magically turned into a heap of bones.

D2061.1.2.p: Persons are magically forced to dance until they die of exhaustion.

D2061.1.3.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 136ff., 457f. nn. 1—29 passim; Irish myth: *Cross; England, U.S.: Baughman.
D2061.1.3.p: Someone is killed by poison applied through magic.

D2061.1.4.p: Persons are magically made to waste away, rot, and die.

D2061.1.5.p: A plague or epidemic is summoned by magic to kill people.

D2061.2.p: A list of the methods used to carry out a magic murder.

D2061.2.1.r: (Cf. F555.7.) Hartland Perseus III 59f.; *Krappe Balor 1ff.; Penzer II 298, IV 232, VIII 75 n. 1; Chauvin V 16 n. 2, 293; Gaster Rabbis 225 No. 203.—Greek: Fox 35 (Gorgon); Irish myth: *Cross; England, Wales, U.S.: *Baughman; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Persian: Carnoy 336; N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 344 n. 242, (Calif): Gayton and Newman 92; Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 65.
D2061.2.1.p: A person is killed by a single look from someone with magical power.

D2061.2.1.1.p: The evil eye sets a bird on fire.

D2061.2.2.r: *Cox Cinderella 491; Herbert III 200; Oesterley No. 102; *Kittredge Witchcraft 73ff., 411ff. nn. 1—171; Irish myth: Cross; Heptameron No. 1.
D2061.2.2.p: A person is killed by harming an object or animal connected with them, which works through a sympathetic link.

D2061.2.2.1.p: A person falls dead when a spear pierces their shadow.

D2061.2.2.2.p: A spell chanted over a person's shadow causes their death.

D2061.2.2.3.p: A person is killed by abusing or destroying an image representing them.

D2061.2.2.4.p: A person is killed by abuse inflicted on their body or parts of it.

D2061.2.2.4.1.p: A person's hair is burned, and they die as a result.

D2061.2.2.5.p: A person is killed by abuse of their clothing.

D2061.2.2.5.1.p: A person dies when their gloves are boiled.

D2061.2.2.6.p: A candle is burned in a way that makes its victim waste away and die. The victim's decline is caused by the burning candle, which is a form of sympathetic magic.

D2061.2.2.7.p: An animal is mistreated or killed in order to cause a person's death through sympathetic magic.

D2061.2.2.8.p: An ordinary object is mistreated or destroyed in order to cause a person's death through sympathetic magic.

D2061.2.2.8.1.p: A needle is placed under the hearth; as it burns, it causes the victim to burn and die.

D2061.2.3.r: (Cf. D2069.1.1.) N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 345 n. 242a, (Calif.): Gayton and Newman 56, Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 114, 240, 246.
D2061.2.3.p: A person is killed merely by being pointed at with magic.

D2061.2.4.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Hebrew: 2 Kings 2:24, Neuman; Icelandic: Boberg; Eskimo: Kroeber JAFL XII 173, Turner RBAE XI 262.
D2061.2.4.p: A person is killed by a magical curse spoken against them.

D2061.2.4.1.p: A person is cursed so that they die in sin and are damned.

D2061.2.4.2.p: A clergyman's curse causes a man to die from a wound he has received.

D2061.2.5.p: A hunter is burned to ashes by the power of a heroine's chastity.

D2061.2.6.p: A person is killed by a spike that has been magically made to appear on a chair where they sit.

D2061.2.7.p: A man is killed by being shown the caul, the membrane he was born with, which is used as a magic weapon against him.

D2061.2.8.p: A horse is magically made to hang itself on a gate, causing its death.

D2061.2.9.p: Someone breathes on an enemy, and the enemy is driven onto a knife and killed.

D2062.p: A person is wounded, mutilated, or injured by magic rather than by ordinary means.

D2062.1.p: A person's heart is removed by magic.

D2062.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; German: Grimm No. 135; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2062.2.p: A person is blinded by magic.

D2062.2.1.p: A person is blinded by a curse spoken against them.

D2062.2.1.1.p: A person has a crooked or squinting look in one eye as a result of a curse.

D2062.2.2.p: Looking at a holy person causes a person to go blind.

D2062.2.3.p: A person is made to squint as a punishment, through magic.

D2062.2.4.p: Enemies are magically made unable to see each other, so they lose track of one another while hunting.

D2062.2.5.p: A person is magically blinded after being bitten by a snake.

D2062.2.6.p: A thief's cough magically makes the watchmen guarding him go blind.

D2062.3.p: A body part cut off or wounded by magic does not grow back.

D2062.4.p: A person's sexual organs are damaged or removed by magic.

D2062.4.1.p: A witch uses magic on a bride so that she loses her sexual organs.

D2062.4.2.p: A man is castrated through magic rather than by a surgeon or any physical means.

D2062.5.p: A person is magically given temporary growths on the body, such as extra parts that later go away.

D2063.p: A general heading for magic that causes discomfort or torment to a person without killing or permanently injuring them.

D2063.1.p: A person is tormented or made to suffer by magic.

D2063.1.1.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 97ff., 429ff. nn. 173—239 passim; England, U.S.: *Baughman; Feilberg DF X 165ff.; Icelandic: *Boberg.
D2063.1.1.p: A witch or other person is tormented by harming an animal or object that stands for them, such as burning it or sticking it with pins.

D2063.2.p: A person is magically made unable to lie still in bed and keeps tossing and turning.

D2063.3.r: (Cf. D1373.0.1.) Irish myth: Cross; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 105.
D2063.3.p: A person is magically given a thirst that can never be quenched.

D2063.3.1.p: Druids magically cause someone to have an unquenchable thirst.

D2063.3.1.1.p: Saints magically cause someone to have an unquenchable thirst.

D2063.4.p: A person is magically made to itch or scratch uncontrollably.

D2063.5.p: A person is magically made to break wind (pass gas) continually.

D2063.6.p: A man is magically transformed so that he barks like a dog.

D2064.r: (Cf. D1837.) Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Chinese: Graham; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 458, 467, Rasmussen III 67, 292.
D2064.p: A general heading for magic that makes a person fall ill.

D2064.0.1.p: A person is magically made to fall lovesick, pining with unrequited or enchanted love.

D2064.0.2.p: A person becomes sick at heart through magic, a magical sickness of the heart.

D2064.0.3.p: A plague or deadly epidemic is brought on by magic.

D2064.1.r: (Cf. C55, C940.1.) *Type 613; *BP I 322 n. 1; Irish: O’suilleabhain 27, Beal XXI 308.
D2064.1.p: A girl falls magically sick because she has thrown away her consecrated communion wafer.

D2064.2.p: A princess's illness rises and falls with a witch's fire: she is very sick when the witch's fire burns high and recovers when it is put out.

D2064.3.p: Someone's sickness is magically passed on to an animal, which then suffers it in the person's place.

D2064.4.r: (Cf. D2071.) Fb “sygdom” III 700a, “overse” II 771a; England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales, U.S.: *Baughman.
D2064.4.p: A person falls ill because another person has cast an evil eye on them.

D2064.5.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 372.
D2064.5.p: A person falls ill because of a curse laid on them.

D2064.6.p: A sick person is magically made worse by being wounded.

D2064.7.p: A magic sickness results from a piece of a weapon left lodged in the victim's head.

D2064.8.p: Someone magically causes a fruit-bearing plant to dry up and shrivel, and this brings sickness on a person tied to it.

D2065.r: (Cf. D2161.3.8.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 30, *382 n. 51, 124ff., 449f. nn. 1—23 passim; Irish myth: *Cross; Lithuanian: Balys Index 3512; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 167, 259, 368, 445.
D2065.p: Magic is used to drive a person mad or make them insane.

D2065.1.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 124ff., 449f. nn. 1—23 passim; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2065.1.p: A person goes mad because a demon has possessed them.

D2065.2.p: A person becomes insane after seeing a strange or uncanny sight.

D2065.2.1.p: A person is driven insane by magic after hearing a strange or uncanny sound.

D2065.3.p: Druids take away men's senses, making them lose their wits.

D2065.4.r: (Cf. D2064.2.) Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 60 No. 435*.
D2065.4.p: A princess's madness rises and falls with the height of a fire: she is more insane when the fire burns high.

D2065.5.p: A person goes insane because someone has cast an evil eye on them.

D2065.6.p: A person carried off by Echo is left mad and unable to speak.

D2065.7.p: A person goes insane because of a curse laid on them.

D2066.r: (F360.) Magic shooting of small objects into a person’s (or animal’s) body. Kittredge Witchcraft 133, 453ff. nn. 62—82 passim; *Fb “skud” III 333b, “ellefolk” I 241b.—Irish myth: Cross; England, Ireland: *Baughman.
D2066.p: A person or animal is struck down by elfshot, a magic missile fired by elves that causes sudden illness or death.

D2066.1.p: Elves obtain magic stones that have passed from fairies to mermaids, and the devil completes the work on them so they can be used to injure people. Elfshot is harm done by such magic missiles.

D2069.p: A miscellaneous motif about magic that causes a person to die or be physically hurt.

D2069.1.p: Magic makes a person fall down.

D2069.1.1.p: Someone is made to fall down just by another person pointing at a door.

D2069.2.p: Magic forces people to bend their arm against their will.

D2070.r: (Cf. D5, G200.) **Kittredge Witchcraft.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Ynglinga saga 29, Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 200.
D2070.p: Casting harmful spells on people, called bewitching.

D2070.1.r: (Cf. D991.3, D1274.1.) North Carolina: Brown Collection I 668.
D2070.1.p: A magic hairball is used to bewitch someone.

D2071.r: *Krappe Balor 9ff.; *Chauvin V 161 No. 84, VIII 143 No. 144 n. 1; *Fb “öje” III 1167ab, 1168a; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 686; Elworthy The Evil Eye (London, 1895); Jahn Über den Aberglauben des bösen Blicks bei den Alten; Pitre Le jettatura ed il mal occhio in Sicilia (Kolozsvár, 1884); Seligman Der böse Blick und Verwandtes (Berlin, 1910); Maclagen, R. C. The Evil Eye in the Western Highlands (London, 1902); Penzer II 298; *Hertz Abhandlungen 181ff.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2071.p: The evil eye: a person bewitches another just by a glance.

D2071.0.1.p: An evil eye is hidden behind seven veils so it cannot harm anyone.

D2071.0.1.1.p: An evil eye is covered with a bag or hide while its owner is stoned, so the owner is harmless.

D2071.0.2.p: A person gains the evil eye after being exposed to a magic concoction.

D2071.0.3.p: A man with the evil eye cannot look at any living thing before breakfast without making it wither and die.

D2071.1.r: See references for D1070, Magic ornaments, a large number of which are used to keep off the Evil Eye. India: Thompson-Balys.
D2071.1.p: Methods of averting or protecting against the evil eye.

D2071.1.1.r: (Cf. D1001, D1776.) *Fb “spytte” III 514b; Irish myth: Cross.
D2071.1.1.p: The evil eye is averted by spitting.

D2071.1.2.p: The evil eye is averted by swinging a cat over a child's cradle.

D2071.1.3.p: A person pretends to change sex to confuse the evil eye and avoid its harm.

D2071.1.4.p: Wearing or using black is a guard against the evil eye.

D2071.1.5.p: The evil eye is turned back: when its glance is returned, it blights the person who originally cast it.

D2071.2.p: A person kills others by the power of the evil eye.

D2071.2.1.p: A person kills animals just by glancing at them with the evil eye.

D2072.r: (Cf. D1410.) *Type 952; *BP III 453; Chauvin V 16 n. 2; Tawney I 408, 417, 458; *Fb “stjæle” III 575a; Kittredge Witchcraft 201f. nn. 104—110; Alphabet 624; *Loomis White Magic 56f.—Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Göngu-Hrólfs saga 242, Boberg; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 300 No. 10; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2072.p: A general case of magic paralysis: a person or thing is made helpless or unable to move by magic.

D2072.0.1.r: Fb “sværd” III 690a; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman.
D2072.0.1.p: A sword is magically made helpless so it cannot be used in a fight.

D2072.0.2.p: An animal is magically made unable to move.

D2072.0.2.1.r: (Cf. D1654.12.) Fb “hest” IV 212a; Irish myth: Cross; England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales, U.S.: *Baughman.
D2072.0.2.1.p: A horse is enchanted so that it stands still and cannot go forward.

D2072.0.2.1.1.p: A horse or ox pulling a wagon is magically stopped by a witch, so the wagon cannot move.

D2072.0.2.2.p: A bird is magically paralyzed and cannot fly or move.

D2072.0.2.2.1.p: A man whose job is to keep birds away from the crops locks them in a barn, which is usually roofless, using magic, and then goes to town.

D2072.0.2.3.p: A team of oxen is magically paralyzed and cannot move.

D2072.0.2.4.p: A mule is magically paralyzed by a witch and cannot move.

D2072.0.2.5.p: Pigs are magically paralyzed by a witch and cannot move.

D2072.0.2.6.p: A dog is magically paralyzed and cannot move.

D2072.0.3.r: (Cf. D1419.3, F302.3.1.2, F402.1.13.) *BP II 265 n. 1, IV 196 n. 1.—Irish myth: *Cross; Italian: Basile I No. 6; U.S.: Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2072.0.3.p: A ship is magically held back so it cannot sail on.

D2072.0.4.p: A bird is overpowered when someone steps on its shadow, so it drops the meat it has stolen.

D2072.0.5.r: (Cf. D5.1, G256.3, G257.) England, Scotland, U.S.: *Baughman.
D2072.0.5.p: A person is magically paralyzed and cannot move.

D2072.0.5.1.p: A witch magically stops a person from drinking.

D2072.0.5.2.p: A person who yawns is magically unable to close their mouth afterward.

D2072.0.5.3.p: A talkative wife has her tongue magically paralyzed so she cannot speak.

D2072.1.p: A person or thing is paralyzed by the evil eye, a harmful glance believed to carry magic.

D2072.2.p: A person or thing is paralyzed by a curse.

D2072.2.1.p: A witch uses a charm to cause paralysis.

D2072.3.p: A saint's magic leaves someone unable to move or act, frozen in place.

D2072.4.p: Magic is used to stop someone from being able to carry out a task or job.

D2072.5.p: A house protected by magic freezes thieves in place when they enter with criminal intent, while honest visitors are fed and welcomed.

D2072.6.p: A magic song paralyzes those who hear it, leaving them unable to move.

D2074.p: Someone uses magic to draw or pull a person, animal, or thing toward them.

D2074.1.r: (Cf. D1440, D2156.) *Toldo VIII 21; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Þiðriks saga II 271—75, Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 324.
D2074.1.p: Magic is used to call animals to come to the person doing the calling.

D2074.1.1.p: Magic is used to call mammals, such as land animals, to come near.

D2074.1.1.1.p: Magic is used to call buffalo to come to the caller.

D2074.1.1.2.p: Deer are summoned to come by means of singing.

D2074.1.1.3.p: A bear is summoned to come by magic.

D2074.1.2.r: Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 324, (Greenland): Rink 116, 153; Marquesas, Tuamotu: Beckwith Myth 269, 289; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 94.
D2074.1.2.p: Magic is used to call fish or sea animals to come to the caller.

D2074.1.2.1.r: N. A. Indian (Calif.): Gayton and Newman 83.
D2074.1.2.1.p: Coyote uses his magic to call the largest fish to come to him.

D2074.1.3.p: Magic is used to call birds to come to the caller.

D2074.2.p: A general category of magical means used to draw someone or something near.

D2074.2.1.p: A person is summoned simply by someone thinking about them.

D2074.2.2.p: A person is summoned by burning a lock of their hair.

D2074.2.2.1.p: Someone strikes their long braided hair on the ground, and this summons a goddess to help them.

D2074.2.3.p: Something or someone is summoned simply by wishing for it.

D2074.2.3.1.p: A mistress is summoned to come just by someone wishing for her.

D2074.2.3.2.p: A ship is summoned to come to someone just by their wishing for it.

D2074.2.4.p: A spirit or genie is called up by writing its name on slips of paper and burning them.

D2074.2.4.1.p: A foster-mother is summoned simply by speaking her name aloud.

D2074.2.4.2.p: Animals are summoned by pronouncing their names.

D2074.2.4.3.p: A helper appears when the person calls out his name.

D2074.2.4.4.r: *Krappe Archiv. f. d. Studium d. neueren Sprachen CLVIII 16ff.
D2074.2.4.4.p: A written request for a spirit's help is left on a card, so the spirit comes to do the task.

D2074.2.5.p: A spirit or supernatural being is summoned through prayer.

D2074.2.5.1.p: A cleric who was imprisoned is brought to answer a saint's prayers when the saint performs a ritual.

D2076.p: A saint magically causes druids who intended to curse him to bless him instead.

D2078.p: A person is trapped or shut up by magic.

D2078.1.p: A witch is forced by magic into a boulder and kept shut inside it.

D2079.p: Other magical ways of harming or bewitching someone that do not fit the other categories.

D2079.1.r: (Cf. D2063.5.) N. A. Indian (Calif.): Gayton and Newman 83.
D2079.1.p: A person is magically compelled to break wind (pass gas) under certain conditions.

D2080.p: Magic is used to damage or destroy someone's property.

D2081.r: (Cf. D1563.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 171, 488f. nn. 59, 63, 64; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 383 n. 5; Irish myth: *Cross; England, U.S.: *Baughman; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 85 No. 750B.
D2081.p: Land is magically made barren so nothing will grow on it.

D2081.1.p: The earth dries up and becomes barren over three years while the hero is buried under it.

D2082.0.1.p: Trees are magically made to stop bearing fruit.

D2082.0.2.p: A tree withers and dies through magic.

D2082.1.p: A magic glance turns a tree to ashes. Another magic power restores it.

D2082.2.p: A holy hermit burns up a tree with one blast of his fiery breath.

D2083.p: Magic is used maliciously against a household's dairy, spoiling or stealing milk and butter.

D2083.1.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 480 n. 1; Irish myth: Cross; England, Scotland, U.S.: *Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2083.1.p: Magic is used to make a person's cows stop giving milk.

D2083.2.p: Magic makes cows produce milk that is spoiled or unfit to drink.

D2083.2.1.p: A witch uses magic so that the cows give bloody milk.

D2083.2.2.p: A witch uses magic so that a cow gives curdled milk.

D2083.3.r: (Cf. D1605.2, C2087.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 163, 482 n. 4; England, Scotland, Ireland, U.S.: *Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 5653.
D2083.3.p: Magic is used to draw milk out of another person's cow so that the thief gets it.

D2083.3.1.p: Milk is taken from another's cow by squeezing or pulling an axe handle or similar object, which magically draws the milk away.

D2083.3.2.p: A witch uses a rope made of hair to magically draw milk from another person's cows.

D2083.3.3.p: A witch magically moves milk from another person's cows into her own vessel.

D2083.4.p: Butter is magically taken from another person's dairy and transferred to the thief.

D2084.p: Magic stops manufacturing or craft processes from working properly.

D2084.1.p: Magic prevents beer from brewing or fermenting.

D2084.2.r: (Cf. D1573, D2083.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 167, 485f. nn. 30—35; England, Ireland, U.S.: Baughman.
D2084.2.p: Magic prevents butter from forming in the churn.

D2084.3.p: A saint causes dyes to fail to take or to work incorrectly.

D2085.p: Magic makes game animals wary and hard to catch or shoot.

D2085.1.p: A curse placed by a saint makes a river or lake barren so it has no fish.

D2086.p: Magic makes weapons dull or ineffective.

D2086.1.r: **U. Priebe Stumpfmachen der Schwerten durch Zauber (Kiel Diss., Stettin, 1906); Zs. f. Vksk. XIII 213, XV 349, XVII 329; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 46, 302, 260, *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman.
D2086.1.p: Magic makes a sword dull so it cannot cut.

D2086.1.1.p: An executioner's sword is magically changed into wood so it cannot cut the condemned person.

D2086.2.p: A witch uses magic so that guns no longer work.

D2086.3.p: A magic power causes an enemy's weapons to be blown or knocked out of their hands. It is a way of disarming foes without physical contact.

D2087.p: Magic is used to steal things, so that goods vanish without any thief being seen. This is the general heading for magical theft.

D2087.1.p: Someone's crops are taken away by magic rather than by a human thief. The harvest disappears from the fields.

D2087.2.p: A hunter's catch is taken by magic during the night. The game he caught disappears overnight.

D2087.3.p: Sheep or cattle vanish every night through magic. The animals are lost again and again.

D2087.3.1.p: A cow and its herder vanish together every New Year's night. Both the animal and the person are taken by magic on that night.

D2087.4.p: Men vanish every night by magic. People are taken away one after another without explanation.

D2087.5.p: Gold is stolen by magic. The treasure disappears without any visible thief.

D2087.6.p: Food is taken by magic. Stores of provisions disappear through supernatural means.

D2087.7.p: Witches go through the drawers of chests in a house and rifle through them. Their search of the household goods is done by magic.

D2087.8.p: A witch steals potatoes and leaves no trace of the theft. The potatoes simply go missing.

D2088.r: Krappe Balor 2 n. 9; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
D2088.p: Locks open by magic, without keys or force. Doors and chests unlock themselves through supernatural power.

D2088.0.1.p: On the night of Christ's Nativity, every lock in the land opens by itself. Locks everywhere are unfastened on Christmas night.

D2088.1.p: A fairy gets into a city that is locked up, using magic to pass through its closed gates. The fairy enters despite the locks.

D2089.p: A miscellaneous heading for magic used to harm property in ways not covered by other headings. It covers various damaging spells against goods and possessions.

D2089.1.p: A man uses magic to make all the iron in an enemy's storehouse vanish, so that the enemy cannot make weapons. The iron disappears and weapons become impossible to forge.

D2089.2.p: A curse makes stones useless for their purpose. Stones stop working or serving as intended.

D2089.3.p: Animals are struck dead by magic. The creatures die suddenly through supernatural power.

D2089.3.1.p: Magic keeps swine from getting fat. The pigs stay lean no matter how they are fed.

D2089.4.p: A saint makes a mill wheel turn backwards. The mill runs in reverse by holy power.

D2089.5.p: A curse makes written books unreadable, so their text can no longer be read.

D2089.6.p: Magic destroys a house, reducing it to ruin or collapse.

D2089.7.p: Magic makes a person's goods or supplies steadily shrink and disappear.

D2089.7.1.p: Food shrinks away to nothing as soon as it has been cooked.

D2089.8.p: Magic sets a person's clothing on fire and burns it.

D2089.9.p: Magic closes a trail or path so that it can no longer be followed.

D2089.9.1.p: Magic covers a trail with thorns so that it cannot be followed or passed.

D2089.10.p: Magic stops fire drills from working, so no fire can be made by friction.

D2090.p: Other magic powers that destroy or harm, not covered by the preceding headings.

D2091.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 516.
D2091.p: Magic is used as a weapon to attack an enemy.

D2091.1.p: Magic calls down fire from the sky onto an enemy.

D2091.2.p: Magic calls down a plague of frogs on an enemy.

D2091.2.1.p: Magic calls down an army of snakes and frogs on an enemy.

D2091.3.p: Magic makes streams of blood pour down upon an enemy.

D2091.4.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 189; Africa (Duala): Lederbogen Fables 62, (Ekoi): Talbot 127.
D2091.4.p: Magic makes enemies turn on each other and fight among themselves.

D2091.5.p: Magic calls down storms upon an enemy.

D2091.6.p: Magic makes enemies suffer from raging thirst.

D2091.7.p: Magic sends a lake or river against an enemy to overwhelm them.

D2091.7.1.p: Magic makes a river rise up against an enemy.

D2091.8.p: Magic brings a drought upon an enemy to destroy them.

D2091.8.1.p: Magic priests (druids) dry up the water supply in an enemy's camp, leaving the enemy without drink.

D2091.9.p: A magician brings down paralysis on an enemy, leaving them unable to move.

D2091.10.p: Magical heat is sent against enemies so that they melt away or wither.

D2091.10.1.p: Stones or similar objects are magically made hot so that they burn the feet of enemies.

D2091.11.p: A magician blows a black cloud onto an enemy to overwhelm or harm them.

D2091.12.p: Magic makes plants and animals shriek, so that the sounds frighten an enemy.

D2091.13.p: An army is halted in its tracks by a curse pronounced by a saint.

D2091.14.p: A magician shoots a magic arrow from each of his fingers to attack an enemy.

D2091.15.p: Magical slipping or collapse of the earth swallows or overcomes enemies.

D2091.16.p: An enemy is magically shut in by walls, trapped inside.

D2092.p: A magician causes a man to sink into mud and become stuck or drowned.

D2093.r: *Saintyves Essais 180ff.; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman.
D2093.p: Walls are knocked down by magic, as the walls of Jericho were.

D2094.p: A plague or disease is magically sent upon domestic animals, killing or sickening them.

D2095.p: Someone or something vanishes by magic.

D2095.1.p: A whole village and its people vanish by magic.

D2096.p: A magician causes something to rot or decay rapidly.

D2097.p: A magician stirs up trouble or discord by magic.

D2098.p: A ship is sunk by magic.

D2099.p: A miscellaneous magic power that destroys or harms, not covered by the more specific headings.

D2099.1.p: A person loses a skill or ability through magic.

D2099.2.p: A person is banished from a place by magic.

D2099.3.p: A magic power causes a house to collapse or be crushed.

D2099.4.p: A magic power breaks calabashes (gourd vessels).

D2100.p: Wealth that comes through magic, such as treasure or riches produced by supernatural means.

D2100.1.r: (Cf. D1652.) Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys, Tawney I 350f., 471.
D2100.1.p: A treasure that never runs out, no matter how much is taken from it.

D2100.2.r: (Cf. D1288, D2106.) *Loomis White Magic 87; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2100.2.p: A coin that duplicates itself, so that spending it leaves more coins.

D2101.r: *Type 613. See also N530—N549, Discovery of treasure.
D2101.p: Treasure is found through magical means rather than by chance or search.

D2101.1.p: Treasure is located by sprinkling the ground with the blood of a white rooster.

D2101.2.p: Jewels fall as a shower from the sky, drawn down by magic.

D2102.1.p: Gold comes out of someone's mouth by magic.

D2102.2.p: A valley fills with gold when someone commands it.

D2102.2.1.p: A field turns to gold after a holy ascetic plows it.

D2102.3.p: A saint produces treasure by supernatural power.

D2102.4.p: A son born of a supernatural bride to a king has the power to make gold, including gold buildings and ornaments.

D2102.5.p: Magic corn turns to gold when an animal eats it.

D2105.r: (Cf. D1470.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; German: Grimm Nos. 90, 121, 179; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 229, 325, 422, 454, Holm 40; Rasmussen I 239, 374, III 51, (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 63, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM 245; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 484, (Toba) ibid. (1) 368; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 115 No. 9, (Ibo): Thomas 119.
D2105.p: Food and other supplies appear by magical means.

D2105.1.p: Food or supplies are given in answer to someone's prayer.

D2105.1.1.p: Starvation is averted because someone composes a hymn.

D2105.2.p: A messenger from heaven brings food or supplies.

D2105.3.p: Rubbish or refuse is magically transformed into edible food and wearable clothing.

D2105.3.1.p: Trash is magically transformed into food that can be eaten.

D2105.4.p: Drink is produced by magic, appearing without being brought or bought.

D2105.5.p: A holy man makes fish come up out of a lake to feed guests when he has no other food to offer.

D2105.6.p: Magic brings down a shower of grain, so that food appears without being grown or gathered.

D2105.7.p: Magic makes fruit appear on a tree or be taken from it without ordinary growing or picking.

D2106.p: Magic makes objects increase in number, so that a small amount becomes many.

D2106.1.r: (Cf. D2100.2, V220.) *Toldo VI 289; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2106.1.p: A saint uses magic to make objects multiply in number.

D2106.1.1.p: A saint works magic so that a body of water becomes full of fish.

D2106.1.1.1.p: Fish are caught in a field that has no water, because a saint has made the fish appear there.

D2106.1.2.p: A saint miraculously multiplies animals so that their number greatly increases.

D2106.1.3.p: A saint multiplies a quantity of metal, making more of it appear.

D2106.1.4.p: After a saint dies, his corpse multiplies so that several communities each receive a body to claim.

D2106.1.5.p: A saint multiplies a supply of food so there is enough to feed everyone.

D2106.2.p: A single sack of charcoal magically multiplies into one hundred sacks.

D2106.3.p: A tree grows from a single cake and bears cakes of every kind hanging from its branches.

D2107.p: A warrior's weapons, armor, and other gear appear by magic when he needs them.

D2107.1.p: A hero who offers incense to the sacred bull Nandia is given a horse and the weapons he needs.

D2120.r: *Type 400, 566; Chauvin V 231 No. 130 n. 1.—Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 84 No. 750A*; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 676; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 102; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 53.
D2120.p: A person or thing is moved from place to place by magic rather than by ordinary travel.

D2121.r: *Type 400; *Huet RTP XXXII 97, 145; Wesselski Theorie 23.—Irish myth: Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Ferguson 128; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 219; Africa (Benga): Nassau 214 No. 33.
D2121.p: A journey is made by magic, covering distance quickly or effortlessly.
