D2151.0.1.p: A saint magically changes the temperature of water.

D2151.0.2.p: Water is magically made to dry up.

D2151.0.3.p: A wall of water is magically kept off or driven away.

D2151.1.r: (Cf. D911.) Irish: Plummer cxlvii, *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 230, 453.
D2151.1.p: A magical power to control the sea.

D2151.1.1.p: A sea is created by magic.

D2151.1.2.p: The tide is magically held back from coming in or going out.

D2151.1.2.1.r: (Cf. V250.) *Ward Catalogue of Romances II 602; Crane Miraculis 91 No. 22.
D2151.1.2.1.p: The Virgin Mary holds back the tide.

D2151.1.2.2.r: (Cf. D1713, V220.) *Loomis White Magic 40; Irish myth: *Cross.
D2151.1.2.2.p: A saint holds back the tide.

D2151.1.2.3.p: A grave on the shore rises up with the incoming tide.

D2151.1.3.r: (Cf. D1766.1, D2151.3.) Irish myth: Cross; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G 3/109).
D2151.1.3.p: The sea is calmed in answer to prayer.

D2151.1.4.p: Through magic, the sea turns into a level field of flowers, as if it were a meadow rather than water.

D2151.2.r: *Loomis White Magic 40f.; Irish: Plummer cxlvii—cxlviii, *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; Persian: Carnoy 339.
D2151.2.p: A magic power controls the flow and course of rivers.

D2151.2.1.r: *Loomis White Magic 40; Irish myth: Cross; Korean: Zong in-Sob 70.
D2151.2.1.p: Through magic, a river's current is made to flow backward, in the opposite direction.

D2151.2.1.1.r: (Part stands still, rest flows.) Africa (Wakweli): Bender 87.
D2151.2.1.1.p: Through magic, a river is split so that its flow divides and parts to leave a path through it.

D2151.2.2.p: A holy person causes a river to swell and flood over its banks.

D2151.2.3.p: Through magic, rivers are dried up so that their water disappears.

D2151.2.3.1.p: An evil spirit holds back the water of a river so that it stops flowing.

D2151.2.4.p: A holy person causes a river to freeze over even though it is summer.

D2151.2.5.r: N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 31.
D2151.2.5.p: A stream of water suddenly appears by magic where none was before.

D2151.2.5.1.p: When desert travelers pray, a river magically appears to supply them with water.

D2151.2.6.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 484.
D2151.2.6.p: Through magic, a river is made wider than it was.

D2151.3.p: A magic power controls the waves of the sea or other water.

D2151.3.1.r: Marquesas: Handy 65; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G 3/109); Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 300, (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 516; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 386.
D2151.3.1.p: Through magic, a huge tidal wave is raised.

D2151.3.2.r: (Cf. D1388.) Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 875.
D2151.3.2.p: Crashing waves do not touch a holy person, who stays dry despite the storm.

D2151.4.r: Irish: Plummer xxxi, *Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 841.
D2151.4.p: Through magic, a whirlpool is calmed and its swirling stops.

D2151.5.p: A magic power controls the water in a pond or tank.

D2151.5.1.p: Water is drawn up out of a tank by singing, without any other means.

D2151.5.1.1.p: Water is raised from a tank by burying a ring in it, with magic doing the work.

D2151.5.2.p: Through magic, a pond is made to dry up completely.

D2151.6.r: (Cf. A941.5, D927, D1567, F933.) Irish myth: Cross.
D2151.6.p: A magic power controls wells and springs, causing them to flow or dry up.

D2151.6.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G 3/403); N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 31.
D2151.6.1.p: A holy man magically causes wells or springs to stop producing water.

D2151.6.2.p: A man magically draws all the water of a spring into a small brass pot.

D2151.7.p: A magician or holy person controls the water of a lake by magic.

D2151.7.1.p: A saint magically makes a lake dry up.

D2151.8.r: (Cf. D1542.3, D1549.3.1.) Mangaia (Cook Islands): Beckwith Myth 103; Samoa: Clark 74; Marquesas: Handy 109.
D2151.8.p: Someone causes a flood by magic.

D2152.p: A magician or holy person has power to control mountains by magic.

D2152.1.r: Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 190; Irish myth: *Cross; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 236; Africa (Bakuba): Einstein 160.
D2152.1.p: A magician levels a mountain by magic, making it flat.

D2152.2.p: A magician is able to throw mountains down on enemies.

D2152.3.p: A mountain is blown away by magic.

D2152.4.r: Irish myth: Cross; N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 31.
D2152.4.p: A magician makes a mountain grow taller by magic.

D2152.5.p: A saint moves a mountain from one place to another.

D2153.p: A magician or holy person has power to control rocks by magic.

D2153.1.p: A rock standing in the sea is created by magic.

D2153.1.1.p: An island is created by magic.

D2156.p: A magician or holy person has power over animals by magic.

D2156.1.p: By magic power, a person makes does (female deer) give milk.

D2156.2.p: A single cow miraculously produces an abundance of milk.

D2156.2.1.p: A single cow miraculously gives enough milk to feed a saint and all his disciples.

D2156.3.p: A saint compels a wild beast, such as a leopard or wolf, to return a child or domestic animal it has stolen to its mother or owner.

D2156.4.p: A saint scolds a wild boar for its raids and damage, and the boar obeys him.

D2156.5.p: A saint has magical power over dangerous snakes, which become easily controlled and harmless at his word.

D2156.5.1.p: A saint commands a serpent that has bitten a man to take back its venom, and the poison is withdrawn.

D2156.5.2.p: A saint, by his intervention, drives snakes out of a person's body.

D2156.6.p: A saint magically destroys harmful insects that are damaging people's crops or lives.

D2156.7.p: A saint orders cicadas either to sing praises of God or to be silent, since their noise disturbs his preaching.

D2156.8.p: A saint forces a wolf to take the place of a calf the wolf has eaten, so the wolf becomes a substitute for the lost animal.

D2156.9.p: A saint causes a cuckoo to call out in winter, when cuckoos normally do not sing.

D2156.10.p: Horses or oxen coming from the sea are magically put temporarily at a man's service, then released.

D2156.11.p: A saint kills a lion by striking it with his slipper.

D2157.p: A person magically controls the fertility of the soil and the growth of crops.

D2157.1.r: (Cf. D1563, D2081, F349.4, F733.) Dickson 122 nn. 69, 70; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 145; Loomis White Magic 82; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 85 No. 750B; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2157.1.p: Land is magically made fertile so that it becomes productive.

D2157.1.1.p: A saint scratches the surface of the earth with his spear, and buried treasures of gold and silver are revealed.

D2157.2.r: Dh I II 61ff.; Irish: Cross, O’Suilleabhain 15, 18, Beal XXI 305f.; Icelandic: *Boberg; England, Scotland: Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 200ff.; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 120.
D2157.2.p: Crops grow magically and quickly, far faster than normal.

D2157.2.0.1.p: Rice grows to maturity within a single day by magic.

D2157.2.1.p: A saint's crops grow magically and quickly.

D2157.2.2.p: During a famine, a saint causes wheat to ripen early so that people have food.

D2157.3.p: Withered and dead trees suddenly bloom and come back to life when a saint commands it.

D2157.3.1.p: Apple trees bear fruit because of a saint's blessing.

D2157.3.2.p: A tree that had hidden treasure in its roots regains life and green leaves after the treasure is given away.

D2157.4.p: A tree grows to full size miraculously and very quickly.

D2157.5.p: Poor, barren soil is magically turned into a beautiful garden overnight.

D2157.6.p: A field is plowed and sown by magic, without any human labor.

D2158.r: (Cf. D1271.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
D2158.p: A magic power to control fire, either starting it or putting it out.

D2158.1.p: Fire is created by magic, without ordinary means such as flint or matches.

D2158.1.1.p: A fox makes fire by striking its tail against the ground.

D2158.1.2.p: A saint sets a stone on fire.

D2158.1.3.p: Fire obeys holy men: it does what saints command.

D2158.1.3.1.p: A saint, either personally or through his relics, brings a large fire under control.

D2158.1.3.2.p: Fire will not catch on or burn holy garments, wooden altars, or similar sacred objects; it turns away from them.

D2158.1.4.p: A magician opens his eyes and a forest bursts into flame twenty-four miles ahead of him.

D2158.1.5.p: A saint produces fire by supernatural means whenever it is needed.

D2158.1.5.1.p: A saint lights her lamp or candle without using any fire.

D2158.1.5.2.p: Food is cooked and bread baked without any fire being used.

D2158.2.r: (Cf. D1656, Q492.) Köhler-Bolte I 417; *Oertel Studien zur vgl. Littgsch. VIII 113; Irish: Plummer cxxxviii, *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 816; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 176.
D2158.2.p: A magic power to put out fires.

D2161.r: *Type 712; *Kittredge Witchcraft 30, 385 n. 64; *Fb “sygdom” III 699b; *Weinrich Antike Heilungswunder (Giessen, 1909); Wesselski Mönchslatein 136 No. 116; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 118; Eskimo (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 170, 193, 240, 248, (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 43, 82, (Greenland): Rink 279, 327, 370, 431, 440, 459, 467, Rasmussen III 172, 190, 209.
D2161.p: A general magic power to heal the sick and injured.

D2161.1.p: A magic cure that works for particular named diseases.

D2161.1.3.p: A woman's pain in childbirth is magically eased.

D2161.2.r: (Cf. D1503.) Finnish: Kalevala rune 9; English: Wells 80 (Sir Tristrem); Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1224; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 113, 440.
D2161.2.p: A wound is healed by magic.

D2161.2.1.p: A cow is cut up for steaks while alive, yet she heals herself by magic and is whole again. The motif describes a wound-healing miracle in which the animal survives being butchered.

D2161.2.2.p: Bleeding from a wound is stopped by magic.

D2161.3.p: A physical defect or disability is removed by magic.

D2161.3.1.r: (Cf. D1505.) Fb “blind” IV 45b; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1153, 1234.
D2161.3.1.p: A person who is blind is made to see again by magic.

D2161.3.1.1.p: Eyes that have been torn out are magically restored in the person's head. It is a form of magic cure for blindness.

D2161.3.2.r: Krappe Zeitschrift für Englische Philologie XLIX 361—369; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Lagerholm 66—68, Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule, Nouvelles de Sens No. 12; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2161.3.2.p: A hand that has been cut off is magically reattached or restored.

D2161.3.3.r: Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 43.
D2161.3.3.p: Broken bones or limbs are healed by magic.

D2161.3.3.1.p: A witch burns her child's legs to use as firewood, then covers the child with a sheet and the child is whole again. The child's legs are restored by her magic.

D2161.3.4.p: Baldness is cured by magic, so that hair grows back.

D2161.3.4.1.p: Skin covered with feathers is magically grafted onto a bald head, so the person grows a covering. It is a magic cure for baldness.

D2161.3.5.p: Deafness is cured by magic, so the person can hear again.

D2161.3.6.p: Muteness, the inability to speak, is cured by magic.

D2161.3.6.1.p: A tongue that has been cut out is magically restored, so the person can speak again.

D2161.3.7.p: Lameness, the inability to walk properly, is cured by magic.

D2161.3.7.1.p: A lame animal is cured by magic and can walk normally again.

D2161.3.8.p: Madness or mental illness is cured by magic.

D2161.3.8.1.p: A magical remedy that cures epilepsy, the disorder causing seizures, is described.

D2161.3.9.p: Bad breath is cured by magic.

D2161.3.10.p: Infertility, the inability to have children, is cured by magic.

D2161.3.11.p: A barren woman or man is magically made able to have children.

D2161.4.p: This heading collects the various ways a magical cure can be carried out.

D2161.4.0.1.p: A sick person is cured by doing what a saint told them to do in a dream.

D2161.4.1.r: (Cf. D1500.3.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 94, 424f. nn. 137—145; England, U.S.: *Baughman; Irish myth: *Cross.
D2161.4.1.p: A disease is cured by passing it on to an animal, which then takes the sickness away.

D2161.4.2.p: A disease is cured by moving it into some inanimate object, which then carries the illness away.

D2161.4.2.1.p: A ghost takes a boil away from a sick person and moves it onto a wooden post.

D2161.4.2.2.p: A saint moves a person's disease into his bell (bachall, a staff or crozier), which takes on the sickness.

D2161.4.2.3.p: A saint removes a thorn from someone's foot and moves it into a rock.

D2161.4.2.4.p: A disease is cured by moving it into a tree, which takes on the sickness.

D2161.4.3.p: A sick person is cured by passing through the earth at a crossroads.

D2161.4.4.p: A person is cured by repairing an image (such as a statue or doll) that has the same deformity as their body.

D2161.4.5.r: (Cf. F950.3.) *Kittredge Witchcraft 148, 467 n. 92; *Oertel Studien zur vgl. Littgsch. VIII 115; Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 477 s.v. “durchkriechen”; A. F. Schmidt Hultræer i Danmark (Danske Studier 1932, 33ff.); Kr. Nyrop Kludetræet (Dania I (1890), 1ff. and 309); Irish myth: Cross; England, U.S.: *Baughman.
D2161.4.5.p: A patient is cured by being passed through a cleft in a tree, a form of ritual passing through an opening.

D2161.4.6.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 95ff., 424f. nn. 146—154; *Fb “levende” II 403b—404; Feilberg Levende begravet (Aarbog for dansk kulturhistorie 1892).
D2161.4.6.p: A living animal is buried alive as a way to cure a disease.

D2161.4.7.p: An animal is burned to cure a disease, especially a disease among animals.

D2161.4.8.r: (Cf. D1787.) Or where he is buried. Kittredge Witchcraft 31, 386 n. 68.
D2161.4.8.p: Grain is burned on the spot where a man has died, as a way to cure a disease.

D2161.4.9.r: (Cf. V81.) Kittredge Witchcraft 145, 464 n. 61; England: Baughman.
D2161.4.9.p: Baptism itself is used as a magical cure for illness.

D2161.4.9.1.r: Sign of cross, prayer, etc. Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
D2161.4.9.1.p: Some other religious ceremony, not baptism, is used as a magical cure for illness.

D2161.4.10.p: A disease is cured by the same person or thing that caused it.

D2161.4.10.0.1.p: Only one particular person has the power to heal a certain wound.

D2161.4.10.1.p: A wound is healed by the same spear that inflicted it.

D2161.4.10.2.r: D2161.2.) *Schoepperle Tristan and Isolt 375ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
D2161.4.10.2.p: A wound can be healed only by the person who inflicted it (or by a member of that person's family). Compare the idea that a disease is cured by the same agent that caused it.

D2161.4.10.2.1.p: A fairy who has been wounded by a human can be healed only if the fairy gets that human's blessing.

D2161.4.10.2.2.p: A snake draws the poison out of a snake bite by sucking on it, curing the wound caused by a snake.

D2161.4.10.3.p: A bite is cured by putting hair from the dog that bit the person onto the wound.

D2161.4.10.4.p: A father who has been weakened by grief over a lost son is magically restored to health as the son comes near home. In the note, he had lost his strength, sight and hearing when the son left.

D2161.4.10.5.p: Blindness is cured by killing the snake that caused it.

D2161.4.11.p: A sick person is cured by placing children on the roof, or in the oven, as a magic treatment.

D2161.4.12.p: A person is magically cured while asleep.

D2161.4.13.p: A person eats human hearts to cure insomnia, so that he or she can sleep.

D2161.4.14.p: A sick or injured person is magically cured by bathing.

D2161.4.14.1.p: A magic cure is achieved by bathing in milk.

D2161.4.14.1.1.p: Wounds caused by poisoned arrows are healed by a bath of milk.

D2161.4.14.2.p: A sick person is magically cured by bathing in holy water, such as in a sacred lake.

D2161.4.14.3.p: A person is cured by washing in morning dew.

D2161.4.15.p: A sick person is cured by lying in the shadow of a saint.

D2161.4.16.p: A sick person is cured magically just by being touched.

D2161.4.16.1.p: A healer cures the affected parts of the body by passing a hand over them.

D2161.4.17.p: A sick or injured person is magically cured by being licked.

D2161.4.18.p: A patient's lock of hair is put into a hole in a post or tree, and the hole is plugged with wood, to cure the patient.

D2161.4.19.p: A catch-all heading for magic cures of various other kinds that do not fit the more specific categories.

D2161.4.19.1.p: A barber starts to recover from an illness or injury once he reveals a raja's secret, which is treated as a magic healing.

D2161.5.p: A disease or injury is cured by magic performed by a particular person.

D2161.5.1.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 124ff., 449f. nn. 1—33 passim; *Toldo I 331; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman.
D2161.5.1.p: A disease or injury is cured by a holy man.

D2161.5.2.r: (Cf. V256.) *Ward Catalogue of Romances II 609 No. 23, 617 No. 38, 619 No. 22, 630 No. 23, 649 No. 47.
D2161.5.2.p: A disease or injury is cured by the Virgin Mary.

D2161.5.2.1.r: Ward II 648 No. 40 and passim; *Crane Miraculis 89 No. 17.
D2161.5.2.1.p: A cure takes place at a shrine dedicated to the Virgin Mary.

D2161.5.2.2.p: A cure is effected through a relic of the Virgin Mary.

D2161.5.2.3.r: Ward II 613 No. 32; *Crane Miraculis 95 No. 30; English: Wells 167 (Vernon Miracles).
D2161.5.2.3.p: A sick person is cured by drinking or being given milk that belongs to the Virgin Mary.

D2161.5.2.4.r: (Cf. D2161.3.) *Crane Miraculis 89 No. 18; Wells 167 (Vernon Miracles), 169 (The Clerk who would see the Virgin); Spanish Exempla: Keller.
D2161.5.2.4.p: Severed limbs are restored to the body by the Virgin Mary.

D2161.5.2.5.p: A spider bite is cured by the Virgin Mary.

D2161.5.2.6.p: Severe headaches are cured by the Virgin Mary.

D2161.5.3.p: A disease or injury is cured by a deity.

D2161.5.4.p: A disease or injury is cured by Moses.

D2161.5.5.r: (Cf. V232.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
D2161.5.5.p: A disease or injury is cured by an angel.

D2161.5.6.p: A sick person is cured by a surviving twin, after the other twin has died.

D2161.5.7.p: A disease is cured by the seventh son of a seventh daughter, who is believed to have healing powers.

D2161.6.p: Diseases are cured at a particular time rather than by a particular person.

D2161.6.1.p: All diseases are healed at the moment of Christ's birth.

D2161.6.2.p: Diseases are cured during the Messianic era, the future age of the Messiah.

D2161.6.3.p: Diseases are cured at the birth of a holy man.

D2162.p: A person uses magic to control or stop a disease.

D2162.1.p: A saint stops an epidemic by fasting.

D2162.2.p: A saint commands that an epidemic stop at a river or the sea, and the plague goes no further.

D2162.3.p: A place is made safe from plague by an angel, because its people pray and fast.

D2162.4.p: The people living on a mountain dedicated to an angel are spared from plague.

D2163.p: Magic is used to protect a person or army in battle.

D2163.1.p: Weapons that have been broken in battle are magically made whole again.

D2163.2.r: Icelandic: Boberg; Finnish: Kalevala rune 27; Maori: Dixon 61.
D2163.2.p: Magic brings extra fighters to the hero's side, either by multiplying his followers or by conjuring a whole new army.

D2163.2.1.p: Heaven sends help to fighters in battle.

D2163.3.p: The Virgin Mary catches an arrow aimed in battle, so it does not harm its target.

D2163.4.p: A magic mist is raised to shield fighters from the enemy in battle.

D2163.5.p: A saint's prayer brings victory in a battle.

D2163.5.1.p: At a saint's prayer, a great flock of birds comes and drops stones from their claws on the enemy, filling them with terror.

D2163.5.2.p: A saint changes a cruel king's heart so that he gives up violence and thinks peaceful thoughts.

D2163.5.2.1.p: A holy man reads a letter that stops an emperor from laying waste to a country.

D2163.6.p: Magical obstacles are created in front of an enemy to block their advance.

D2163.6.1.p: A saint makes a large forest grow up suddenly between two opposing armies.

D2163.6.2.p: A saint makes a wall of cakes rise up between two opposing armies.

D2163.7.p: An enemy army is tricked by an illusion created by a saint.

D2163.8.p: A saint's blessing gives victory to those who receive it.

D2163.9.p: A saint protects his followers from bullets by spreading a sheet over their heads.

D2165.r: (Cf. D1395.) English: Wells 43 (Arthour and Merlin); Irish: Plummer cxxxix, *Cross; Icelandic: Þorsteins saga Vikingssona 400, Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2165.p: A person escapes from danger by magic.

D2165.1.p: A character escapes from danger by flying through the air using magic.

D2165.2.p: A character escapes from drowning by magically drying up all the water around them.

D2165.3.p: Magic is used to stop or prevent others from chasing the character.

D2165.4.p: A character magically makes an opening in a house so they can get out and escape.

D2166.p: Magic keeps a person from being hurt when they fall.

D2167.r: (Cf. V52.14.) Tawney II 540; Saintyves De l’incorruption des corps saints (Bull. et. Mem. de la Soc. d’Anthrop. des Paris, 7th ser. IV [1923] 84—100).—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “cadavre”; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 311.
D2167.p: A dead body is magically kept from rotting or decaying.

D2167.1.p: Food is magically kept from spoiling or going bad.

D2167.2.p: A book is magically kept from decaying or falling apart.

D2167.3.p: Flowers are kept fresh and do not wilt through magic.

D2168.p: Magic is used to counteract or neutralize poison.

D2168.1.p: Poison is magically removed or separated from a drink.

D2171.r: (Cf. D1413.) *Type 593; Fb “holde” IV 219b; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 102; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2171.p: Objects are magically made to stick to people or things.

D2171.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 394, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 66 No. 9.
D2171.1.p: An object magically attaches itself to a person so it cannot be removed.

D2171.1.1.p: A seat or chair is magically made to stick to a person so they cannot get up.

D2171.1.2.p: A tankard or drinking cup is magically made to stick to a person's lips.

D2171.1.3.r: Irish myth: Cross (D2171.7); Jewish: *Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 325, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 237.
D2171.1.3.p: A person is magically made to stick fast to the floor or ground.

D2171.2.r: (Old Man of the Sea, Burr-Woman). *Basset 1001 Contes I 190f; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 126 No. 58; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 42 No. 30; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 330 n. 191e.
D2171.2.p: A person is magically made to stick to a monster such as a witch or ogre.

D2171.3.p: A person is magically made to stick to an animal.

D2171.3.1.p: A person is magically made to stick to a goose.

D2171.3.2.p: A person is magically made to stick to a swan.

D2171.3.3.p: A person is magically made to stick to a turtle.

D2171.3.4.p: Magic makes a hose, or piece of cloth, stick to an animal's body so it cannot be pulled off.

D2171.4.p: Objects are magically made to stick together so they cannot be separated.

D2171.4.1.p: A pitcher is magically stuck fast to the ground and cannot be lifted.

D2171.4.2.p: A cauldron is magically stuck to a wall and cannot be taken down.

D2171.4.3.p: A witch uses magic to make a towel stick to a wall.

D2171.5.p: Magic causes people to stick together so they cannot be pulled apart.

D2171.6.p: Clothing clings to a person's body by supernatural means and cannot be pulled off.

D2171.7.p: A man's feet are magically fixed to the pavement so he cannot walk until he makes a vow.

D2171.8.p: A witch uses magic to keep milk in an overturned pail so it does not spill.

D2172.p: Magic acts continue on their own, so that a person keeps doing something once started.

D2172.1.r: Type 593; Lang Eng. Fairy Tales 74; Lithuanian: Balys Historical.
D2172.1.p: A person is magically forced to keep repeating an action or words until someone releases them.

D2172.2.r: BP II 215, 438; *Hdwb. d. Märch. s.v. “Erste” nn. 112—149; Irish: Beal XXI 306; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 750A@1*.
D2172.2.p: A magic gift lets a person keep on all day with whatever task they begin, such as measuring linen or throwing water on a pig.

D2173.p: Someone's singing has magical power or effect.

D2174.r: Type 306; BP III 78; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XIX 309 n. 1; England, Wales, U.S.: *Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2174.p: Enchanted people are forced to dance by magic and keep dancing until released.

D2175.r: Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 299, 268, 111; Jewish: Neuman; Irish myth: Cross.
D2175.p: A curse is placed on someone by magical means.

D2175.1.r: (Cf. D926, D1766.2.1, D1792.2, V134.) Kittredge Witchcraft 34, 394 n. 113.
D2175.1.p: A curse is worked by means of a well.

D2175.2.p: A saint's bachall, or crozier staff, is used to lay a curse.

D2175.3.p: A magic satire or magic song is used as a curse against someone.

D2175.4.p: A saint's bell is used to lay a curse.

D2175.5.p: A curse is magically turned into a blessing.

D2176.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
D2176.p: Evil spirits are driven out by magical means.

D2176.0.1.p: A saint makes a place holy so that death cannot come there, or so that evil spirits are driven out of it by magic.

D2176.1.r: Irish: Plummer clxx, *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 66; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 310 No. 33.
D2176.1.p: Through magic, snakes are forbidden from entering or living in a place.

D2176.2.p: Through magic, lice are forbidden from entering or living in a place.

D2176.3.p: An evil spirit is driven out of a person or place by magic.

D2176.3.1.r: *S. Prato La Tradition III No. 2 (1889) (Tobit); Jewish: *bin Gorion Born Judas@2 II 360f.
D2176.3.1.p: An evil spirit is driven out by burning fish, the smoke being the means of expulsion.

D2176.3.1.1.p: An evil spirit is driven out by burning medicine, the smoke being the means of expulsion.

D2176.3.2.r: (Cf. V10ff.) Holy name, sign of cross, prayer, etc. Fb “Jesus” II 41; Irish: Beal XXI 325; Italian Novella: Rotunda; *Chauvin VIII 41 No. 8AB; India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer III 37; Korean: Zong in-Sob 60, 128.
D2176.3.2.p: An evil spirit is driven out through a religious ceremony.

D2176.3.3.p: An evil spirit is driven out by a saint.

D2176.3.3.0.1.p: Evil spirits are driven out when a saint dies.

D2176.3.3.1.p: Demons inhabiting stone images are driven out by a holy man or saint.

D2176.3.3.2.p: A saint makes a spring clean again by driving out a demon that inhabits it.

D2176.3.3.3.p: A saint throws an ink bottle at a devil who is bothering him.

D2176.3.3.4.p: A saint's breath alone is enough to drive the devil away.

D2176.3.4.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3368; Legends Nos. 702—710.
D2176.3.4.p: A devil is cast out of a person who is possessed.

D2176.4.p: A magic book is made to vanish by throwing it into a stream.

D2176.5.p: Cut hair is burned to keep witchcraft from being worked with it.

D2176.6.p: An invisible man is exorcised by flailing the air around him with a peach branch.

D2177.p: Someone is imprisoned or shut away by magic.

D2177.1.r: *Type 331; *Goebel Jüdische Motive im märchenhaften Erzählungsgut (Gleiwitz, 1932) 52ff.; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 311 No. 39, 314 No. 105, 320 No. 34; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Graham; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 439.
D2177.1.p: A demon is shut up inside a bottle by magic.

D2177.1.1.p: Demons are imprisoned by magic, in the manner of being enclosed in a bottle.

D2177.2.p: A demon is shut up inside a pomegranate by magic, trapped there so it cannot get out.

D2177.3.p: Evil spirits are locked inside stone by magic, so they are confined and cannot harm anyone.

D2177.4.p: A stone wall built by magic or as protection keeps evil spirits from entering a place.

D2178.p: Ordinary objects, animals, or people are brought into being by magic rather than by natural means.

D2178.1.p: A whole city is made appear through magic instead of being built by people.

D2178.2.p: Cattle are created out of nothing by magic.

D2178.3.p: Tents or pavilions are conjured into existence by magic.

D2178.4.p: Animals are created by magic rather than born.

D2178.4.1.r: N. A. Indian (Calif.): Gayton and Newman 82.

D2178.4.2.p: Harmful or poisonous creatures are produced by magic.

D2178.5.p: People are created by magic rather than born.

D2178.6.p: Gifts meant for ceremonial occasions are produced by magic.

D2178.7.p: Whatever a goldsmith intends to make appears by itself in the forge without his working it.

D2178.8.p: A tree is produced by magic.

D2178.9.p: A flower is produced by magic.

D2182.r: (Cf. D1052, D1652.3.) Irish: Plummer clxxxi, Cross.
D2182.p: A cow gives more milk after licking a saint's garment, which is a magical increase in milk.

D2182.1.p: A saint, rather than a garment, causes a cow's milk flow to increase.

D2182.2.p: A cow's milk flow is increased by singing or music.

D2183.p: Spinning is done by magic, with the thread made without ordinary spinning work. It is usually done by a supernatural helper.

D2184.p: People are magically made to keep hurting themselves: they try to drive an ox but drive themselves, or try to stab an animal but stab themselves.

D2184.1.p: People are magically forced to strike themselves with blows that were meant for someone else.

D2185.p: A magician carries a woman sealed in a glass coffin, and she can come out whenever he wills it.

D2185.1.p: A fairy or divine being keeps a mistress safe by housing her in a crystal bower.

D2186.p: A cat hidden in a woodpile stops an axe from cutting the wood, so the chopper cannot make progress.

D2188.r: (Cf. D1641.) Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 484; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 457, Rasmussen III 264, (Kodiak): Golder JAFL XVI 25, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 257.
D2188.p: Someone or something vanishes by magic.

D2188.1.p: A person has the magical power to disappear or reappear whenever they choose.

D2188.1.1.p: A garment vanishes or reappears when its owner gives the command.

D2188.2.r: Jewish: Neuman; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 48, 54, Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 3/1241).
D2188.2.p: A person disappears from sight by magic.

D2188.2.1.p: A man vanishes by magic, leaving only his ring behind.

D2188.3.p: A whole village vanishes by magic.

D2191.p: Roast ducks fly away by magic.

D2192.r: *Fb “kirke” II 125 a; Wells 42 (Arthour and Merlin); Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3602; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 465; Ellice Island: ibid. 270; Marquesas: ibid. 269; Tuamotu: ibid. 267; Tahiti: ibid. 266; Maori: ibid. 265; Africa (Duala): Lederbogen Fables 59.
D2192.p: Work done during the day is magically undone at night.

D2192.1.p: A supernatural force moves the foundation of a new church, or its building materials, to another site during the night.

D2193.p: Flowers fall onto a person's hands when they wash them.

D2194.p: Dung falls onto a person's hands when they wash them.

D2195.p: A withered, blighted garden is magically restored to beauty.

D2195.1.p: A flower bursts into bloom when touched.

D2196.p: A saint causes a fiery sword to stand between a hostile king and queen.

D2197.p: A person gains power to control or rule over animals through magic.

D2198.p: A person has magical control over spirits, specifically angels.

D2199.p: Other magical manifestations that do not fit the preceding categories.

D2199.1.p: A bottomless tub or vat holds water through the power of a saint.

D2199.2.r: Slaves forced to hew down yew tree with dull tools: hands bleed. (Cf. H1110, P170.) Irish myth: Cross.
D2199.2.p: Tools are sharpened through the power of a saint.
